title: CEE MORNING BRIEFING: Czech, Hungarian 1Q GDP Details Due
text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
0700/0900 Hungary April foreign trade data 
0700/0900 Hungary first quarter final GDP data 
0700/0900 Czech first quarter final GDP data 
0700/0900 Czech unemployment in May 
 

Final readings of first quarter gross domestic product data in the Czech Republic and Hungary are due Friday, along with Czech May jobless reading and Hungary's foreign trade balance in April.

In Prague, the revised GDP reading is expected to be little changed from the preliminary first-quarter reading, which came in worse-than-expected with contractions of 1% in both annual and quarterly terms.

Dalimil Vyskovsky, a fixed-income trader at Komercni Banka in Prague, said the sharp decline in the flash reading was puzzling and said the bond market will be closely watching Friday for any revisions.

The economic growth data is likely to play a larger-than-normal role in the Czech central bank's monetary policy decision later this month, Mr. Vyskovsky said.

Any upswing in Czech May unemployment, which is expected at 8.2% from April's 8.4%, will add to pressure for the central bank to cut interest rates on June 28, which would be the first change to monetary policy in more than two years, analysts said.

In Budapest, investors are eying Hungary's detailed gross domestic product data to capture which factor pulled Hungary's economy into recession in early 2012.

Preliminary GDP data showed a 0.7% contraction in unadjusted terms, mainly due to a plunge in construction in February and March, as well as on further declining consumption and investments, Takarekbank said.

title: News Highlights: Top Economic Stories Of The Day
text:
TOP STORIES 
 
US STOCKS EDGE LOWER AFTER RALLY, EURO-ZONE WORRIES 
 

U.S. stocks move lower as euro-zone liquidity concerns prompt investors to consolidate some of the sharp gains registered a day earlier. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is off more than 50 points.


 
US AUTO MAKERS SEE 2011 SALES GAINS INTENSIFYING IN 2012 
 

Auto makers cap off 2011 with strong a strong December and now expect the recovery in U.S. sales to intensify in 2012 as a stabilizing economy and ongoing job creation continue to encourage shoppers.


 
US NOVEMBER FACTORY ORDERS RISE 1.8% 
 

Factory orders increase for the first time in three months on greater demand for aircraft and other goods, the latest indication the manufacturing sector is slowly gaining momentum. Orders rise to $459.18 billion; economists were expecting an increase of 2.1%.

CURRENCY-TRADE CONTROVERSY SWELLS AROUND SNB PRESIDENT 
 

A controversy surrounding transactions made by the wife of Swiss National Bank President Philipp Hildebrand swells after media reports that he profited from a large dollar purchase around the time of the central bank intervention.


 
INVESTORS LOSING CONFIDENCE IN HUNGARY

Investors' confidence in the Hungarian government is evaporating, sharply raising pressure on policy makers here as they struggle to contain the spreading economic damage from the Continent's debt woes and stalling euro-zone growth.


 
OIL SLIPS AMID EU BAN OF IRANIAN OIL 
 

Although oil prices spiked in mid-morning trading to highest level in nearly eight months on reports that EU officials agreed in principal to an embargo on Iranian oil imports, they fall back on an apparent lack of concrete details.


 
BANKS PARK RECORD FUNDS WITH ECB 
 

European banks parked a record amount of funds at the European Central Bank's overnight deposit facility Tuesday while short-term emergency borrowing from the central bank remained elevated.


 
GREEK PM EXPECTS DEBT PLAN DEVELOPMENT IN 15 DAYS 
 

The Greek government appears to be nearing a deal with banks in negotiations on writing down their Greek bonds, a union leader says, citing Prime Minister Lucas Papademos.


 
MORTGAGE APPLICATION VOLUME FALLS 3.7% 
 

The number of mortgage applications filed in the U.S. falls 3.7%, the Mortgage Bankers Association says, even after adjusting for the seasonal effects of the Christmas and New Year's holidays.


 
ECB BALANCE SHEET GROWS SLIGHTLY, GOLD RESERVES INCREASE 
 

The Eurosystem's balance sheet grows slightly, topping a previous all-time high as the ECB continues buying government bonds on the secondary market and as the value of its gold reserves increases.


 
 
   ======== DOW JONES NEWSWIRES ANALYSIS AND COMMENTARY ======== 
 
Election 2012 
ROMNEY WINS IOWA CAUCUSES BY EIGHT VOTES 
 

Mitt Romney pulls out a razor-thin victory by just eight votes in the Iowa caucuses, edging out former Pennsylvania Sen. Rick Santorum with a dose of momentum going into a New Hampshire primary he is heavily favored to win.


 
Analysis 
PIMCO'S GROSS: BUY TREASURYS, AVOID EURO ZONE 
 

After getting burned by selling Treasury securities in the early part of 2011, bond investor Bill Gross is placing the asset class at the top of his shopping list for 2012.


 
The Wall Street Journal 
HUNGARY WILLING TO BE FLEXIBLE IN EU, IMF TALKS 
 

Hungarian economic officials stress their willingness to be flexible in negotiations with the EU and IMF over a precautionary credit line the country is seeking as insurance against market turmoil.


 
 
TRANSFER PAYMENTS WON'T RESCUE THE EURO ZONE 
 

The divide between the German and Spanish economies fuels the argument that a single currency needs a single fiscal policy, including fiscal transfers. But as the U.K. has demonstrated, fiscal transfers can actually prevent economic readjustment.

title: DJ UPDATE Hungary Won't Allow Outside Interference In Lawmaking -PM
text:
--Hungary PM determined to go ahead with central bank bill ratification

--PM Orban continues to reject foreign calls to change domestic policies

--Hungary central bank questions legitimacy of new bill prior to ratification 


 
   By Gergo Racz 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

(rewrites throughout, adds details, background, comments from central bank and analyst)

BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--Hungary won't allow outside forces to intervene in the country's policymaking, Prime Minister Viktor Orban said Friday.

"There is no person in the world who could tell elected representatives of the Hungarian people what laws they can or can't create," he said.

Orban reacted to criticism targeted at the government from abroad, including calls from European Commission President Jose Manual Barroso and United States Secretary of State Hilary Clinton to amend bills submitted to Parliament. Pieces of legislation revising the operation of the central bank proved a dealbreaker earlier this month when delegations from the International Monetary Fund and the European Union terminated negotiations early with the Hungarian government.

"If Hungary's parliament were to create a law that would be in breach of the country's obligations laid out in international treaties, than the aggrieved party may take steps, but only after ratification, not before," Orban said.

The bill allows the government to delegate new members to the central bank's rate-setting council while another, related bill allows merging the finance market regulator and the central bank. In this case, the current post of central bank governor would be demoted to deputy.

"The laws about to be passed go against legal security and allow the government to realize its short-term political goals through influencing the central bank's decision-making," the National Bank of Hungary said Friday, prior to parliament's closing vote in the matter. "It hurts the economic interests and stability of the country," the central bank added.

Despite the apparently rigid negotiating positions, PM Orban said Hungary's delegation will conduct talks with the IMF sometime at the start of January.He added, however, there is no fixed schedule yet, and stressed that an agreement with the Fund isn't a necessity.

"Hungary has an excellent budget for 2012 and the country can stand on its own without the IMF," he said on public radio.

However, markets would apparently be more confident regarding Hungary's outlooks if it had the IMF in its corner, as reflected by an unsuccessful government bond auction on Thursday and the continued weakness of the national currency.

"Investors are rapidly losing confidence in Hungarian policymaking and are beginning to shun the country's bond market. The standoff is escalating by the day and unless negotiations with the IMF resume and a workable agreement is reached fairly quickly, Hungary will have a full-blown debt crisis on its hands," said Nicholas Spiro, managing director at Spiro Sovereign Strategy.

Parliament is set to ratify the central bank bill later Friday.

title: CEE MARKETS 3- Hungary  debt yields jump, Poland talks of new  interventions
text:
(Adds Polish cbanker, updates levels)

* FX markets fragile, Polish cbank warns may intervene again

* Czech, Polish debt stable after selloff; Hungary down

* Spreading euro zone crisis weighs

By Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST/WARSAW, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Hungarian bond yields soared to 2-1/2 year highs on Thursday and Poland's central bank warned of further interventions as emerging European currencies remained under pressure on concerns the euro zone debt crisis is threatening even Germany.

The yield at an auction of 12-month Hungarian Treasury bills rose to its highest since September 2009, at 7.07 percent, although the debt agency managed to sell all 30 billion forints of paper on offer.

On secondary bond markets, Hungarian yields rose up to 20 basis points to highs last seen in the summer of 2009 following a similar rise in the previous session, when a German bond auction described as "disastrous" hit central European debt.

"We saw an almost continuous rise in yields," one Budapest-based fixed income trader said. "I hope this will not continue next week as that would already be real big trouble... European markets are in a panic which has spilled over into our market."

"I hope things will improve next week when U.S. investors return from their holidays," he added.

Hungary has been the central European market most vulnerable to investors cutting back their exposure to risk, and the forint, which lost more than 1 percent on Wednesday, stayed near record lows, slipping 0.3 percent to 310.99 per euro.

In Poland, where the zloty hovered close to multi-month lows, the central bank's deputy governor in charge of interventions told Reuters it was likely to intervene again after stepping into the market on Wednesday for the fourth time in less than three months.

The Polish currency was nearly flat at 4.49, a nudge below the key psychological level of 4.50 and year-lows just beyond.

"The comments by the deputy governor temporarily supported the zloty," one Warsaw trader said. "I think a further retreat of the zloty towards this year's minimum of 4.42-4.53 to the euro is still possible."

"The question is whether the central bank will defend these levels," he added.

Both the zloty and forint have lost more than 10 percent in 2011, mostly in the latter half of the year.

The Czech crown slipped 0.4 percent against the euro to 25.76, and a Prague-based dealer said it could be heading towards 26.300-500 if it stays weaker than 25.300-400, an area that has offered support.

A Hungarian dealer said the forint had no room to firm in the short term as concerns remain that Standard & Poor's may cut Hungary's debt rating to junk even though the government has applied to the IMF for a precautionary credit line.

"The forint has almost lost all its gains posted since the news about the (planned) IMF deal, but can firm in the longer term on the news flow about the talks and the deal," another dealer said.

Romania's leu, which has seen support from prospects of intervention there, firmed 0.1 percent.

Fears that the worsening euro zone sovereign debt crisis will cripple economic activity, leaving central Europe's export-reliant economies vulnerable, have hammered the region's markets.

The Czech 10-year yield was quoted up 6 bps at 4.489 pct

after a jump of 40 basis points on Wednesday in a usually stable market.

The region's main equity indices were little changed.

text:
16 Nov 2011 08:04 EDT *DJ  Hungary MPC Divided On Future Monetary Policy Conditions

16 Nov 2011 08:07 EDT *DJ  Some Hungary MPC Members: Monetary Policy Can't Offset Euro Zone Crisis

16 Nov 2011 08:09 EDT *DJ  Hungary MPC Members Agree In Wait-and-See Monetary Policy Stance

16 Nov 2011 08:13 EDT *DJ  Hungary MPC To Assess CPI Outlook After Econ Policy Details Public

16 Nov 2011 08:14 EDT *DJ  Hungary MPC To Watch Spillover Effects Of Weak HUF, Taxes In CPI

16 Nov 2011 09:17 EDT DJ  Hungary MPC Voted 6 To 1 In Favor Of Oct Rate Hold Decision

BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--Six of the seven members of the Hungarian central bank's Monetary Policy Council voted in favor of leaving the key rate on hold in October, citing increasing economic headwinds.

The central bank kept interest rates unchanged at 6%, in line with analysts' expectations. One panel member, Julia Kiraly, wanted to raise rates by 0.25 percentage point, the meeting's minutes showed Wednesday. Kiraly is the central bank's deputy governor and is in charge of financial stability.

The majority of MPC members agreed to adopt a wait-and-see stance, though they were divided over future monetary policy conditions.

The bank's lowered its economic outlook because of the country's exposure to the euro-zone debt crisis as well as a government measure aimed at paying off household foreign-currency mortgages at the expense of the banking sector. And the MPC agreed to monitor possible inflationary effects stemming from the weak forint and tax changes.

It also said it would reassess its mid-term inflation outlooks, once the government finalizes its economic policy, when the bank comes to compile the December inflation forecast.

The minutes of the meeting come a day after the MPC verbally intervened to protect the forint against further depreciation against the euro, after it hit historic lows around HUF317 Monday. The MPC said that if investor risk aversion persists, this could warrant gradual monetary tightening.

The minutes are released two weeks after the rate-setting meeting and therefore don't reflect changes that have occurred in the intervening period, such as prospective downgrades to Hungary's sovereign rating and forint weakening.

title: CORRECTED-UPDATE 1-Hungary cbank steps in to prop up weak forint
text:
(Corrects size of t-bill sale in paragraph 6)

* C.bank says forint falls not in line with fundamentals

* Says "gradual tightening" of monetary conditions may be needed

* Verbal intervention gives scant immediate support to forint

* Gradual rate hikes may come if forint fails to recover -analyst

By Gergely Szakacs and Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank intervened verbally on Tuesday to prop up the weak forint, which fell to record lows to the euro late on Monday, and said a gradual tightening of monetary conditions may be needed if risk aversion in European markets is lasting.

Hungarian five-year credit default swaps traded above 600 basis points, close to their March 2009 record high after Standard & Poor's and Fitch both put Hungary on negative credit watch on Friday, increasing the chances of a cut to "junk" rating status.

The central bank will hold its next regular policy meeting on Nov. 29 after keeping rates unchanged at 6 percent last month .

"If the increase in risk aversion affecting European financial markets proves lasting, a gradual tightening of monetary conditions may be necessary," the rate-setting Monetary Council said after a regular non-rate meeting on Tuesday.

Hungary's forint, the weakest performer in central Europe this year, sank to a fresh record low at 317.9 to the euro on Monday after the two rating agencies warned Budapest it may lose its investment-grade status.

Poor demand also forced the debt agency to scrap a six-week bill auction on Monday. It sold 40 billion forints of three-month bills on Tuesday.

The market falls prompted the Monetary Council to issue a statement saying the forint's recent decline was unjustified.

"In the Monetary Council's assessment, the recent depreciation of the forint is not in line with the fundamentals of the Hungarian economy," the panel said, adding that forint falls also worsened the inflation outlook.

The Monetary Council said the government's commitment to bringing the budget deficit below 3 percent of economic output next year and efforts to reduce debt meant a spillover of fears about debt sustainability from the euro zone was misplaced.

The comments provided scant relief for the forint, which traded at 314.75 versus the euro at 1337 GMT, a shade stronger than 314.90 before the bank's verbal intervention.

One analyst said gradual rate rises could be on the cards if the forint fails to recover meaningfully.

"I agree that the market falls are caused by speculation rather than fundamental factors. A one-off big interest rate hike is not the solution," said analyst Zsolt Kondrat at MKB Bank.

"They must say what they just said and if the exchange rate does not rebound, they must start to lift interest rates gradually, saying that these exchange rate levels already carry inflation risks," he said.

Central bank Governor Andras Simor had warned after the October policy meeting, when the forint traded at stronger levels of around 300 to the euro, that the weak currency could push meeting the bank's inflation target further into 2013.

Inflation will rise next year on the back of government tax hikes to rein in Hungary's budget deficit and keep European Union development funds flowing in at a time when the economy heads into a period of near stagnation.

(Reporting by Gergely Szakacs, Sandor Peto; Editing by Catherine Evans)

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Zloty eases on caution ahead of EU summit
text:
(Adds FX regaining some ground, bonds)

* Zloty erases previous session gains on euro angst

* FX still off recent lows, interventions unlikely for now

* Hungary cuts longer-term debt sales

* Stocks also drop as expectations fade for euro summit

By Sam Cage

BUCHAREST, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty erased the previous day's gains on Thursday as traders took defensive positions ahead of a key European summit, while fears of a ratings cut hit a Hungarian debt tender.

European policymakers are struggling to reach agreement on how to address the debt crisis, and the euro and stocks fell on French President Nicolas Sarkozy's comments that Paris and Berlin were at odds before the weekend meeting.

Events in the euro zone are dominating central European markets because of their close trade and banking ties, and currencies regained some ground as the euro rallied on clearer signs of how European officials plan to tackle the debt crisis.

"Failure to come up with a plan brought back risk-off," a Bucharest dealer said.

Polish and Romanian central banks have intervened to support their currencies, helping to move them away from 27-month and 15-month lows respectively. Dealers said while currencies were still not far from intervention territory, action seemed unlikely unless losses accelerated.

"We believe that CEE currencies will be unable to develop any significant appreciation beyond short spells of central banks' interventions," BNP analysts said in a note.

Hungary sold less 5- and 15-year debt than it had originally planned to as fears of a ratings downgrade and euro zone turmoil reduced demand for longer paper. It sold 20 billion forints ($93 million) worth of 3-year bonds as planned.

"Some in the market are afraid of a ratings downgrade, some fear an emergency rate hike, and there are those who think the fears are unjustified," a Budapest-based dealer said.

Concerns Hungary may lose its investment-grade rating also pressured the forint in early trade before it recouped early losses to trade 0.3 percent higher on the day.

ROMANIA YIELDS RISING

The zloty shed 0.3 percent, erasing all of the previous day's gains, and the Czech crown -- the region's best-performing currency this year -- was flat at 24.877 per euro.

A Prague dealer said the crown will again test its September low of 25.015 and if it breaks that, it could fall towards previous lows hit in January.

The region's stock markets were all in the red, also led by Poland, where the Warsaw bourse shed more than 1 percent.

Romania's leu was a touch higher at 4.33 per euro and markets will eye a tender for 600 million lei in three-year bonds, expecting the finance ministry will have to stump up higher yields than 7.49 percent when it last sold similar paper, or sell less than planned.

"I think there will more or less be a 4.33-4.35 interval today, on hold for the weekend events, provided the Germans and French don't express more disagreements in the meantime," said a second Bucharest dealer.

title: WRAPUP 1-Inflation eases in CEE, rate paths may diverge
text:
* Hungary CPI at 3.6 pct y/y flat from Aug, cbank's hands tied

* Romania's inflation drops sharply, cbank may have room to cut

* Czech inflation falls 0.2 pct m/m in Sept

By Krisztina Than

BUDAPEST, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Lower food prices helped keep a lid on inflation in Romania and Hungary last month and inflation pressures remain muted across the EU's eastern wing, but some central banks may still have to hold or even raise interest rates to counter growing market risks.

In Romania inflation slowed sharply to 3.5 percent in September -- the lowest annual rate since the 1989 fall of communism -- entering the central bank's target band and indicating it might have room to start cutting rates soon.

Romania's borrowing costs are the highest in central Europe at 6.25 percent but its central bank has had to intervene to support the currency in the past month and analysts say that has stayed its hand on cutting rates.

In neighbouring Hungary, inflation at 3.6 percent in September also came in slightly below analysts' forecast for 3.7 percent, but the central bank there has no room for manoeuvre at all due to a recent surge in the country's risk premia and the forint's weakening .

"We see a relatively significant easing of inflation going forward and countries like Poland and the Czech Republic clearly have room for monetary easing," said Lars Christensen at Danske Bank.

"The story is slightly different in Romania and Hungary."

In the Czech Republic consumer prices fell 0.2 percent in September on a month-on-month basis, putting the annual inflation rate at 1.8 percent, which analysts said would allow the bank to keep rates stable at a record low of 0.75 percent or even consider a cut down the line.

The minutes of the last rate meeting there showed on Sept. 30 that the bulk of the Czech central bank's board believed risks to the bank's inflation outlook were slightly on the downside.

September inflation data for Poland, by far the region's largest economy, is due on Oct. 13.

Minutes from the Polish central bank's latest meeting showed that the balance of risks for inflation had become more even but did not point to a need for rate cuts. The bank has also intervened to support the zloty.

HUNGARY HANDS TIED

With the global growth slowing and markets worried that the euro zone's debt problems will spread into a full scale banking crisis to rival that in 2008, policymakers across the region's developing markets would like to do more to bolster growth.

Hungary's government will hike its top value added tax rate to 27 percent from 25 percent from January, raising inflation. But inflation pressures from the demand side continue to be extremely low, and the economy is slowing -- with some analysts now forecasting zero growth next year or even a recession.

The central bank, whose base interest rates stand at 6 percent , has said once the effects of the tax hikes wear off inflation could ease back to its 3 percent target by the beginning of 2013.

But the forint is trading close to 300 versus the euro

and Hungary's 5-year credit default swaps are at around 524 basis points, near their highest levels since March 2009.

"In the next 3 months inflation is expected to remain between 3.5-4.0 percent and then jumping above 4 percent in January due to the VAT-hike," said Zsolt Kondrat at MKB Bank.

"The central bank cannot reduce interest rates primarily due to financial stability risks, and secondly because it will wait to see potential second-round effects from next year's tax hikes on inflationary expectations," added Gergely Suppan at Takarekbank.

Analysts at Nordea Bank said the Romanian central bank would face a similar dilemma as Romanian households also have a large amount of foreign exchange loans and the country has a high proportion of Greek and Italian banks operating there.

"Although the improved inflation outlook and subdued domestic demand would argue for a rate cut, it is difficult with the markets' risk perception of Romania," it said.

(Reporting by Krisztina Than)

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary would like higher forint but can manage-minister
text:
* First government comment on weak currency after recent falls

* Would be more satisfied with 268 EUR/HUF level -state sec

* Says 2012 budget reserves can handle exchange rate changes

* Even more important is less exchange rate volatility -state sec

BUDAPEST, Oct 5 (Reuters) - (Adds further details, comments)

BUDAPEST, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Hungary's government would be happier with forint levels of around 268 to the euro, but the 2012 draft budget has large reserves to handle exchange rate risks from a weaker forint, a top Economy Ministry official said on Wednesday.

The remarks by State Secretary Zoltan Csefalvay are the first comments to made by the Hungarian government on the weakness of the currency after recent heavy falls which sent the forint to 29-month lows at 300 to the euro this week.

Poland's central bank and government stepped in to prop up the ailing zloty in the past two weeks and dealers say the Romanian central bank may also be supporting the leu through market interventions.

The National Bank of Hungary launched weekly euro tenders for commercial banks this week to supply lenders with liquidity and temper exchange rate volatility as foreign currency debtors repay their loans at discounted rates under a government scheme.

"It would not be good if the forint was stuck at levels around 300 (to the euro)," state secretary Zoltan Csefalvay was quoted as saying by private broadcaster Gazdasagi Radio on its website when asked about the impact of the euro's strength on the 2012 budget, which was built on an assumed 268 euro/forint exchange rate.

"But next year's budget contains a fund worth 300 billion forints ($1.33 billion), or slightly above 1 percent of GDP, which for the most part can be devoted to this end, if the exchange rate changes," he said.

The forint sank to fresh 29-month lows of 300.65 against the euro on Wednesday, pressured by growing fears over the euro zone debt crisis and a controversial Hungarian foreign currency loans repayment scheme, which compounds global risks.

The government submitted the 2012 budget draft to parliament on Friday, targeting a deficit of 2.5 percent of GDP.

Asked whether the government had an exchange rate target, Csefalvay said:

"We have already touched upon what next year's budget reckons with (268 to the euro), we would be satisfied with that," he said.

"But what is even more important, an even bigger issue is the strong volatility, which foreign currency debtors can feel day by day, but obviously the Hungarian economy also feels this strong volatility."

He said a weaker currency could help make Hungarian exports more competitive, adding however, that genuine competitiveness could be achieved only if goods and services in Hungary can be marketed even at a stronger forint exchange rate.

title: DJ FOCUS: Hungary Could Be Next To Join New  Currency  War
text:
-- Forint at critical level that could spur central bank action

-- Hungary central bank seen intervening on spot market first, with rate hikes seen as last resort 


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--With the forint sinking fast, Hungary could become the latest emerging-market country in Eastern Europe and Asia to try to prop up its currency in the wake of mounting concerns over Greece and the global economy.

The Hungarian forint sunk Tuesday to its weakest level against the euro since April 21, 2009, having broken the critically important HUF300 level, which market participants anticipate could trigger action from the central bank. Hungary is more sensitive than most to currency weakness, because it makes it much more expensive for Hungarian households to pay back the foreign-currency mortgages that the majority of them hold.

With the forint under increased pressure, it might be "time to pull the emergency brake," said Nordea economist Elisabeth Andreew, adding that the possibility of emergency interest rate raises is also increasing.

Back in October 2008, the National Bank of Hungary raised interest rates by 300 basis points to support the forint. While such aggressive monetary action can't be ruled out this time around, Hungary's central bank is likely to try other options first, market participants said.

"The economy is very weak and the National Bank of Hungary may resort to foreign-exchange intervention first," said Murat Toprak, a foreign-exchange strategist at HSBC in London.

The Hungarian forint--like other emerging-market currencies in Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe and Africa--have been under heavy selling pressure in recent weeks as a toxic combination of fears about the global economy and escalating euro-zone debt worries lead investors to fold their bets in emerging markets on a colossal scale.

As a result, the currency wars of the recent past have metamorphosed, with authorities in emerging markets this time embarking on currency-strengthening programs, having previously battled to hold their currencies down to keep a competitive edge.

Authorities in Poland, Romania and Russia have all stepped in to defend their currencies in recent days, while Turkey's central bank holds daily foreign-exchange auctions to stem lira weakness.

Countries across Asia have also been very active in defending their currencies, with South Korean, Malaysian, Indonesian, and Philippine central banks all suspected of intervening Tuesday.

Sudden currency weakness can pose inflationary problems by lifting the cost of imported goods, and for those countries burdened with large amounts of debt denominated in foreign currencies, it is particularly harmful because these debts become much more expensive to pay back.

-By Clare Connaghan, Dow Jones Newswires; +44 (0) 20 7842 9496; clare.connaghan@dowjones.com

title: CEE MARKETS 4-C.banks seen  intervening  to support zloty, leu
text:
(Adds analyst comment, Hungary c.bank, updates prices)

* Zloty, leu trim losses after cbank interventions

* Hungary c.bank to launch euro sale tenders, seen helping forint

* Bond yields rise, stock markets down across board

By Sam Cage and Luiza Ilie

BUCHAREST, Sept 30 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty and Romanian leu trimmed losses against the euro on Friday after dealers said both countries' central banks intervened on the spot market to support the ailing currencies.

Markets are testing the thresholds at which emerging Europe's central banks will step in to bolster currencies hit by fears about a spiralling debt crisis in the euro zone -- the region's main trading partner -- and a slowing global economy.

The zloty and Hungary's forint have lost 12 percent and 10 percent respectively since July 1.

"I think central bank interventions will be more common if market panic continues," said Nordea's Elisabeth Andreew. "The CEE region has in general much better fundamentals than the euro zone and it is not fundamentally correct that these currencies should be sold off that sharply."

"The way it will happen will probably vary though. Poland has a lot of EU funds while I think Hungary for example would do an emergency hike in interest rates if pressure rises too much on the forint."

A week ago, Poland's central bank and state-owned bank BGK launched their first coordinated intervention in the foreign exchange and fixed income markets to support the zloty and government bonds, which were pummelled by the global flight from risk.

On Friday, two Warsaw dealers said the central bank intervened on the spot market selling euros. By 1415 GMT the zloty was quoted at 4.423 against the euro, down 0.2 percent on the day, having earlier traded as much as 0.6 percent lower.

Though the Romanian leu has so far been one of the region's most stable currencies, its losses have accelerated and it fell to a 15-month low of 4.3725 per euro before dealers cited central bank buying through local banks which pushed it to 4.353, down 0.1 percent.

Romania's central bank held rates unchanged at 6.25 percent on Thursday, later suggesting slowing inflation might give room to ease borrowing costs. Finnish handset manufacturer Nokia's decision to stop production in Romania also damaged sentiment.

"I'm thinking this is about as far as the leu goes," a Bucharest dealer said. "A new ceiling for the leu could be 4.38."

BOND YIELDS RISE, STOCKS FALL

Elsewhere in the region, Hungary's central bank said it will launch euro sale tenders on Oct. 3 for commercial banks to help them finance the repayment of households' foreign currency mortgage loans under a government scheme.

Analysts said the sales would help prevent a plunge in the forint. The bank earlier said that it would use its foreign currency reserves to prevent forint volatility as the repayments are seen boosting demand for foreign currencies.

By 1400 GMT the forint was down 0.6 percent on the day, while bond yields rose.

"You can see that shorter yields are going up now and long yields are static," one Budapest fixed income trader said.

"(Interest rate) swaps keep going up, they are at 6.75 pct for 2 years and 7.00 pct for five years. The markets have clearly priced in two 25 basis point central bank rate increases for the next one year."

The risk-averse mood weakened the Czech crown -- the region's best performer in 2011, down only 1.7 percent since July. It was 0.6 percent down on the day, though it largely shrugged off minutes from the central bank's last meeting.

The majority of the bank's board believes that risks to the bank's inflation outlook are slightly on the downside, the minutes showed, adding to signs rates may yet head lower.

The crown is now weaker than the Czech central bank's outlook for 24.2 for the third quarter, but analysts said it would tolerate a much deeper fall.

Stocks fell across the region with Prague's shedding 1.1 percent and leading losses.

title: CEE MONEY-Hungary cbank would love to cut but hands tied
text:
* Economy needs lower rates, market risks do not allow easing

* Hasty cut could dent bank's credibility if euro crisis deepens

* Bank must "warm up" markets before any cuts -analysts

By Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Much has been made of the split between Hungary's government and central bank, but the truth is that the bank would now love to cut interest rates to help the economy.

The Swiss National Bank's move to weaken the franc on Tuesday may just conceivably have given them some room to do so - but not much and not in a rush.

Inflation is not an especially large problem in an economy that is almost static, but the heavy exposure of central Europe's most volatile emerging market to Swiss franc loans means the bank cannot afford to risk a forint sell-off.

Growth-smothering interest rates of six percent -- among the highest in Europe -- seem to be the cost the country now has to pay.

That arithmetic may have changed a little with the SNB's shock move, which knocked 8 percent off the franc's value to the euro, though most analysts say it could still take years before Hungary will have room to ease the cost of borrowing by a full percentage point or more.

"The currency risk (for households' mortgage loans) has decreased with that (SNB move)," said Zsolt Kondrat, analyst at MKB Bank in Budapest.

"I see no rate cut in September, a small cut may come late this year, but the bank must (first) prepare the ground for it."

DOMESTIC SPLIT

When Prime Minister Viktor Orban appointed four new members to the seven-seat Monetary Council in March, investors expected the body's new majority to loosen policy this year to support the ruling Fidesz party's pro-growth agenda.

Growth stalled in the second quarter, prompting ministers to renew calls for lower rates as they pledged new tax hikes to help plug the resulting hole in budget revenues.

The central bank itself is now likely to cut its growth and inflation forecasts in a quarterly report this month, something policymakers could normally follow with hints of lower rates.

But the euro zone debt crisis has spooked investors and those seeking safe havens for their cash, driving the franc higher versus the euro and closely-linked currencies like the forint .

Even with the Swiss central bank intervening, Hungary has little choice but to keep the premium for holding the forint high.

"The bank has no good options. It must choose the lesser evil," said Zsolt Papp, fund manager at UBP SA, which manages $1 billion in emerging fixed income assets.

"Cutting rates would be better but that's hard in an uncertain market environment."

Any falls for the forint mean higher monthly repayments for the tens of thousands of Hungarians who hold franc-denominated loans, and would further hurt already low domestic demand.

They would also raise pressure on Hungarian banks, which face rising non-performing loan rates. According to the financial market watchdog PSZAF, loans overdue more than 90 days accounted for 13.9 percent of all loans to households at the end of March.

The forint -- which traded at around 150 against the franc three years ago -- was bid around 228 on Tuesday, off from record lows at 271.62 four weeks ago, but much weaker than April's 200.

Hungary already leads its neighbours in terms of vulnerability, which the market expresses in the cost of insuring its debt. Five-year credit default swaps are now bid at 432 basis points, the highest level since April 2009 and much higher than Poland or the Czech Republic.

That means that a hasty rate cut now could later force the bank into a new hiking cycle if there is a serious spillover of euro zone market risks into Hungarian assets.

"WARMING UP" MARKETS

The weak growth figures and the proximity of the next inflation report have raised expectations of a cut in the past few weeks with interest rate swaps (IRS) now pricing in 25-50 basis points in cuts for the next couple of months.

That is still likely contingent on a calming of the euro zone crisis and/or the U.S. Federal Reserve launching new monetary stimulus. The bank may also wait to see whether the government's 2012 budget poses additional inflation pressures vis-à-vis Orban's pledged tax hikes.

Barring extraordinary comments by policymakers, the next opportunity to prime market expectations for a shift to easing would be after the bank's next rate meeting on Sept. 20.

Many analysts argue, however, that a small cut may simply have no impact. Hendrik Scheerlink, CEO of KBC unit K&H Bank, says it is rather rising non-performing franc loans, an extraordinary banking tax, and the economic slowdown in European export markets that are crushing new credit.

"These factors are more relevant at the moment than the interest rates set by the central bank," he said.

($1 = 192.151 Hungarian Forints)

(Reporting by Sandor Peto; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: UPDATE:  Hungary Central Bank  Declines Comment On Euro  Intervention  Talk
text:
-- Hungary's central bank declines to comment on intervention on forex market

-- Traders say Hungary central bank intervention is a rumor

-- Raiffeisen said central bank intervened to keep EUR/HUF below 275

(Adds traders' comments in paragraphs five to 11, background in paragraphs six and 12.)


 
   By Veronika Gulyas and Gergo Racz 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--The Hungarian central bank Wednesday declined to comment on talk that it would buy the Hungarian forint against the euro to keep the exchange rate below HUF275, while traders said there had been no intervention.

The central bank's response came after a Raiffeisen Bank analyst said the bank was attempting to keep the euro-forint cross at bay amid a nervous market environment and a surging Swiss franc, which strengthened to an all-time high of HUF273 early Wednesday.

"The central bank doesn't comment on foreign currency market moves and it never commented in the past either," the bank told Dow Jones Newswires.

Other market analysts dismissed the idea that the central bank would intervene at current, relatively benign euro-forint levels. At 1150 GMT, the euro was trading at HUF272.97 from around HUF278 Tuesday.

"The central bank could intervene, but it has no reason [to do so] looking at the current forint-Swiss franc exchange rate," said Equilor analyst Szilard Buro.

Traders contacted by Dow Jones Newswires were unanimous that there had been no intervention.

A Commerzbank trader said such a move was highly unlikely since events are driven by global developments and not happenings in Hungary's economy.

Despite disappointing industrial output and foreign trade data suggesting that the country's growth is likely to slow earlier than predicted, the government is sticking to its strict fiscal policy and has pledged to keep the budget deficit below 3% of gross domestic product in 2011 and future years.

The forint hasn't yet reached a level against the euro which would warrant intervention, said Peter Attard Montalto of Nomura International in a note to analysts.

"Above HUF280 we'll see the central bank start to verbally intervene, around HUF290 they'll be in the market more aggressively first on the quiet and then making a public splash, around HUF300 they will raise rates," Attard Montalto said.

A trader also said the forint is holding stable against the euro, therefore intervention is unlikely. Furthermore, it would actually make the forint vulnerable as it would make the currency appear weak and a possible subject for speculation.

Hungary's central bank reportedly last intervened in 2009 when the euro reached an all-time high of HUF317.10 against the forint March 6. At the time, traders and analysts had mixed opinions as to whether there was indeed any intervention and the bank never acknowledged that had done so.

title: CEE MARKETS 4- Currencies  recover on weak dollar, forint leads way
text:
* Dollar weak as U.S. debt deadlock in focus

* Hungary cbank holds interest rates on hold at 6 percent

* Poland cbank says does not rule out FX intervention

(Adds Hungary central bank governor, updates prices)

By Jason Hovet and Luiza Ilie

PRAGUE/BUCHAREST, July 26 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint trimmed gains against the euro on Tuesday after the central bank left interest rates flat, while other emerging European currencies gave up their earlier gains.

Hungary's central bank kept rates on hold at 6 percent

on Tuesday for the sixth month running to curb price growth to the bank's 3 percent inflation target.

By 1340 GMT, the forint had edged down to 267.96 to the euro, still up 0.3 percent on the day.

The Czech crown edged up 0.3 percent to near its 55-day moving average of 24.357 per euro. Poland's zloty

lost some steam and was hovering around the psychologically key 4.0 per euro level, up 0.1 percent on the day.

Stock markets in central Europe were weaker on the day across the region, led by Prague , which was off 1.3 percent.

Deadlock in talks in Washington over raising the debt limit to avoid a first-ever U.S. default has pushed investors away from the dollar, which fell broadly on Tuesday and lifted appetite for emerging European assets.

While markets last week gave a cautious welcome to a euro zone deal giving heavily indebted Greece easier borrowing terms and fresh aid, implementation risks remain and dealers said central Europe can still feel pressure from this.

But for now, focus has shifted to the one-week deadline to lift the U.S. debt ceiling.

"Until the U.S. debt ceiling issue is clarified it will be very hard to see sustainable risk appetite in the region or elsewhere," one Bucharest-based trader said.

HAWKISH HUNGARIAN CENTRAL BANK

Hungary's central bank Governor Andras Simor said that in order to meet a 3 percent inflation target for 2012 "keeping interest rates at the current level may be necessary." He added that the euro zone debt crisis was the key risk for interest rates.

Investors were listening to Simor for hints on whether the bank will maintain a neutral monetary policy stance or signal an easing bias.

"The tone was a bit more hawkish than at the previous meeting, probably because the central bank can't afford a dovish tone at this point, which may put the HUF at risk of weakening," said Nordea's Elisabeth Andreew.

Some analysts were expecting a rate cut before the end of this year, with earlier expectations that the bank may raise rates -- after a 75 basis point tightening cycle that ended in January -- having evaporated.

Elsewhere in the region, monetary tightening remains on the cards later this year in Poland and the Czech Republic. In Romania, where the key rate at 6.25 percent is higher than in Hungary, recent central bank comments have triggered some modest expectations of a rate cut.

Romania's leu added 0.6 percent to the euro, recovering after the government's failure to sell a minority stake in oil and gas giant Petrom last week tumbled shares in the unit.

Romania aims to push on with the sale of stakes in energy firms, the economy ministry said on Tuesday, despite the failed attempt to list Petrom shares on the bourse.

Meanwhile, Poland's central bank Governor Marek Belka said he did not rule out interventions on the foreign exchange market, but only to limit volatility, not to defend a specific level of the zloty.

"It is no surprise that he says they are ready to do FX intervention; he is the fourth or fifth management board guy to say this in the last 2.5 weeks," said Nomura's Peter Montalto.

"We think that means they'll strongly defend 4.1 and try and keep EURPLN around or below 4.0."

text:
* Bucharest dealers says c.bank likely intervened

* Forint down half percent, sticks at lows after rates held

* Zloty dips on dovish cbank comments

(Adds suspected leu intervention, more details)

By Jason Hovet and Dagmara Leszkowicz

PRAGUE/WARSAW, Feb 21 (Reuters) - The Romanian leu rose to a five-month high on Monday in what dealers said looked to be central bank intervention, while Hungary's forint held near session lows after the central bank left interest rates on hold.

Intervention by the central bank, which never comments on market activities, was the first this year and helped the leu to buck a weakening trend in emerging Europe caused by falling risk appetite.

The region's currencies came under pressure from falling stock markets, a drop in the euro, spreading anti-government protests in Libya and the Middle East, and ongoing concern over euro zone peripheral Portugal's high budget deficit.

To counter this, Bucharest dealers said the central bank looked like it stepped in the market indirectly through banks.

"We suspect the central bank indirectly sold euros through two local banks," said one dealer with a foreign bank in Bucharest.

Another dealer said volumes were twice those of a normal trading day.

"It seems they are afraid of inflationary pressures ... looming food inflation is a reality," the dealer said.

Dealers have said the bank intervened last year to keep the currency in a tight band of around 4.1-4.3 per euro and the government frequently baulks at selling debt at high yields.

By 1551 GMT, the leu <EURRON=> added 0.3 percent to bid at 4.227 to the euro. The Czech crown <EURCZK=> was flat, while the forint <EURHUF=> fell 0.5 percent from Friday, but remained steady after the rate decision.

HUNGARY RATES

The Hungary central bank, as expected, kept interest rates unchanged at 6 percent in its last meeting before four new members join the Monetary Council, after a string of three-quarter point rate rises. [ID:nLDE71K1J6]

The bank said these rate increases would help inflation fall to its target as the direct impacts of cost-side shocks fade.

"That is no surprise to us -- or anybody else for that matter," said Lars Christensen, economist at Danske Bank. "With growth still lacklustre and inflation set to moderate there is really no reason for hiking rates at the moment."

Analysts have said board changes could lead to looser policy as appointments will be made by the centre-right Fidesz government which has openly criticised the bank for raising interest rates.

Bond yields remained unchanged after the decision. Forward rate markets still priced an additional hike in three months, but dealers have said this would likely be priced out if government reform plans, due to be unveiled next month, meet market expectations.

Hungary and Poland are the only two central European countries to have started raising interest rates, with the Czechs likely on hold in the coming months. Romania is expected to try to loosen policy to boost its economy.

The Polish zloty <EURPLN=> lost 0.6 percent to the euro on weakening market sentiment and comments of Poland's central bank governor that pointed to a more moderate pace of its own monetary policy tightening.

Markets have raised bets the Monetary Policy Council will follow a January rate rise from a record low with another hike at the council's March meeting. [ID:nLDE71K0GL]

Central bank head Marek Belka said on Monday it should act with moderation if there is no wage pressure and the January rise would not be followed by a "cascade" of further hikes.

"We're less confident now with a possible rate hike in March (after Belka's comments), but we also bear in mind that his comments are more ambiguous recently," said Rafal Benecki, senior economist at ING bank in Warsaw.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks hit 2-wk high, forint recovers
text:
* Emerging stocks rise nearly 1 pct, spreads tighten

* Emerging currencies rally, forint up after c.bank comments

* Lithuania sounding investors out for Eurobond

By Carolyn Cohn

LONDON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks hit two-week highs and several emerging market currencies rose 1 percent on Thursday, boosted by strong U.S. and Chinese data, and the Hungarian forint recovered after central bank comments. Wall Street posted its best day in eight weeks on Wednesday following higher than anticipated U.S. and Chinese purchasing managers' data.

That renewed investor appetite for riskier assets following a 2 percent loss in emerging stocks last month.

"Investors were positioned for more bearish news and changed tack when Chinese PMI and U.S. ISM figures came out better than expected," said Kasper Bartholdy, head of sovereign strategy and co-head of economics at Credit Suisse.

"The numbers are no cause for jubilation but they are not as disastrous as some people thought." The MSCI emerging equities index <.MSCIEF> rose half a percent to two-week highs and the Thomson Reuters emerging equity index <.TRXFLDEEPU> gained 0.2 percent.

Emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> tightened 2 basis points to 286 bps after narrowing sharply on Wednesday.

Investors expect fresh emerging debt supply over the next few months.

Lithuania has sounded investors out over a seven-year euro-denominated bond, that would raise at least 500 million euros, during a roadshow this week, fund managers said. [ID:nLDE6801QJ]

FORINT RECOVERS

Most emerging European currencies rose ahead of the European Central Bank meeting later on Thursday.

The forint climbed nearly 1 percent against the euro <EURHUF=> and held above record lows against the Swiss franc <CHFHUF=> after central bank spokesman Andras Simon told Reuters on Wednesday that the strong Swiss franc posed risks to Hungary's economy, comments which Unicredit described in a client note as "quasi-verbal intervention".

Simon also said Hungary may need the support of an IMF and European Union safety net if global investor sentiment turns negative.

Hungary's talks with the IMF and EU about a review of its current financing deal collapsed in July. This deal, which it took to fend off a currency crisis in October 2008, runs out next month.

Reflecting the continued nervousness, Hungary sold 15 billion forints less than its original offer in a 12-month T-bill auction on Thursday.

"We recommend using the current rally to rebuild long EURHUF or PLNHUF positions," said BNP Paribas analysts in a client note.

The Polish zloty <EURPLN=> and South African rand <ZAR=> also rose at least 1 percent, but the Romanian leu hit fresh five-week lows <EURRON=> as investors fret about political will to implement austerity measures.

(Additional reporting by Sujata Rao and Sebastian Tong; editing by Patrick Graham)

title: 3rd UPDATE: IMF Breakdown Whacks Hungarian Forint, Debt Markets
text:
(Adds background on currency intervention risks, analyst comment, and updates levels.)


 
   By Katie Martin 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--The Hungarian currency and debt markets have slipped sharply after the country failed over the weekend to reach a funding deal with the International Monetary Fund and the European Union.

The euro shot almost 3% higher against the forint at the start of European trading hours to reach just over HUF290, taking the forint back down to its lowest levels in over a year, as Hungary failed to deliver the austerity measures required for it to receive the remainder of its existing EUR20 billion standby credit line.

The cost of insuring Hungarian government bonds against default rocketed higher, with five-year credit default swaps quoted 43 basis points wider at 365 basis points. That means it now costs $365,000 a year to insure $10 million of such debt against a failure to repay.

The forint and CDS levels are now back at the weak points they reached last month, when Hungarian officials warned that the country may be heading towards a Greek-style debt crisis.

The country's key stock market index also declined 4% at the open Monday, with shares in Hungary's biggest bank, OTP, shedding some 8.5% of their value. Prices later sprang back a little, indicating that early panic-style trading was moderating.

The currency markets offered a sign that the blow to Hungarian assets was sending ripples throughout the region, as the Polish zloty and Czech koruna also weakened, though declines for these currencies were much more modest.

Further losses are seen ahead for Hungarian markets, with analysts predicting that the breakdown in IMF/EU talks will hit investors' confidence in Hungary for the long term.

"The market has drawn a clear conclusion: without additional IMF and EU support, Hungary will be hard pressed not to default," said analysts at Commerzbank in Frankfurt in a note to clients. "In this situation, the central bank will doubtless not cut its key rates today, even though the government wants it to."

Further sustained currency weakness could trigger intervention by Hungary's central bank to try to inject some stability, several analysts suggested. A weak forint brings headaches for Hungary by ramping up repayment costs on outstanding foreign currency-denominated loans.

"There is the very clear risk that further weakness in the forint will prompt central bank intervention," said Neil Mellor, a currencies analyst at The Bank of New York Mellon in London. "The market is clearly fully aware of this probability, with the upward spike in the euro today coming to a dramatic halt just south of the June high of HUF290.30."

The breakdown in talks between Hungary and the multilateral bodies has implications beyond Eastern Europe, as it offers a clear sign that international aid is tied to strict conditions.

"Hungary said it was already in the fifth year of austerity measures and it was not possible to tighten the screws any further. That's critical because it's exactly the problem the euro zone faces; austerity measures... are not one-offs, they are multiyear projects," said Simon Penn, an analyst at UBS in London.

"The IMF and EU have not fudged a solution. Hungary won't play ball so the funding line is suspended," he added. "Remember, Greece's fiscal position is far worse than Hungary's."

At 1105 GMT, the forint was still wedged at its lower levels, with the euro trading at HUF288.02. The Polish zloty and Czech koruna had bounced back somewhat, with the euro trading at CZK25.462 from a peak of CZK25.517 and at PLN4.1168 from a peak of PLN4.1548.

title: CEE MARKETS 5- Hungary  assets dive, cbank threatens  intervention
text:
* Forint, stx, bonds hammered; cbank threatens intervention

* Other CEE assets gain back some morning losses

* Romania sells less T-bills than planned as expected

(Updates with Hungary cbank's intervention comments)

By Marius Zaharia

BUCHAREST, July 19 (Reuters) - Hungarian assets plunged on Monday following the suspension of IMF/EU funding talks over the weekend as markets shrugged off central bank warnings it could intervene or raise interest rates.

The central bank left borrowing costs unchanged at 5.25 percent on Monday but said it would resume transfers of EU funds in the currency market to fight forint volatility, adding that higher interest rates may also be needed. [ID:nBUS002150]

The forint <EURHUF=> was untouched by the comments, and traded 3.1 percent down on the day at 290.46 per euro at 1341 GMT, even weaker than levels seen before them.

"While these comments and actions might limit speculative pressure against the forint, it doesn't provide much relief against the external funding pressures ... or shore up the government's credibility during the current impasse with the IMF," said Koon Chow of Barclays Capital.

Hungarian bond yields rose 20-30 basis points across the curve on Monday, while Budapest stocks <.BUX> fell 2.3 percent. Yields on Hungary's Eurobond maturing June 2011 <HU013159386=RRPS> shot up to their highest since June 2009, while five-year CDS spreads rose 58 basis points, according to Markit.

Regional currencies tracked the forint's decline in overnight trade, but later recovered.

Dealers say central European assets are decoupling from Hungary's problems as Poland and the Czech Republic have sounder fundamentals than Hungary and Romania, while the latter has overcome significant hurdles to keep its own IMF deal on-track.

The Polish zloty <EURPLN=> was down 0.8 percent, trading at 4.14 per euro, significantly off overnight lows of 4.1540. The Romanian leu <EURRON=> was a touch lower, while the Czech crown <EURCZK=>, seen as a regional safe haven, was 0.4 percent higher.

In Romania, the finance ministry stuck to its self-imposed cut-off yield of 7 percent -- half of 2009 peaks -- and sold roughly a fifth of what it planned at a one-year T-bill auction. [ID:nBUC003742]

Such a result was widely expected, since the ministry has either rejected all bids or cut tenders across maturities since early May, when investors began demanding higher yields in response to worries over the success of the government's austerity drive.

As an alternative way to seek funding, the ministry said on Monday it plans to sell one-year euro-denominated paper on local markets worth 400 million euros. [ID:nBUC003743]

In Poland, June industrial output data came in significantly better than expected, highlighting the country's economic outperformance in the region. [ID:nWSF009293]

MARKET PRESSURE

Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy said he still expected to reach an agreement with the International Monetary Fund and the European Union as talks may resume in September, but markets face uncertainty until then. [ID:nLDE66I0VT]

Some economists said the forint may test levels close to 300 per euro before the government decides to resume negotiations, but many say it is to early to assess how far the sell-off would go, especially with the central bank on its toes.

Hungary faces no immediate pressure on state finances and its 2010 position looks safe, but economists agree it needs to keep the IMF deal on track as an external anchor of credibility.

An immediate risk from the suspension of IMF/EU talks was depreciation against the Swiss franc, also seen in the zloty.

While currency depreciation against the euro may have helped Hungary to tame a recession and Poland to avoid one, weakening against the Swiss franc has caused big pain for these countries as a large chunk of household loans taken when their economies were booming are denominated in francs.

On Monday, the forint fell more than 3 percent against the Swiss franc <CHFHUF=> from Friday to 211.6, while the zloty was quoted 0.6 percent weaker at 3.0362 <CHFPLN=>.

Cheuvreux noted the forint was now around 38 percent weaker than levels at which many mortgage loans were taken.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Assets fall on risk aversion, Romania hit hard
text:
* Fx, stocks, bonds fall on renewed euro zone worries

* Romanian stocks nosedive 11 pct on strike concerns

* Polish cbank keeps rates on hold

(Recasts with new prices, comments)

By Dagmara Leszkowicz and Sandor Peto

WARSAW/BUDAPEST, May 25 (Reuters) - Central European assets fell on Tuesday as risk aversion grew globally and markets in the neighbouring euro zone got an additional hit from fears that the debt crisis in its southern peripheries was widening.

Romania's stock index <.BETI> was worst hit, plunging 11 percent due to concern about looming strikes against drastic budget cuts agreed with the IMF. [ID:nLDE64O13K]

Central Europe's reference currency, the euro <EUR=>, touched a four-year trough against the dollar after Spain's weekend takeover of a small savings bank and political tension on the Korean peninsula added to global risk aversion. [ID:nN25121933]

The region's main equity indices, excluding Romania, fell 2.4-5.2 percent to about three-month lows.

Elsewhere, Bulgarian credit default swaps rose 25 basis points to 280 as the country said its budget deficit could be 4.8 percent of gross domestic product in 2010, far above initial estimates. [ID:nLDE64O0KP]

While the strong presence of Greek banks make Romania and Bulgaria more vulnerable to the euro zone crisis than other emerging economies in the European Union, deficit and debt levels in central Europe are healthier than in many euro zone countries.

However, the region is heavily reliant on exports to western Europe, and its assets are vulnerable to risk aversion.

Currency losses were led by the region's most liquid unit, the zloty <EURPLN=>, which fell 1.7 percent against the euro by 1502 GMT. Hungary's forint <EURHUF=> shed 0.9 percent, while the Czech crown <EURCZK=> was down 0.4 percent and Romania's leu <EURRON=> dipped 0.2 percent.

Analysts said nervousness over Romania's political situation was better reflected in stocks as the leu may be protected by the central bank if it weakens markedly.

Serbia's dinar <EURRSD=> hit record lows and it was bid at 102.51, slightly off lows at 103.37. Serbia's central bank has sold 856.5 million euros this year to support the currency, including its latest 20 million euro sale on Monday.[ID:nLDE64O0QN]

POLAND HOLDS RATES

Hungarian government bond yield spreads over corresponding Bund yields rose 19-26 basis points, Polish yields rose 13-18 basis points, while Czech yields rose 10-14 basis points. Bond prices at the long end of the curve suffered mostly.

Poland's central bank kept its key interest rate <PLINTR=ECI> on hold at a record low 3.5 percent. It said inflation was likely to ease in coming months. [ID:nLDE64N11C]

The bank's statement had little comment on the zloty's retreat after strong gains earlier this year, although the minutes of the bank's April meeting showed that rate setters paid significant attention to the zloty.

Rate setter Jan Wijniecki said the weakening zloty was beneficial to the economy. [ID:nLDE64N11C]

Some Budapest-based dealers said central banks in the region might intervene in the market if the current turmoil continues. Hungary's central bank never comments on market intervention, and dealers said the bank was unlikely to cut rates further at a meeting on Monday.

Current forint levels against the euro and the Swiss franc are already painful to Hungarian households who hold a large amount of foreign currency loans.

"Even without central bank intervention, market players have become very cautious (in the region)," one currency dealer said. "There have been big swings in both directions and many people have burnt themselves."

"If there are even bigger falls in developed equity markets, let's say about 10 percent, the forint may try to settle in weaker territories at 285-290 (from around 280)," the dealer said.

title: =DJ UPDATE: Hungary MPC: Further Rate Cuts Hinge On Risk Assessment
text:
(Adds comment from central bank governor.)

By Margit Feher and Veronika Gulyas

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--Interest rates, rather than direct intervention in the forint market, will remain the Hungarian central bank's main policy tool and further rate cuts will continue to hinge on investors' risk perception of the country, National Bank of Hungary Governor Andras Simor said Monday.

Following direct currency market intervention in Poland and in light of the recent, relative strength of the forint, expectations have been growing that the Hungarian central bank will also use direct intervention.

"The central bank's main policy tool is its rate policy, but we don't exclude direct intervention from our policy tools," Simor said.

The Hungarian central bank has no exchange rate target, Simor reiterated. However, "there are such exchange rate levels which are detrimental to the economy and pose a risk to the country's financial stability," Simor said when asked to reveal conditions under which the central bank may directly intervene in the forint market.

Simor also said there could be sharp or sudden volatile forint movements which the corporate sector couldn't accommodate, which could also serve as a reason for direct intervention.

Simor was speaking at a press conference after the bank's monetary policy council decided in a vote with a decisive majority to cut the policy rate by 0.25 percentage point rather than by 0.50 percentage point, the other option it discussed.

"Inflation and the real economy outlook would justify further rate cuts, which could take place if Hungary's risk perception (among investors) makes that possible," the MPC said in a statement.

The MPC Monday cut the policy rate for the tenth month in a row, to another record low of 5.25% from 5.50%.

"There's reason that would justify tighter monetary conditions. The economy has only been recovering slowly and the inflation outlook also shows that inflation will dip below the target--those would justify not a tightening but a loosening of the conditions," Simor added.

The MPC maintained that inflation will slow this year close to the central bank's 3% inflation target and dip below that level next year, Simor added.

He noted, however, that worries persist on financial markets over Greece's debt situation.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Forint holds post-election gains after cbank
text:
* Forint holds post-election gains after cbank cut

 * Stocks throw support behind other FX

 * Greece, intervention worries weigh

 (Updates Hungary cbank, prices)

 By Dagmara Leszkowicz and Jason Hovet

 WARSAW/PRAGUE, April 26 (Reuters) - A landslide Hungarian election victory for the centre-right Fidesz party gave a lift to the country's forint and bonds on Monday, as rising stock markets added support to other central European currencies.

 The forint touched its highest level in eight sessions after the Sunday run-off vote that gave Fidesz a clear two-thirds majority in parliament, and was unshaken later on Monday after the central bank cut interest rates to a new record low of 5.25 percent as expected. [ID:nLDE63P1FR]

 "What happens next is a question of monetary policy as well as politics," Raiffeisen Bank analyst Zoltan Torok. 

 "I do not believe this was the last rate cut. There will be at least one more. We think it will come in the third quarter, but the outlook is very uncertain on that horizon."

 The forint <EURHUF=> added 0.1 percent over Friday's close, bid at 263.1 to the euro by 1412 GMT. Bond yields held around multi-year lows hit this month.

 Analysts expected a post-election bounce for Hungarian assets after Fidesz won the majority needed to launch vital reforms to get the economy back in gear after the country was near financial collapse two years ago. 

 But they said the grace period could be short and the new government's relationship with the central bank would be tense.

title: ANALYSIS-Forint gains could hurt economy, cbank may step in
text:
* Forint seen extending gains after April 25 election

* New Fidesz govt, c.bank likely to oppose more forint gains

* Strong forint would hurt exports, engine of recovery

By Marton Dunai and Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST, April 21 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint is expected to rise further after Sunday's election, which could prompt the incoming pro-growth Fidesz government and the central bank to try to stem currency gains to help the economy.

An expected two-thirds majority for Fidesz, enough to launch deep reforms in the recession-hit economy, has beefed up market optimism, and the forint <EURHUF=> has outperformed its regional peers since the first round of voting on April 11, which Fidesz won by a landslide.

Since then the forint has firmed 1 percent to 263.70 versus the euro by 0630 GMT on Wednesday. The zloty <EURPLN=> of Poland, the only European economy to avoid recession, was flat while the Czech crown shed 0.3 percent in the same period.

Analysts say problems in the euro zone will not erode gains as investors have begun to differentiate between emerging Europe and Greece and the forint could rise further to levels which could hurt exports, the engine of recovery.

"At the current level it's not obvious a strong forint is in anyone's interest," Morgan Stanley analyst Pasquale Diana said.

"First, you don't need it from an inflationary standpoint," he said. "Second ... this economy is frankly humming on one cylinder (exports). This is not a time you need EUR/HUF heading south, especially if it is not warranted by fundamentals."

The forint's recent gains are inconsistent with levels seen in the previous 9 months, when it hardly deviated from the 270 per euro level. The currency is also stronger than seen in the most recent Reuters forecasts. <FXEURHUF>

Before Fidesz's big victory in the first election round, most analysts predicted the forint would stay around 270 per euro in the next six months at least.

Now most of them see it rising further in the short term.

"In my view the forint will ... firm to between 250 and 260 in the short term," Concorde Securities analyst Janos Samu said. "Regional currencies will again see appreciation pressure."

Hungary's external financing capability, after deep budget cuts last year, is among the best in the region, also seen as a positive for the forint.

Hungarian bonds are also seen extending their strong rally that pushed yields to all-time lows. [ID:nLDE62U1OZ]

Credit default swap spreads have hit their lowest since before Hungary resorted to an IMF and EU bailout in 2008.

CENTRAL BANK TAKES NOTE

Hungary's central bank has also noted the forint's strength. Vice Governor Ferenc Karvalits told Reuters last week there was no need for tighter monetary conditions. [ID:nLDE63F0XW]

Karvalits said the Hungarian bank "generally refrains" from using intervention but "does not categorically exclude" the use of this tool if needed.

He also said further cautious rate cuts from the current record low of 5.5 percent <NBHI> were on the cards.

Emboldened, markets may price deeper rate cuts than the bank is willing to deliver -- even after rate setters shifted toward a more dovish stance in March. [ID:nLDE63D1LR]

"We think that there is scope for front-end rates to overshoot on the downside, especially if the forint remains strong," Morgan Stanley's Diana wrote in a recent note.

The NBH is fairly tolerant towards a strong forint, analysts said, but persistent pressure on the currency could force rate cuts and possibly even direct intervention around 255 forints to the euro.

"The NBH can't fine-tune the exchange rate through interest rate cuts, so I'm inclined to think there will be intervention as well," MKB Bank analyst Zsolt Kondrat said.

Poland and Romania have already intervened to cool markets.

"(Hungary) is the exception, not the rule, as we have not deployed intervention yet," Kondrat added.

Fidesz, whose top priority is economic growth, is likely to favour lower rates as well. That would boost corporate lending and weaken the forint to benefit exports, the sole driver of economic growth amid sluggish domestic consumption.

"For the economy, (EUR/HUF) 270 would be good," Samu said. "I think Fidesz will want an even weaker exchange rate."

An exceedingly strong forint may prompt the new Fidesz government to try to talk down the currency, said Balint Hada, an analyst at Quaestor Financial Consulting in Budapest.

But a positive scenario for Hungarian markets, including the forint, hinges on a healthy global background.

Analysts said risks could re-emerge in the second half of 2010. Liquidity in global markets may tighten and the new government may loosen the fiscal grip to restart growth.

"The current (global) optimism is fragile," Hada said. "My fear is that something might come, perhaps as early as this quarter, a bad economic figure which would shatter optimism. It would be much harder to navigate the (Hungarian) economy then."

A significant forint weakening towards 300 versus the euro would unnerve the central bank and put an end to monetary easing as it could threaten financial stability. According to a recent central bank study, it could also hurt the economy by forcing banks to tighten credit. (Editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: ANALYSIS-C.Europe to fight  FX  gains with  intervention , low rates
text:
* Further FX gains to reduce chances for economic recovery

* Central banks talk down currencies to staunch firming

* Markets may turn more dovish on interest rates

* http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/310/EZ_CEEFX0310.gif 

(Adds graph of currencies)

By Marius Zaharia

BUCHAREST, March 10 (Reuters) - The rebound in the EU's emerging currencies may hurt economic recovery this year and policymakers look set to fend off investors by keeping interest rates low and threatening market intervention.

Although the currencies of Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Romania are still well below pre-crisis highs, weak demand for the region's exports in the euro zone has officials worrying that excessive strength could hurt growth.

Drawn by a solid economic outlook, investors propelled the zloty and the crown to 15-month and four-month peaks this week, while the forint and leu have been helped by their official interest rates of 5.75 and 7 percent.

The zloty surge, a 23 percent gain in 13 months, has prompted two ministers to talk down the currency this month and central bankers there have cast doubt on the timing of rate hikes that would raise the zloty's allure. [ID:nLDE6281MH]

For a graph of currency moves in the region, click on: http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/310/EZ_CEEFX0310.gif ("http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/310/EZ_CEEFX0310.gif")

Romania's central bank governor also signalled last week he was concerned the leu could firm too far, spreading fear among dealers that the bank could intervene between 4 and 4.1 lei per euro, virtually freezing the currency. [ID:nLDE62313Q]

"We are at a stage where they are afraid that their currencies are going too strong," said Gyula Toth, EMEA economist and strategist at UniCredit in Vienna.

"You have a situation when there is a constant inflow of currency into the country, and from this perspective they will have to fight quite heavily (against FX firming.)"

UNDESIRED FIRMING

Analysts think Poland and Czech Republic will hike rates twice in the second half of the year, and markets expect Romania to cut by one percentage point in 2010 and Hungary by 25-75 basis points, depending on developments after an April election.

But according to a Reuters poll <CEEFXPOLL01>, all of the currencies are expected to appreciate this year.

Even turmoil tied to debt-stricken Greece is seen helping, as it has pushed some investors away from troubled euro zone periphery states into more solid-looking economies further east.

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Waldemar Pawlak said a zloty level of around 4.0 per euro was desirable, a statement bringing to mind the government's forays into the foreign exchange market last year when it tried to keep the zloty from weakening by converting European Union development funds.

The Czech central bank discussed intervention against crown firming last year and analysts said they could do so again if the unit approached 25 per euro. [ID:nL58899]

"In Romania there was already a hint the central bank might intervene. In the Czech Republic... we saw verbal interventions last year and those might come back, and in Hungary it is already possible to see verbal intervention," said Elisabeth Gruie, FX strategist at BNP Paribas in London.

She believes markets are pricing in excessively high levels for rates and sees no hikes in the region this year, a thought echoed by others.

"Strong currencies in the end will tend to delay rate hikes," said Timothy Ash, an analyst with RBS in London.

INVESTMENT FLOWS

Raising rates would attract more flows into straight FX plays. Otherwise, if investors are not going to get more gains from currencies, they may switch more focus to debt and equities trades.

BNP Paribas sees more flows into regional debt than FX instruments in the short term, and Barclays is especially upbeat on Romanian bonds, as rates have more room to fall there and the country is pursuing budget cuts backed by the International Monetary Fund.

Low currency volatility would also redirect flows to other emerging markets such as Asia or Latin America, which are more tolerant to FX strength.

If growth does stay strong, governments may also have more political room to carry out further fiscal reforms, although elections this year across the region may prove a bigger barrier to any such tightening of public purse strings.

Locking in a competitive advantage against euro zone countries and shoring up growth will also benefit incumbent administrations.

"If you're looking for a soft patch and not a double dip recession, FX strength already starts to become an issue," said BNP Paribas's Gruie. (Editing by Michael Winfrey and Patrick Graham)
