title: Calming Words From Italy Could Bring Only Temporary Relief: DZ -- Market Talk
text:
1016 ET - The extent of the market movement in Italian government bonds witnessed over the past few days "reveals that the escalation in the political situation caught many investors on the wrong foot," says DZ Bank analyst Daniel Lenz. Should soothing words come through from the incoming premier or from the president, a noticeable counter-movement in yields could even be forthcoming, Lenz says. This would, however, "by no means put an end to the risk emanating from [Italian government bonds] BTPs," he says, adding that when the new government begins to implement its plans, at least in part, a second phase of reassessment will be likely to kick in, driving up risk premiums to levels even higher than at present. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0934 ET - With a 14.6% yield, the Turkish 10-year government bond offers big returns to investors, especially to those who do carry trades--selling low-yielding currencies and buying high-yielding ones. But a carry trade generates fewer gains if prices of those currencies move in the wrong direction. "The Turkish lira screens very well on a carry to risk ratio, but that carry means little when spot forex can move so much day after day," says RBC. The lira has hit another record low Tuesday, sending USD/TRY to 4.6640 and EUR/TRY to 5.4948. USD/TRY last trades up 1.6% at 4.6474 and EUR/TRY up 1.5% at 5.4746. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

0935 ET - US government bonds wobbled around the flatline ahead of a series of Treasury auctions for short-term notes. The yield on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury note recently traded at 3.062%, compared with 3.065% Monday. Yields, which fall as bond prices rise, slipped overnight as Italian government bonds recovered some of their losses. On tap later Tuesday: auctions for the 4- and 52-week bill, as well as the 2-year note. Signs of weak demand could stoke selling pressure, although some analysts anticipate a relatively quiet trading session ahead of Wednesday's FOMC minutes. (akane.otani@wsj.com; @akaneotani)

0806 ET - Brazil's central bank says it is likely to keep interest rates steady at 6.5%, a historic low. The message came in minutes to last week's meeting, when the Selic rate was held after 12 consecutive cuts. But it's unclear how markets will react to the communication. Pundits were led to believe the bank would cut last week and many criticized the bank for surprising them. Instability comes from a weakening currency, which could fuel import prices and inflation. The bank said it is monitoring the FX impact on prices and will react accordingly. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

0752 ET - Most emerging market currencies were up against the dollar earlier on Tuesday, including the Turkish lira, but the fall in TRY has resumed again, with USD/TRY up 1% at 4.6234, after reaching a new all-time low of 4.6251. "The vulnerable EM currencies with material idiosyncratic issues continue to underperform," ING says. USD/IDR is also up, albeit by less--0.1% at 14,120. And USD/BRL rises as well, by 0.1% to 3.6778. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

0746 ET - The National Bank of Hungary is only likely to verbally intervene in the fall of the Hungarian forint, says ING, adding it doesn't "expect no actual NBH response" to the fact that EUR/HUF has risen to 317 from 310 in a month. The three-month Budapest interbank offered rate, or Bubor, has also shot up to 0.1% from 0.02% just a few weeks ago and the 10-year Hungarian forint interest rate swap has risen to 255 basis points on Tuesday, the highest level in a year. "The central bank is likely to remain in wait-and-see mode" at the interest rate decision due 1200 GMT, ING says. A lack of NBH response may push EUR/HUF toward the 319 level again, ING adds. EUR/HUF is last down 0.2% at 317.42. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

0734 ET - The three-month Budapest interbank offered rate, or Bubor, has shot up to 0.10% from 0.02% a few weeks ago, and the 10-year Hungarian forint interest rate swap has risen to 255 basis points, the highest level in a year, says Societe Generale . This raises questions over whether the National Bank of Hungary will "double down on its dovish rhetoric and unconventional means to keep both front and long-end yields suppressed," SocGen says. The central bank, which signaled before that it wants to anchor long-term funding costs and keep the yield curve flat, announces its rate decision at 1200 GMT. EUR/HUF falls 0.2% to 317.36. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

0720 ET - The final steps toward a new antiestablishment Italian government presents challenges for the country's economic and sovereign outlook, and may impede progress on the European reform agenda, according to Scope Ratings. The Italian economy holds structural weaknesses tied to its low growth, high public-deficit of 132% of gross domestic product, alongside institutional bottlenecks, and "the composition and inexperience of this probable new government cast doubt on the country's future commitment and ability to resolves such challenges," say analysts Dennis Shen and Giacomo Barisone. The implementation of even some of the suggested measures, probable inaction on other areas of needed reform, and extended political uncertainty cloud the path ahead for Italy's 'A-/Stable' sovereign rating, Scope Ratings' analysts say. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0654 ET - The difficult outlook for gold remains even as falls in the dollar have halted the descent of the metal's price, says spread-betting company IG. "Gold's decline has stalled, which has given precious metal miners a breathing space, but overall the difficult outlook for the commodity remains," says IG's Chris Beauchamp. "It's not clear whether the recent weakness in the dollar marks a top in the rally of the past few months, but with the market still broadly short USD, it's easy to imagine the greenback perking up in due course, even if tomorrow's Fed minutes are not overly hawkish. Ahead of the open, we expect the Dow to start at 25,056, up 43 points from Monday's close." (philip.waller@wsj.com)

0652 ET - Italian government bonds pare some of Monday's losses but rising five-year credit default swap prices indicate that investors remain concerned over the new government's fiscal plans. "Investors appear concerned over motivations as much as plans," say Brown Brothers Harriman analysts. While a modification of the fiscal plans may appease President Sergio Mattarella , "it may require more to ease investor concerns, where a Greek-like crisis is feared, and worse given the size of Italy's economy and market," BBH analysts say. The 10-year Italian BTP yield is trading 6.2 basis points lower at 2.318% at 1044 GMT, according to Tradeweb . The five-year Italian CDS is indicated at 140.85 bps, up from 124.11 bps at the end of last week, according to FactSet. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

0618 ET - For now, EUR/USD is trading sideways from 1.1750, last up 0.3% at 1.1824 as the spread between 10-year Italian and German government bonds is narrowing, but if the BTP-Bund spread were to widen to 213 basis points, "then EUR/USD could cascade down to 1.15," according to Societe Generale . "For now though, the rot in the single currency seems to have been stopped." Whether "a tactical bounce follows may boil down to the eurozone flash" PMIs and the Federal Open Market Committee minutes on Wednesday, SocGen says. According to a WSJ poll, manufacturing PMI likely has stayed flat at 56 and services PMI likely has fallen to 54.5 in May. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

0537 ET - Eight years ago today, on May 22, 2010, the programmer Laszlo Hanyecz bought two pizzas using 10,000 bitcoin. This is widely recognized as the first real-world transaction using bitcoin. If those pizzas were bought now, with bitcoin trading at $8,268, they would cost $82.7 million--a rather pricey lunch. Commemorating that day puts into perspective how much the cryptocurrency has gained in value since then, and highlights potential issues surrounding its purchasing power in the future. Many critics say, however, that bitcoin could never be a currency because its value fluctuates too much. (olga.cotaga@wsj.com; @OlgaCotaga)

title: *S&PGR Affirms Hungary At 'BBB-/A-3'; Outlook Positive
text:
16 Feb 2018 16:05 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Affirms Hungary At 'BBB-/A-3'; Outlook Positive


 
 
The following is a press release from Standard & Poor's : 
 
Ratings: 
Foreign and Local Currency: BBB-/Positive/A-3 
 
For further details see ratings list. 
 
OVERVIEW 
 
     -- Hungary is entering another year of strong, cyclical economic recovery, 
with real GDP growth projected at 3.5% in 2018. 
     -- Its current account has started to erode, but the external profile 
remains strong, and while bank lending remains slow, we see structural 
improvements in the banking system. 
     -- We are affirming our 'BBB-/A-3' sovereign credit ratings on Hungary. 
     -- The outlook remains positive. 
 
RATING ACTION 
 
On Feb. 16, 2018, S&P Global Ratings affirmed its 'BBB-/A-3' long- and 
short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on Hungary. The 
outlook remains positive. 
 
We have withdrawn our 'BBB-' ratings on the National Bank of Hungary  (Magyar 
Nemzeti Bank ; MNB or central bank) at the bank's request. 
 
OUTLOOK 
 
The positive outlook primarily reflects the possibility that Hungary's 
strengthening economic metrics might support ongoing improvements in the 
banking sector, thereby reinforcing the monetary transmission channel. 
 
We could raise the ratings in the next 12-18 months if recent improvements in 
the financial sector enhanced the authorities' ability to influence domestic 
monetary conditions. This would be signalled, for example, by a stronger 
recovery of bank lending alongside continued economic growth, accompanied by 
current account surpluses and contained fiscal deficits. 
 
We could revise the outlook to stable if lending growth remained subdued and 
banks' nonperforming loans (NPLs) started increasing. In addition, we could 
take a negative rating action if Hungary's public finances weakened, external 
vulnerabilities increased, exchange rate policy became more interventionist, or 
its institutions weakened, for example in Hungary's relationship with the EU , 
especially if we anticipated fiscal risk associated with such developments. 
 
RATIONALE 
 
Hungary's strong external profile and track record of fiscal restraint support 
the sovereign ratings. Relatively weak checks and balances between government 
branches, moderate long-term growth prospects, high public debt, and so far 
impaired monetary transmission mechanism are key constraints. 
 
Institutional and Economic Profile: Strong cyclical growth amid a weaker 
institutional setting 
     -- Cyclical upswing benefits from external environment and government 
stimulus. 
     -- Structural challenges may contain longer-term growth. 
     -- Weakened checks and balances constrain the predictability of 
policymaking. 
 
Like its regional peers, Hungary is undergoing a strong cyclical recovery. We 
expect real GDP growth will approach 3.5% in 2018, only modestly lower than in 
2017. This is due to booming consumption, triggered by real wage and employment 
gains; fiscal stimulus and minimum wage hikes; substantial recovery in EU  
structural and cohesion fund inflows; rising expenditure on housing subsidies; 
stronger private-sector balance sheets; and the ongoing recovery in the 
eurozone. In 2017, after a 10-year lapse, real consumption and investment in 
Hungary recovered to precrisis levels. 
 
However, our growth projection for this year exceeds the country's long-term 
growth potential. Over the medium term, we expect Hungary's structural 
challenges will likely slow the pace of average GDP growth to just under 2.5% 
per year in 2019-2021. These include poor demographics, resulting partly from 
the government's reluctance to accept migrant workers; a large public sector; 
weaknesses in the business environment; low productivity; and an overheating 
labor market. 
 
Moreover, given the prominence of EU  funds in Hungary's public investments, the 
country's growth outlook after 2020 will be exposed to risks of post-Brexit 
funding cuts and likely changes to the EU 's structural fund allocation 
criteria, not least because of the explicit disagreements between Hungary and 
the EU  on some policy issues. 
 
We think that some unconventional policies of the current government, aided by 
a favorable external environment, have helped reduce Hungary's external 
vulnerabilities and secure macroeconomic stability. We also acknowledge the 
government's ambitious reform agenda, aimed at boosting competitiveness and 
productivity. However, we also think institutional changes implemented since 
the early 2010s, which re-codified legal frameworks for Hungary's key 
institutions (for example, the MNB and constitutional court) have weakened the 
checks and balances between branches of government. In particular, the 
consequent concentration of power has expanded the influence and size of the 
public sector at the expense of governance, in our view. 
 
Moreover, restrictive actions taken against the independent mass media and the 
clamp down on nongovernmental organizations have resulted in further political 
centralization, undermining the effectiveness of Hungary's institutions and the 
predictability of its policymaking. Three ongoing infringement procedures 
against Hungary could destabilize Hungary's relationship with the EU , 
potentially derailing EU  investment projects and eroding private-sector 
investor confidence. In our base-case scenario, we assume that such policies 
will continue to constrain Hungary's ability to implement structural reforms 
and effectively address periods of economic distress. At the same time, we 
believe significant financial sanctions or cuts in structural funds to Hungary 
for noncompliance with EU  policy are less likely before 2020, when the EU 's 
current financial framework ends. 
 
Flexibility and Performance Profile: Signs of a solid lending growth recovery 
     -- Procyclical fiscal stance will unlikely allow government debt to drop 
below 60% of GDP in the medium term. 
     -- Surging domestic demand and higher energy prices will start consuming 
current account surpluses. 
     -- Stronger lending demand, historically low interest rates, gradually 
reducing NPLs, and several government-sponsored and -initiated schemes support 
credit growth recovery. 
 
Despite the government's intentions to continue its fiscal stimulus via tax 
cuts and higher spending, we assume in our base case that fiscal slippage will 
be contained, resulting in general government deficits of 2.2% of GDP on 
average in 2018-2021. This is despite a slightly wider fiscal deficit in 2018 
due to upcoming parliamentary elections, compared with 2% of GDP on average in 
2016-2017, which was supported by asset sales and strong consumption-related 
tax receipts. The 2018 budget targets a deficit of 2.4% of GDP, excluding 
revenues from potential privatization receipts, which could therefore augment 
budgetary performance. 
 
We forecast that general government debt, net of liquid assets, will reduce 
somewhat, but stay above 60% of GDP throughout our forecast horizon. At the 
same time, we note improvements in Hungary's central government debt profile. 
Concentrated policy efforts--particularly the authorities' self-financing 
program initiated in 2014--have yielded a reduction in Hungary's foreign 
currency-denominated debt to about one-fifth of total outstanding debt. 
Nonresidents' holdings of central government debt have also declined, reaching 
about 37% in 2017 compared with 40% in 2016, while resident commercial banks 
increased their exposure to the sovereign to over 20% of total banking system 
assets. Hungary has also benefitted from the decline in global interest rates 
and has been able to refinance its outstanding commercial debt with cheaper 
borrowings. This prompted a reduction in general government interest costs to 
about 6.6% of general government revenues in 2017 from its peak of nearly 10% 
in 2012. 
 
Our fiscal forecast does not factor in any contingent risk, such as capital 
injections into development institutions, new state acquisitions, or spending 
on visible capital projects. If these developments crystalize, they could weigh 
on the government's fiscal and debt profiles. 
 
Hungary's external financial profile--which has improved considerably since 
2009--remains a credit strength. Successive current account surpluses since 
2010, the repayment of a large portion of banks' external debt, the redemption 
of official loans contracted in relation to balance-of-payments assistance, and 
the government's substitution of external debt with domestic borrowings have 
all aided external deleveraging. The banking sector is now in a net external 
creditor position. 
 
At the same time, we consider that higher global energy prices and surging 
domestic demand will reduce current account surpluses to below 1% of GDP in 
2021 from an exceptionally strong 6% in 2016. However, this will likely be 
counterbalanced by other non-debt inflows, primarily EU  funds via the capital 
account, resulting in the continued reduction of our preferred external debt 
measure and narrow net external debt, which has more than halved since 2009. 
 
We continue to believe that Hungary's monetary transmission channel remains 
hampered by a still sizable, although reducing, amount of legacy NPLs in 
commercial real estate and banks' residual dependence on foreign currency 
financing. However, these constraints--which have contained the MNB's monetary 
policy effectiveness for years--have started to subside, in our view. 
 
Following a visible recovery of bank lending in 2017 (in absolute terms), when 
credit to the private sector increased by over 4%, we see a higher likelihood 
of sustainable lending growth, including to households. This reflects the 
impact of the central bank's credit-boosting programs (such as the Market-Based 
Lending Scheme for small and midsize enterprises, and certified consumer 
friendly housing loans) and strengthening credit demand, notably thanks to 
historically low interest rates. For 2018-2021, we forecast positive credit 
growth (averaging 4.5%-5%) after a contraction in 2011-2016. We note, however,

title: CEE MARKETS-Crown hits 4-year high, rate hike bets weigh on bonds
text:
* Crown strongest since intervention regime was launched in
2013
    * Moody's may improve Hungary's rating this week-trader

 (Adds Polish economic figures, weakening of Czech 10-year
bonds)
    By Sandor Peto and Jason Hovet
    BUDAPEST/PRAGUE, Oct 18 (Reuters) - The Czech crown hit a
four-year high and the zloty tested 3-month highs against the
euro on Wednesday as Polish retail and industrial data confirmed
robust economic growth in Central Europe. 
    The crown firmed past 25.7 for the first time
since the central bank in late 2013 launched an intervention
regime to keep the currency week. 
    In April it removed a cap on the crown at 27, letting it
rise, and in August it started to reverse years of interest rate
cuts. Another hike may come as early as next month, and that
prospect, coupled with strong economic figures, lifts the crown.
 
    Of the bonds offered by the Czech government at its auction
on Wednesday, there were no sales of zero-coupon paper. "With
CNB hikes looming people are not interested in short bonds at
these levels," a dealer said.
    After the auction, the Czech 10-year benchmark government
bond yield, bid at 1.453 percent, reached its highest level
since August 2014.
    The crown shrugged off concerns that the likely election
victory of ANO party at Czech elections over the weekend could
lead to drawn-out coalition talks, Goldman Sachs said in a note.

    "Domestic financial markets are typically resilient to Czech
political events, given the Czech Republic's strong fiscal
position, sound institutions and independent central bank," it
added. 
    Polish and Czech current account data released this week and
recent government budget figures have confirmed that most of the
region's main economies remain well-balanced, analysts said.
    Polish figures released on Wednesday showed 8.6 percent
annual surge in retail sales in September, and 4.3 percent rise
in industrial output.
    The zloty firmed 0.15 percent to 4.2295 against
the euro, still a touch off Tuesday's three-month highs.
    Polish government bonds eased slightly, with the 10-year
benchmark yield rising 3 basis points to 3.317 percent.
    The forint, steady on Wednesday at 308.15 per
euro, reached 5-week highs versus the euro this week. 
    It traded on the firm side of the key psychological line of
310, even though Hungary's central bank has flagged further
monetary easing.
   "Moody's could lift the outlook of Hungary's debt rating (in
its review) to positive on Friday, and based on Hungarian
economic indicators, an upgrade cannot be ruled out either," one
Budapest-based fixed income trader said.
    Regional central bankers also watch European Central Bank
rate setters and any hawkish guidance from the ECB's Oct 26
meeting could reduce appreciation pressure on regional
currencies, analysts said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Stocks march back toward three-year high
text:
* EM stocks head back toward three-year high

* Chilean peso gains as metals rally

* Philippine's peso rebounds after intervention threat

* Hungary expected to keep rates steady

* China sets yuan midpoint rate at 11-month high

By Marc Jones

LONDON, Aug 22 (Reuters) - Emerging markets, one of 2017's best-performing asset classes, advanced again on Tuesday as stocks climbed back towards three-year highs and a rally in metals markets helped Chile's peso to lead gains by currencies.

MSCI's benchmark emerging stocks index gained 0.5 percent with advances in Hong Kong, China, South Africa and Hungary. It was the index's fourth rise in the past five days, reasserting its outperformance over developed market equities.

"At the moment it is the goldilocks scenario," said Crédit Agricole emerging market strategist Guillaume Tresca. "Everything seems fine, the latest macro data was quite good, political risk is declining and volatility is okay."

Tresca said investors were looking to the annual Jackson Hole conference later this week in the United States, which is hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, for insights into global monetary policies.

Emerging markets have been boosted this year by a weak dollar and by low yields for benchmark U.S and European bonds, which tend to drive global borrowing costs, so this week's signals will be monitored closely.

Currency markets continued to feel the effects of a surge in metals prices. Chile, the world's top copper producer, saw its peso strengthen to its highest in more than six months against the dollar, which itself was higher.

The geopolitical tension around North Korea eased as the head of the U.S. military's Pacific Command stressed the importance of using diplomacy rather than military force to counter Pyongyang's missile threat.

In China, the yuan's official midpoint rate was set at its firmest in 11 months. Mainland Chinese stocks rose again after Shanghai posted its strongest weekly gain in four months last week .

The Philippine peso, which has fallen to an 11-year low, snapped a 10-day losing streak, as the country's central bank warned it would intervene in the currency market to curb speculation.

"The BSP will not tolerate ... speculative behaviour and stands ready to use its very ample international reserves and deploy its full policy and regulatory arsenal if necessary," Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Nestor Espenilla said.

Indonesia was expected to keep its key interest rate at 4.75 percent, although the governor of its central bank has hinted at a potential cut "if all indicators support it". Last week, he said the bank was "pretty happy" with the inflation rate, which was 3.88 percent in July.

In emerging Europe, Hungary's central bank, which has been in stimulus mode for years, was also expected to leave its base rate unchanged, at a record-low 0.9 percent.

The Czech Republic became the first European Union country to raise rates in five years earlier this month, but Hungary is not expected to move until late next year at the earliest .

title: CEE MARKETS 3- Currencies , stocks recoup some losses after initial Brexit shock
text:
(Updates with markets recouping losses, mid-term outlook)
    By Krisztina  Than
    BUDAPEST, June 24 (Reuters) - Central European currencies
and stocks recouped some of their earlier steep losses by Friday
afternoon as the initial shock from Britain's vote to leave the
EU wore off, but markets remained volatile on uncertainty over
the medium-term fallout.  
    Direct trade linkages with Britain account for 3-6 percent
of the foreign trade of central eastern European countries, with
the euro zone having a much bigger role. But Britain is still
Poland's second-biggest export market, with its exports to
Britain in 2015 at around 12 billion euros.
    Investors in Central Europe have been worried that the
impact of Britain's exit could be bigger if it leads later to
cuts in the European Union budget.
    EU development funds play a big role in boosting economic
growth in poorer EU states, so a reduction would be painful.
There are also hundreds of thousands of east Europeans working
in Britain.
    However, some analysts said the region's strong growth
potential still made emerging European assets attractive and
further market losses would likely be contained, especially as
there was further monetary policy easing globally.
    "With central banks anchoring short-term rates at very low
levels, central European bonds may rally once risk aversion
subsides," UniCredit analysts said in a note.
    "Second, expected ECB support for periphery bonds should
help stabilise bond prices in central Europe as well."     
    Early in the morning the zloty tumbled to a 4-1/2
year low of around 4.51 against the euro but later firmed and at
1206 GMT it traded 2 percent weaker from Thursday at 4.457. 
    The forint was one percent weaker. Hungarian five-
and ten-year year government bond yields jumped 15-20 basis
points, and there was a bearish steepening in the yield curve, a
trader said.
    Warsaw's WIG20 blue-chip index, which touched a
7-year low, later recouped some losses and was trading 7 percent
lower at 1200 GMT. Prague stocks were down 6 percent. Budapest
stocks were down 4 percent.
    "The big question is what happens to those who work there

under Brexit, Poland around 0.25 pp and other countries
minimal," Peter Attard Montalto at Nomura said in a note.

zloty was not a risk to the Polish economy. He said he saw no
reason to intervene on the currency market. 
    The National Bank of Hungary said it had all the necessary
tools to continuously ensure financial stability. 
    The Czech crown, which is considered as a safe
haven currency in the region, eased only 0.1 percent.

said will last probably until the middle of 2017.

slower growth in Germany and other euro zone trade partners
because of Britain's looming EU exit will hit the Czech economy
as well, slowing inflation growth.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Stocks plunge, zloty near 4-1/2 year low on British vote to leave EU
text:
(Adds stock markets, Polish tender, analyst on growth)
    By Krisztina  Than
    BUDAPEST, June 24 (Reuters) - Central European currencies
fell and stock markets plunged on Friday after Britain voted to
leave the European Union, with the Polish zloty tumbling to a
4-1/2 year low against the euro and some stock markets to
multi-year lows.
    Direct trade linkages with Britain account for 3-6 percent
of the foreign trade of central eastern European countries, with
the euro zone having a much bigger role. 
    But Britain is still Poland's second-biggest export market,
with its exports to Britain in 2015 at around 12 billion euros.
    Investors in Central Europe have been worried that the
impact of Britain's exit could be bigger if it leads later to
cuts in the EU budget.
    EU development funds play a big role in boosting economic
growth in poorer EU states, so a reduction would be painful.
There are also hundreds of thousands of east Europeans working
in Britain.
    "The big question is what happens to those who work there
(in the UK)," said Janos Samu, an analyst at Concorde Securities
in Budapest. "What hits us badly now is all this uncertainty."
    "We see overall growth impact as biggest in (the) Czech
(Republic) and then Hungary at around 0.5pp shaved off of growth
under Brexit, Poland around 0.25pp and other countries minimal,"
Peter Attard Montalto at Nomura said in a note.
    The zloty fell to 4.52 to the euro in early trade
but recouped some of its losses by 0711 GMT, to trade at 4.456.
The forint fell 1.7 percent to 320, but firmed back
to 318.20 later in highly volatile trading.
    Warsaw's WIG20 bluechip index touched a 7-year low,
but later recouped some losses. The broader market WIG 
fell to a 5-month low. Prague stocks fell to a 7-year low. 
    Shares in Poland's biggest bank, the state-controlled PKO BP
 fell more than 10 percent in early trade, becoming the
biggest drag on the WIG20 index. 
    The Bucharest stock exchange's blue chip index fell
4.5 percent to a four-month low. Budapest stocks were
down 4.6 percent at a three-and-half-month low.
    Poland's finance ministry has called off a switch treasury
debt tender initially planned for Monday due to market
volatility.
    "I don't think the zloty could weaken further than 4.60 per
euro," said Piotr Poplawski, senior economist at ING BSK in
Warsaw.
    "Due to our FX-loan problem we're very dependent on the SNB.
The zloty has regained some ground just after they intervened
and as long as they keep defending the franc the zloty should be
relatively stable," he added.
    He added he did not see a chance of a currency intervention
by the Polish central bank in the near term. 
    Poland's deputy finance minister said the weakening of the
zloty was not a risk to the Polish economy. He said he saw no
reason to intervene on the currency market. 
    The National Bank of Hungary, which left interest rates on
hold at a record-low 0.9 percent on Tuesday, said it was
closely monitoring the British vote and related market
developments and had all the necessary tools to continuously
ensure financial stability. 
    The Czech crown, which is considered as a safe
haven currency in the region, was relatively steady, easing only
about 0.2 percent.

text:

By Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST, April 20 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary is expected to cut its base rate by 15 basis points at its April 26 meeting and lower it further in the next months, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

In the April 18-20 poll, 19 out of 21 analysts projected a 15-basis-point reduction to 1.05 percent in the 1.2 percent base rate next week, and two analysts forecast a 10-basis-point cut.

Inflation, kept in the negative by a decline in crude and commodities prices, has fuelled expectations for central bank policy easing, mainly in Hungary, but also in Poland.

Robust economic growth in the region has buoyed currencies in Central Europe, also pressing the Czech crown to the central bank's intervention cap, and weighing on price levels.

Hungary's central bank, after months of easing through unconventional policy tools, lowered its main interest rate last month, by 15 basis points, resuming the rate cuts which it ended in July last year.

It also flagged further easing measures including rate cuts and its deputy governor Marton Nagy said a weaker forint would support exporters and help "desired inflation" return.

The forint weakened to 315 against the euro from about 310 after the rate cut, but returned to levels on the firm side of 310 by this week, buoyed by improving economic fundamentals and hopes for upgrades in Hungary's credit ratings.

"The exchange rate will absolutely remain a key factor... as long as the forint stays at 310 or firmer, the bank can cut rates further," said Gergely Szabo Forian, portfolio manager of Pioneer Investments.

"A change in the international inflation environment, a reversal in the commodities price decline could also bring forward the end of the rate cuts," he added.

An interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve in the next months would make Hungary's central bank more cautious, said K&H Bank analyst David Nemeth.

"Hungarian and U.S. rates arriving to similar levels would make them thoughtful," he said.

According to the median forecasts in the poll, the base rate could bottom out at 0.75 percent in the next months, stay at that level through this year and rise to 0.9 percent by the end of next year.

The analysts forecast a pick-up in inflation to 1.6 percent by December this year, 2.4 percent by end-2017 and 2.65 percent by end-2018, still below the central bank's 3 percent target. (Editing by Jeremy Gaunt)

text:
(Adds Serbian intervention, Hungary bond auctions, new slug)
    By Krisztina  Than
    BUDAPEST, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Hungarian government bond
auctions attracted good demand on Thursday especially from local
banks keen to invest extra funds freed up by several central
bank measures.
    The forint traded 0.2 percent firmer after the
auctions while the region's other currencies were broadly flat.
Serbia's central bank bought euros on the domestic interbank
currency market to stem gains by the dinar, dealers said.
    The central bank, which on Wednesday cut its benchmark
interest rate to 4.50 percent, intervened with the dinar
 trading at 119.70 to the euro, 0.25 percent stronger
than a day earlier. After the intervention, at 1132 GMT the
dinar was trading more weakly at 119.90.
    The Hungarian central bank has made a series of changes in
recent months to squeeze liquidity out of its own instruments
and encourage banks to buy government debt instead. In its
latest move, it lowered the reserve ratio for commercial banks,
launching a uniform 2 percent ratio. These measures have boosted
local banks' appetite for government securities.
    "There has been significant local demand for government
papers," a fixed income trader said. "This (in past weeks) has
been pushing down yields from 3-month treasury bills up to 3-5
year bonds."
    The trader said the impact from increased local demand was
less palpable on 10-year gove rnment bonds.
    Hungary sold 56 billion forints worth of bonds at an auction
on Thursday, more than the offer of 47 billion forints
. It sold more of the 3-year and 5-year bonds than
planned. 
    The central bank held IRS (interest rate swap) tenders
 on Thursday, which are intended to be a hedging
instrument, supporting banks in increasing and stabilising their
holdings of long-term government securities.
    The central bank accepted 48.3 billion forints worth of
bids, versus its offer of 65 billion.
    In Poland, debt yields fell on Wednesday, tracking core
markets, and eased further on Thursday. 
    Disappointing economic data from the United States resulted
in yield drops abroad and Polish bonds followed suit.
    The Polish debt market is expected to remain under the
influence of core markets, where expectations for an early rate
rise by the Federal Reserve have been weakening, PKO BP analysts
wrote in a note.

reading for Poland, which was to be published at 1200 GMT.

title: CEE MARKETS 1- Currencies  hover near highs, Serbia seen cutting rates
text:
* Serbian central bank seen cutting rates by 25 or 50
bps-poll
    * Zloty off 3 1/2-year high, testing 4.0 vs euro
    * Investors watch central banks as CEE currencies are strong

    By Sandor Peto and Jakub Iglewski
    BUDAPEST/WARSAW, April 9  (Reuters) - Central European
currencies changed little on Thursday after a Wednesday's surge
brought them to levels that may prompt central banks to curb
their strength.
    Serbia's central bank is expected to cut interest rates on
Thursday as its currency remains strong, even though it sold
dinars in recent weeks. A loan agreement with the International
Monetary Fund opened the way for the bank to cut its key rate
last month, by 50 basis points to 7.5 percent.
    Most analysts in a Reuters poll forecast another cut for
Thursday. The dinar gained 0.1 percent
against the euro to 119.95 by 0739 GMT.
    "While caution is surely well-advised amidst a turbulent
global environment and remaining domestic uncertainties, pausing
at this stage would unnecessarily postpone economic recovery,"
Societe Generale said in a note.
    Serbia has the highest interest rates in the region and its
rate cuts aim at helping the weak economy. Elsewhere in the
region, economic growth is buoying currencies.
    The European Central Bank's asset purchases also help, but
concerns that the U.S. Federal Reserve may start raising rates
in June caused wobbles in regional markets in recent weeks.
    Poland's central bank said last month that it had finished
its rate cuts. That has strengthened the zloty, which
hit 3 1/2-year highs against the euro on Wednesday. It traded
flat at 4.105 on Thursday, testing a key level at 4.0.
    "We are getting close to the point where (Poland's) NBP will
have to swallow the bitter pill and say something about the
currency," RBS analysts said in a note. "This may not be enough
to stem the trend but should serve as a wake-up call."
    A rebound of Russia's rouble has also helped the zloty, said
Marcin Turkiewicz, head of currency dealing at mBank in Warsaw.
    "We are linked to that market due to geopolitical
proximity," he said, adding that the zloty may pierce 4.0 and
even move to 3.97-3.96 this week.
    The forint eased 0.1 percent against the euro to
297.50, after touching its strongest levels since late 2013 on
Wednesday.
    The leu was flat at 4.4, beyond which the Romanian
central bank may intervene to curb its strength.
    Hungary is seen cutting rates further. Romania's central
bank may also ease monetary screws as the government has brought
forward a deep cut in value-added tax on food to June.
 
    In the Czech Republic, the crown weakened to 27.36 to the
euro -- keeping it within the Czech central bank's cap on the
crown's value of 27 to the euro. Appetite for testing the cap is
fading, dealers and fund managers say.

text:
* Serbia seen keeping rates on hold for now, dinar firms
    * Crown eases again Czech president comments
    * Inflation weighs on currencies, Polish CPI due at 1300 GMT

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Serbia's dinar firmed on
Thursday ahead of a meeting of the Serbian central bank, which
is expected to keep interest rates on hold like Poland's central
bank did on Wednesday.
    A renewed decline in the Czech crown indicated
that speculation for more monetary easing in Central Europe was
set to prevail, continuing to weigh on the region's currencies.
    Those expectations have been were fuelled by December annual
consumer price index (CPI) figures -- a low 0.1 percent in
Prague and -0.9 percent in Hungary. Poland will publish its own
data at 1300 GMT.
    The Polish central bank is widely expected to cut its record
low interest rates further, a move which could trigger strong
demand at the country's first bond auction this year on
Thursday.
    "(The) zloty can keep part of the gains against main
currencies, but the risk of weakening after the CPI data is
high," Pekao bank analysts said in a note, adding that bond
yields could stay near record lows.
    The zloty edged higher to 4.257 against the euro
by 0853 GMT and Hungary's forint firmed a quarter of a
percent. 
    The dinar firmed 0.1 percent to 122.47, still
staying near record lows even though it extended Wednesday's
gains as companies were selling euros to cover VAT payments due
on Jan. 15.
    Serbia's central bank, worried about the fragility of the
dinar, is seen keeping rates on hold on Thursday.
 
    "Despite recent headwinds, we reaffirm our bullish view on
local bonds," Societe Generale analyst Roxana Hulea said in a
note dated Jan 14.
    "Abating import demand and (expected) official approval of
the SBA (an IMF credit line) will likely give way to the
stabilisation of the dinar and the resumption of the easing
cycle," she added.
    The Czech crown eased 0.1 percent to the euro to
28.104.
    Czech President Milos Zeman talked the currency up on
Wednesday, saying the central bank should halt its policy of
keeping the crown weak through a pledge to intervene on the
currency market. 
    "While Hungary and Poland still have room to manoeuvre with
their interest rates, the Czech Central Bank would have to opt
for a new FX regime border (currently at EUR/CZK 27),"
Raiffeisen said in a note.
    "Whereas we project high probability of more short-term
pressure on CZK, we would currently not expect the central bank
to adjust the FX regime border higher," it added.

title: CEE MARKETS 1-Zloty extends rebound, minister's comments provide support
text:
* Zloty firms, finance minister says pace of fall worrying
    * Forint flat, cbank may support it by year-end -dealers
    * Dinar rises, IMF says Serbia budget in line with loan deal

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Dec 30 (Reuters) - The zloty firmed against the
euro on Tuesday after Poland's finance minister Mateusz Szczurek
said the pace of last week's currency fall might give cause for
concern.
    Szczurek repeated late on Monday that he was not worried by
the zloty's recent weakening to 4.3 to the euro, which would
support the economy, but he saw cause for concern in the pace of
the currency's fluctuations. 
    Central Europe's most liquid currency extended its rebound
on Tuesday for a second day, after losing almost 3 percent in
December on expectations the central bank could cut interest
rates again.
    The zloty <EURPLN-=> firmed 0.2 percent to 4.305 against the
euro by 0905 GMT after gaining on Monday as exporters bought the
currency. 
    It shed about 2.5 percent last week, and touched a
two-and-1/2-year low at 4.3983, after a fall in Polish retail
sales in November fuelled expectations that the central bank
will resume interest rate cuts.
    The Hungarian forint was flat at 315.35, off a
three-year low of 317.40 hit last week.
    Some market participants also expect Hungary to cut its
record low 2.1 percent base rate further next year to help
revive inflation and the slowing economy. 
    In the next few days, however, the Hungarian central bank
could still try to strengthen the forint via market
interventions before the year-end to help the government reduce
state debt from end-2013 levels, traders said.
    A firmer forint reduces Hungary's debt as about 37 percent
of the country's state debt, amounting to 24 trillion forints
($92.6 billion), is denominated in foreign currencies.
    Hungary's central bank never comments on currency market
interventions.
    "I guess the central bank could try to push the forint to
308-310 (by Wednesday's fixing) but I don't expect a bigger
change, like past 305," one Budapest-based trader said.
    The Serbian dinar firmed against the euro on
Tuesday, by 0.1 percent to 121.09, after the International
Monetary Fund said late on Monday that Serbia's 2015 budget was
in line with the terms of a 1 billion euro ($1.22 billion) loan
agreement with the Fund. 
    Passage of the budget has lifted confidence in the dinar,
pushing it off record lows touched in mid-December, and the
central bank, which keeps the currency in tight ranges,
intervened last week to curb its rise.

18 Dec 2014 04:06 ET  Hungary Hit by Russian Currency Crisis But Economy Stable -Matolcsy

By Veronika Gulyas and Margit Feher

BUDAPEST--The Hungarian central bank is under no obligation or pressure to defend the Hungarian currency, the country's central bank governor said on Thursday after the forint weakened to multi-year record lows against major currencies due to contagion from the Russia's ruble crisis.

"There's no forint story, just a ruble story," National Bank of Hungary governor Gyorgy Matolcsy said at a press conference.

The Hungarian forint weakened Wednesday to a three-year low against the euro and a 12-year low against the dollar on the Russian ruble's woes.

Despite this the economy is stable and the currency movements are solely due to the ruble movements, Mr. Matolcsy said.

The governor confirmed that the central bank has no currency exchange rate goal, its only anchor is the medium-term inflation target.

"There's neither obligation nor pressure to intervene in market developments," Mr. Matolcsy added.

The Hungarian economy is affected negatively by the Russian currency crisis since the forint is vulnerable due to Hungary's high public debt and its households' foreign-currency debt, Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban said at the same briefing.

Hungary had also planned to increase its exports to Russia but the extreme ruble weakening against core currencies and the European Union's sanctions against Russia over Ukraine hit Hungary's plans, Mr. Orban added.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Dinar hits two-week high as Serbia vows spending cuts
text:
(Adds bond markets, central bank rate meetings)
    * Budget cut plan lifts Serbia's dinar, stocks
    * CEE assets mostly up, bonds firm as Scots decide to stay
in UK
    * Hungarian, Czech central banks seen holding fire next week

    By Sandor Peto and Ivana Sekularac
    BUDAPEST/BELGRADE, Sept 19  (Reuters) - The dinar jumped to
a two-week high against the euro on Friday after Serbia
announced spending cuts that may open the way to credit talks
with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
    Serbia and neighbouring Croatia are struggling with
recession and high budget deficits. Measures announced by
Serbian Prime Minister Aleksandar Vucic late on Thursday offer
Belgrade the chance of an escape from rising debt. 
    Central European assets mostly gained after Scottish voters
rejected independence, ending the threat of the United Kingdom's
breaking up, which had created uncertainty throughout European
markets.
    The Belgrade stock exchange led a rise, with the index of
its top 15 shares surging 1.6 percent, while a 3 percent dip of
volatile Magyar Telekom stocks pulled down Budapest's
main index by 0.8 percent.
    The dinar, which had dropped to two-year lows to
the euro in recent months as Serbia put off fiscal reforms,
gained a quarter of a percent to 118.25.
    "The announcement of saving measures lifted the dinar," one
Belgrade-based dealer said. 
    The Serbian prime minister announced pension and public-
sector pay cuts on Thursday, hoping to shrink a budget deficit
of more than 8 percent of output and convince the IMF to agree a
new loan deal. 
    Vucic "will hope that the structural reforms being pushed
forward will deliver growth quickly enough to allow Serbia to
grow out of its debt sustainability concerns," said Timothy Ash,
analyst of Standard Bank in a note.
    Serbia's public debt is more than 70 percent of economic
output. Record floods in the Balkans in May led to more
spending, pushing Serbia into recession, and the region is again
struggling with serious floods.
    "Even though these are steps in the right direction, one
should not ignore the fact that the measures and budget
rebalance are delayed and thus reducing the chances of securing
the IMF deal in this year," Hypo-Alpe-Adria bank said in a note.
    "We see the EUR/RSD upwards potential staying in place given
dinar negative factors stemming from banks' external
de-leveraging and aggravated goods (foreign) trade trends," the
bank said. "However, we don't see any abrupt EUR/RSD rise given
the NBS (central bank) active liquidity management, both via FXinterventions and weekly REPO auctions."
    Hungary's forint rose 0.2 percent against the euro
to 311.15, briefly touching eight-week highs at 310.30. It
extended Thursday's 0.2 percent gain amid hopes that Standard &
Poor's would raise the country's credit rating on Friday. 
    Hungary's debt is the highest in central Europe, at around
80 percent of gross domestic product. But its economy has been
growing robustly, bucking the regional trend of economic
slowdown.
    Standard & Poor's has a 'BB' rating on Hungary's long-term
foreign currency debt. It improved the outlook to "stable" from
"negative" on March 28. 
    "However, in our assessment it is more likely that the
rating agency will not change our country's rating," CIB Bank
analysts said in a note.
    
    BONDS FIRM
    Hungarian bond yields dropped as much as 10 basis points

title: POLL-Loose monetary policy may limit CEE  currency  gains
text:
* Zloty seen flat in coming weeks, gradually firmer next year

* Gains smaller, risks are loose monetary policy, Ukraine, Fed

* Hungarian forex loan conversion could cause forint jitters

By Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST, Sept 4 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty may gain more than 3 percent against the euro over the next 12 months as currencies in Central Europe firm up, a Reuters poll of analysts showed.

The region's biggest economies have grown faster than those of euro zone states while inflation across the region is low or even in negative territory in Poland's case.

Their recovery from the previous decade's global economic crisis is slowing and central banks in the region find themselves being nudged towards looser monetary policy, also partly due to the Ukrainian crisis.

That risk is reflected in the forecasts in the poll, which show weaker exchange rates for the zloty and the forint than the median forecasts in a survey conducted a month ago.

The Sept 2-3 poll of 21 analysts showed that the zloty is expected to move sideways near 4.2 to the euro in the coming weeks and firm up to 4.074 by September next year, compared with 4.03 projected in the previous poll.

The forint is expected to firm up by 1.7 percent from Wednesday's close to 309 by next September, a slightly softer forecast than last month's 305. The Czech crown could gain 2 percent to 27.15, and the leu 0.3 percent to 4.39.

Tit-for-tat sanctions between the European Union and Russia have clouded the economic outlook for Central European states and caused some jitters in their markets in recent weeks.

Regional currencies and stocks jumped on Wednesday after Ukrainian and Russian leaders said they were moving closer to a political solution to the battle between Kiev's forces and Moscow-backed rebels in eastern Ukraine. But doubts remain.

"The conflict over Ukraine may not yet be over, so short-term risks (to the zloty) remain," said Piotr Poplawski, analyst at BGZ Bank in Warsaw.

The European Central Bank unveiled a four-year funding plan called TLTROs for banks in June and may flag more monetary stimulus on Thursday, which could also fuel appetite for the assets of the European Union's emerging markets.

"The ECB's TLTRO operations should help the zloty gain," said Poplawski.

The Polish central bank kept its own 2.5 percent main interest rate on hold on Wednesday but Governor Marek Belka said rate cuts were likely if economic figures in the coming weeks continue to indicate weakness.

Belka said that economic weakness in the euro zone had a much bigger impact on Poland than the Ukrainian crisis and that the exchange rate was not an important factor in rate decisions.

Top Polish economic policy makers have said several times, though, that a firming of the zloty would be more worrying for the economy than a depreciation.

"We believe the central bank has little tolerance for a strengthening of the PLN (zloty)," said Nordea analyst Anders Svendsen in a note. "A move towards 4.10 could be enough to prompt a rate cut given the circumstances."

FORINT VULNERABLE

The zloty, as the region's most liquid currency, is particularly exposed to any downturn in international market sentiment if the Ukraine crisis deepens or expectations for an early start to Federal Reserve rate hikes strengthen.

The forint is also vulnerable as junk-rated Hungary has the highest debt in the region at more than 80 percent of economic output. In addition, its central bank has steadily cut its main interest rate to 2.1 percent, below investment grade Poland's main rate.

The median forecasts in the poll show a slight weakening of the forint to 315 by October, a 1 percent gain to 311-311.50 on the 3- and 6-month horizons and further gains thereafter.

Several analysts warned, however, that those forecasts for given points in the calendar hide likely forint jitters.

"I expect a weakening in January that could push the forint to about 320 against the euro due to the planned conversion of banks' foreign currency loans (worth around $15 billion)," said Andras Balatoni, analyst at ING Bank.

Some analysts expect the first wave of forint weakening to come late this month or in October if the government announces the details of the conversions.

However, the government will do its best later this year to strengthen the forint by policy measures or by trying to talk it up, and the central bank may even intervene, analysts said.

Part of Hungary's debt is in foreign currencies and only stronger forint levels could reduce the level of state debt below 80 percent of output by the end of the year, averting the threat of financial sanctions from the European Union.

"By my calculations only forint levels at 307 would result in a decline in debt (from end-2013 levels)," said Gergely Gabler, analyst of Erste Group in Budapest.

title: Canadian Dollar Rallies on Strong Domestic Data -- Market Talk
text:
9:06 EDT - The Canadian dollar extends earlier gains after a duo of strong domestic reports, with June CPI and May wholesale sales rising more than expected. In theory, the CPI increase shouldn't be that supportive for the loonie since the Bank of Canada made it abundantly clear Wednesday it considers the recent uptick in inflation to be transitory, and today's numbers weren't that higher than expected. But with wholesale-sale growth nearly quadrupling expectations, the combination gave a nice jolt of positive energy to the Canadian currency. The US dollar is at C$1.0730 versus C$1.0761 late Thursday. (don.curren@wsj.com @dbcurren)

1255 GMT [Dow Jones]--UniCredit expects Italy to cancel some upcoming government bond auctions, says the bank's rates strategist Luca Cazzulani. He expects the Italy Treasury to cancel the mid-August auction of conventional government bonds, or BTPs, which is scheduled for Aug. 13, and possibly also the end-July auction of inflation-linked bonds, scheduled for July 28. August is traditionally the month with the lowest gross government bond supply during the year. Several countries either don't plan bond auctions at all or cancel some of them. (emese.bartha@wsj.com; @EmeseBartha)

Continued slide in German bund yield adds to the lure of Treasurys as US offers much higher yields. "If we look solely at domestic economic fundamentals, then yields will probably rise slowly and gradually," says Gary Pollack at Deutsche Bank's private wealth management unit. "However, the US Treasury market is truly an international market." He expects yields to stay low, and adds, "we could test 2.40%" -- this year's low set in late May. Expects Hungary's GDP growth to slow down from here in the coming quarters after +3.5% on the year in 1Q, and sees it at 2.9% on the year in 2014 and 2.0% on the year in 2015. title: What To Expect from Another Hungary Fidesz Government? -- WSJ Blog
text:
The incumbent Fidesz party is widely expected to win Hungary's general elections handily on Sunday, possibly matching its current two-thirds majority in parliament. Since it took over government in 2010, the party has tightened its grip on the country's legal system and economy, picked fights with the European Union with a new constitution that critics say limits basic rights and imposed a statist economic policy, much to the consternation of the European Union and foreign investors. Here is a look at what analysts say a second consecutive four-year term in power could bring:

Eurasia Group: Fidesz Win Would Be Investor-Negative

With a feeble center-left opposition, Fidesz looks likely to win the election and "that means more negative news for Hungary and for investors," said Eurasia Group analyst Mujtaba Rahman. Eurasia gives Fidesz a 50% chance of getting another supermajority.

"Another supermajority will serve to validate Fidesz's dismantling of checks and balances since 2010 and likely push the political system further toward centralization," Mr. Rahman added. Even without a Fidesz supermajority, Hungary's macroeconomic conditions will remain mixed and could cause "the business environment to deteriorate in the short, medium and long term."

SocGen: Simple Fidesz Majority Would Be Positive

The election surprise at this point may well be if Fidesz only manages to win a simple majority, which would be a marked positive for market confidence and for Hungarian assets, as it "means that Fidesz would be unable to ram through legislative changes with impunity," Societe Generale economist Phoenix Kalen said.

"Investors remain uncomfortable with Orbán's increasingly autocratic rule, his philosophical turn away from Western Europe, his administration's ad-hoc style of policy-making, frequent changes to the country's constitution, election promises of further bail-out packages for households with foreign-currency mortgages, penalizing treatment of targeted private sectors, and the accompanying erosion of business confidence and private investments," Ms. Kalen added.

BBH: Fiscal Stringency May Prove Hard

"Markets dislike Orbán and his Fidesz party for its confrontational posture with the European Union and the financial system in the past, which included arbitrary taxes on various industries, hurting utility companies by cutting energy costs, undermining the central bank independence, forcing the early retirement of judges who don't conform to the party's views," said Brown Brothers Harriman economist Win Thin.

All that said, it is undeniable that Hungary's economic fundamentals are on good footing, and improving in many aspects. Inflation is low, growth is picking up, unemployment is falling, and the current account is moving further into surplus.

"An argument can be made that the Fidesz choices are just standard populism and that their true costs will not surface for years to come --but when they do surface, history will be re-written," he added.

Nomura: Euro Adoption by End-2018 Unlikely

Under Fidesz, a streak of nationalism has become deep-rooted and euro-adoption at the end of its next parliamentary period--2018--looks unlikely, said Nomura economist Peter Attard Montalto. There will be low growth but higher inflation, with foreign-currency debt reform probably the biggest area of uncertainty for markets.

The key will be if--in order to pay for personal income tax and small and medium-size companies' tax cuts--there are additional changes to the special taxes levied on larger companies, keeping policy uncertainty high for foreign direct investors, he added.

Expect an increase in the amount of government debt held by locals: Fidesz will want more bank assets domestically owned and more key utilities and infrastructure to end up in domestic hands.

Deutsche Bank : More of the Same

Fidesz's election program includes a consolidation of policies introduced in its current term, and the continuation of intervention in the banking and energy sectors. "These policies will not be viewed positively by foreign investors and could worsen the investment climate, " said Deutsche Bank economist Gautam Kalani.

A supermajority would also enable Fidesz to make further amendments to the constitution, including altering the electoral system, which would be difficult to reverse in the longer term, Mr. Kalani added. On the fiscal front, there may be some slippage but the budget deficit is likely to remain below the 3% of GDP threshold, he said.

Morgan Stanley : A Less Eventful Term

"We seriously doubt that the next four years will be as eventful as the last four," said Morgan Stanley economist Pasquale Diana. It seems likely to us that Fidesz will continue to put downward pressure on regulated energy prices, and seek a larger role for the state to play in the energy sector, which could hamper investment. We see no case for Fidesz to indicate a preference for a weaker Hungarian forint," Mr. Diana said, citing that currency strength is no obstacle to exports, a weak forint policy would be hard to control and that the government is still heavily indebted in forints.

4Cast: Risk of Weaker Forint

Financial markets will regard a two-third majority election victory as slightly more negative than a simple majority, said 4Cast economist Gábor Ambrus. "Risks remain that the government--in tacit cooperation with the National Bank of Hungary--would continue to want to keep the forint on the back foot in order to kick start growth and we think that any solution for a drastic reduction in the remaining household foreign-currency debt level would point to this direction."

Citi: Would Fidesz Team With Far Right?

A potential source of surprise could come from Fidesz failing to win a simple majority in parliament, which may force it to seek coalition with the far-right Jobbik party--a clearly unwelcome event for markets, said Citigroup economist Eszter Gárgyán.

Over the next four years, Hungary's economic growth may continue to benefit from firming European growth, slowing deleveraging, and the country's accelerated absorption of European Union support funds. But interventionist government policy could keep Hungary's growth prospects weak relative to its regional peers, Citigroup said.

title: Central Banks Take Advantage of Calm in Markets
text:
Turkey's central bank held interest rates steady and Hungary cut rates for a 19th straight month while leaving the door open to do more, as central bankers took advantage of the recent calm in financial markets to shore up their economies.

Still, the fragilities that sparked a rout in emerging markets last month such as high financing needs and weak currencies haven't been resolved, analysts warned, and could reignite turmoil in many developing economies.

"Some of the vulnerabilities that caused the selloff [in emerging markets last month] are still around," said William Jackson, emerging markets economist at consultancy Capital Economics. "It's premature to say that they're out of the woods."

Turkey's central bank on Tuesday kept its benchmark one-week rate at 10%, as widely expected. Policy makers also left the overnight borrowing rate at 8% and the overnight lending rate at 12%.

"Inflation indicators are forecast to remain above the 5% target for a little while longer...The tight monetary stance will continue until a visible improvement is achieved in the inflation outlook," the central bank said.

The decision came three weeks after an emergency meeting resulted in dramatic rate increases as policy makers scrambled to halt an emerging markets selloff that pushed its currency, the lira, to record lows. The increases also helped restore the central bank's credibility amid concerns that it had bowed to political pressure to keeps rates too low.

Turkey's lira was flat after the anticipated decision. The currency has rallied by almost 5% against the dollar since the central bank's emergency rate rise, the biggest gain among emerging markets.

"Turkey's central bank fixed its credibility in a serious manner with its radical move on Jan. 28," said Nilufer Sezgin, chief economist at Erste Securities in Istanbul.

Still, "what roiled markets and caused the volatility was Turkey's large current-account deficit, its short-term financing and central bank reserves that didn't meet funding requirements. These factors are still in play," Ms. Sezgin said. The current account gap, which hit $65 billion in December, the highest since April 2012, should come down due to slower domestic demand and the weaker lira, she said.

The storm that rocked emerging market assets from Brazil to South Africa to Turkey this year has settled in recent weeks. Investors have become more comfortable with the U.S. Federal Reserve's plan to gradually withdraw its stimulus, while some emerging market central banks have fought back with rate increases and currency interventions.

Meanwhile, Hungary's decision to cut interest rates by 0.15 percentage points to a record-low 2.7% highlights the differences among developing economies, even as many fell victim to the same stampede in January.

Unlike Turkey and South Africa, which run high trade and investment deficits, Hungary runs a current account surplus. Consumer prices were flat last month on an annual basis, far below the bank's 3% target.

"Hungary's position is fundamentally strong compared to other emerging market economies," the central bank said Tuesday, opening the door to additional rate cuts. "Delivering price stability in the medium term points in the direction of monetary easing."

Still, Hungary still must finance a significant amount of external debt, making it sensitive to shifts in investor sentiment toward emerging markets. Its currency, the forint, fell after the central bank's decision, with the euro up 0.8% at 310.87 forints.

The Hungarian central bank "is playing with fire," said Nomura economist Peter Attard Montalto. If emerging markets remain in an episodic wobble over the coming months or even year, each rate cut will mean the next wobble weakens the Hungarian economy further and leaves it at a greater risk of capital outflows, he said.

"They seem to have gotten away with cutting interest rates," said Mr. Jackson of Capital Economics. "The test would come if the forint comes under more pressure."

Margit Feher in Budapest and Tommy Stubbington in London contributed to this article.

title: EU Court Says  Hungary  Can  Intervene  in  Forex  Loans -- WSJ Blog
text:
A senior attorney at the European Union's top court issued a formal legal opinion Wednesday which could clear the way for Hungarian courts to rule on whether exchange rate conditions of foreign currency loans were unfair.

The opinion came as Hungary's Constitutional Court discusses how deep the government can intervene retroactively in the existing loans.

At the end of July 2013, there were around half a million foreign-currency mortgage contracts in Hungary worth 3.5 trillion forints ($15.38 billion), according to the central bank.

The Fidesz party government, which is seeking a second consecutive term in power in elections in eight weeks' time, has said it wants to implement a relief system to ease the burden on borrowers who took out the loans before 2010 and now face high payments after a dramatic slide of the forint.

Foreign-currency loans were vastly popular in Hungary prior to the financial crisis because they were much cheaper to service than forint loans. But the matter became a political issue following the sharp appreciation of the Swiss franc during the global financial crisis.

The European Court of Justice will issue a ruling on the case at a later date, but it often follows the opinions of its advocates general. If the opinion forms the basis of the ruling, Hungarian courts will be able to change foreign-currency mortgage loans if they find exchange-rate stipulations in the loan contracts unfair.

Court decisions annulling the contracts may lead to potentially detrimental consequences for the borrowers as such decisions would force them to pay back the loan in one sum immediately, said Nils Wahl, Advocate General of the European Court of Justice. Hungarian courts easing the loan conditions with modifying the exchange rates would put some of the consequences of the forint's slide on mostly foreign-owned banks in Hungary.

In May 2008, the Kasler family took out a 14.4 million-forint ($63,365) mortgage with OTP, Hungary's biggest bank, with the mortgage calculated in Swiss francs. The contract stated that the amount in Swiss francs was to be calculated on the basis of the buy rate of the bank on the day the funds were made available.

However, reimbursement was to be calculated on the basis of the sell rate of the bank the day before the payment was due. The difference between these two rates was in the bank's favor.

The borrowers challenged this system before Hungarian courts, claiming that it was an abusive clause, an example of an illegal clause detrimental to consumers. The Hungarian Supreme Court, which is now hearing the case, turned to the European Court of Justice, which interprets EU law to make sure it is applied coherently throughout the bloc.

It asked the Luxembourg-based court to rule whether the clause in question was indeed abusive and if so, whether the Hungarian judge can modify it. A complete elimination of the clause would mean that the consumer would have to reimburse the mortgage immediately, in its entirety, which would be beyond the financial capabilities of most borrowers.

Mr. Wahl said Wednesday Hungarian courts could replace the clause, if they find it inadmissible in contracts, with other provisions in the Hungarian law.

"Where the deletion of an unfair term would make performance of the contract impossible, as in the present case, the directive does not preclude the national court from replacing the term at issue with a supplementary provision of national law, where such a replacement is possible under national law," Mr. Wahl said.

He also said foreign-currency mortgage borrowers must understand not only the content of the loan contracts but also the related obligations and rights. In the Kasler case, the contract conditions were set out in plain and simple language, it seems, but there may be doubts as to whether the borrower was "in the position to understand" that he would be subject to additional expense stemming from the difference between the selling and the buying price of the foreign currency, Mr. Wahl added.

In Mr. Wahl's view, Hungary's Supreme Court is to answer that question "in the light of the objective information available when the contract was concluded."

The Court of Justice ruling, which may follow several months from now, may differ from the opinion.

Analysts expect that the Hungarian Supreme Court's decision--the final ruling in the case--will only come at end-May or in June.

    * Forint resilient, investors cut back selling positions

    By Sandor Peto
    BUDAPEST, Feb 12 (Reuters) - Shares in Hungary's biggest
bank fell on Wednesday after a European court opinion that could
clear the way for Hungarian courts to challenge some aspects of
contracts on foreign loans to households.
    OTP Bank fell over 2 percent after the European
Court of Justice issued a non-binding legal opinion that under
European law, Hungary's national courts can intervene where
contract terms are deemed unfair.
    Hungary's government wants to implement a relief scheme for
holders of foreign currency mortgages which have become more
costly to service as the forint has weakened, but is waiting for
legal issues to be ironed out before adopting legislation.
    The plan is expected to prove costly for the country's
mostly foreign-owned banks, even though Hungary's supreme court
has already ruled that lenders were not to blame when borrowers
lost out because the exchange rate changed. The heavily-taxed
banks' reluctance to lend is a drag on economic recovery.
    But the ruling had only a limited impact on the forint,
pressure on which has eased after last month's sell-off in
emerging currencies, which forced Turkey and South Africa into
emergency interest rate hikes. 
    The Hungarian currency was bid at 308.21 versus
the euro at 1521 GMT, up 0.7 percent from Tuesday but off the
day's highs, with some investors reported to have closed short
positions after the sell-off.
    "I think the forint will consolidate unless problems emerge
elsewhere (in other emerging markets) in the world," one
Budapest-based currency dealer said.    
    The forint is seen as vulnerable as investors pull back from
emerging markets. Although Hungary runs a current account
surplus, making it less vulnerable than countries with big

relative to Central European peers.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-In emerging Europe, danger seen in policy rather than capital needs
text:
(Repeats, without changes, story first published on Tuesday)
    * Hungary, Romania seen vulnerable in emerging Europe
    * Politics, influence over central banks worry investors
    * Hungary's debt, percentage of foreign ownership a worry
    * Poland back in favour after pension policy storm

    By Marc Jones
    LONDON, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Central and eastern Europe may
have weathered the latest emerging markets squalls better than
most but Hungary and Romania show the region is not immune and
capital flight is not the only worry on investors' minds.
    While most central European markets have fared better over
the past year than the 'fragile five' countries of Indonesia,
South Africa, Brazil, India, and Turkey with their urgent need
to finance current account gaps, many have still been dragged
through the wringer over the past couple of weeks.
    Hungary has made a particularly convincing case for turning
the 'fragile five' into a 'shaky six'. 
    Despite Budapest's insistence that its current account
surplus makes it far less reliant on the goodwill of foreign
stock and bond investors, its currency  and share
market have sunk further than those of most in the
quintet singled out for their acute dependence on investment
flows.
    The lesson seems to be that messy politics and weak central
banks can be just as damaging for the image as deficits.
    Aberdeen Asset Management fund manager Viktor Szabo said
Hungarian debt ratios near 80 percent of annual economic output,
wrangles with foreign banks and a central bank eyeing more
interest rates cuts meant he was steering clear.     
    "Hungary has no problem on the current account side ...
(but) it has high debt levels, with a significant part of it
denominated in foreign currency," Szabo said.
    "It is becoming more expensive to refinance the debt, and
the risk is that another wave of global risk aversion could lead
to failed bond auctions."
    Hungary and Poland both sailed through bond sales on
Thursday. But the forint remains near a 2-1/2 year low versus
the euro and Hungary's borrowing costs 
have hardly budged from a six-month high, as has the premium
investors demand to buy bonds there rather than from ultra-safe
Germany or Poland.
  
               
    POLAND 'THE BENCHMARK'
    Romania and Serbia are showing some of the same strains as
Hungary, although central bank intervention has helped limit the
impact on the leu  and dinar currencies
.
    Daniel Hewitt, a senior emerging market economist at
Barclays, said the limited use of the dollar in the region
should help but it would be unable to escape another big
sell-off.
    Individual central bank policy stances are increasingly
important for currency defence after abrupt defensive rate hikes
in India, Turkey and South Africa.
    Hungary's monetary policymakers, all appointed by the
current government, have cut rates from a 7 percent 2012 peak to
just to 2.85 percent last month.
    They discuss interest rates again on Feb. 18 and with
inflation extremely low - helped by energy price cuts - the bank
has maintained there is more room to cut rates. But noises from
politicians last week suggest the mood may be shifting.
    "In my world, the difference between Hungary and Poland has
been quite striking in this recent sell-off," said Hewitt.
    "The Hungarian central bank seems to have pushed monetary
loosening too far ... and they have an overhang of liquidity due
to their Funding for Growth scheme, whereas in Poland they have
been pretty restrained."
    Both Hewitt and Szabo tip Polish FX and equities as best
equipped to weather any further unrest.
    Poland, the region's biggest emerging economy, has shaken
off investor disapproval over a pensions nationalisation last
year and its economy is seen growing almost 3 percent this year
even though interest rates are higher than most. Its zloty
 currency has recouped all of its losses from the latest
upset and its main stock index has rebounded.    
    Its links to recovering core European economies like Germany
give the zloty the natural advantage of a central bank likely to
be eyeing rate hikes later in the year.
    "Poland is the real benchmark for me," added Murat Toprak,
emerging market strategist at HSBC in London. "It has good
fundamentals ... if it starts selling off, then we also have to
worry about a lot of different countries."
        
    UNION BENEFITS
    As European Union members, Poland, Hungary and the Czech
Republic are bound by the bloc's rules on fiscal house-keeping.
    For the past several years that has constrained their
governments from running big deficits to boost growth. 
    But it has also restrained current account deficits, sparing
their currencies the worst of the capital outflow risks posed by
the U.S. retreat from easy money.
    Then there are the EU's 'cohesion funds' to help
ex-communist countries rebuild infrastructure. That's investment
for which they don't have to compete with emerging economies
elsewhere.
    "The most important thing for these countries is (economic)
growth. The data we have had recently has been good ...so they
are positioned to outperform," said Hewitt at Barclays.
    "If things do stabilise, even Hungary will strengthen."

 (Additional reporting by Marcin Goettig in Warsaw and Sujata
Rao in London; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)
