title: Emerging-Market  Currencies  Claw Back Some Ground -- Update
text:
Emerging-market currencies recovered from earlier losses on Thursday, as U.S. markets opened to some upbeat economic data and corporate earnings.

But broad risk sentiment recovered later in the session, after data confirmed the U.S. economy grew 3.2% in the fourth quarter of 2013. U.S. stocks opened higher, recovering some of Wednesday's losses, while European indexes bounced back from early declines.

The recent pullback from emerging-market currencies had continued earlier Thursday, after the U.S. Federal Reserve confirmed expectations that it would scale back its bond-buying program by a further $10 billion a month.

The Hungarian forint bore the brunt of the early selling pressure, mimicking large declines in the Turkish lira and South African rand earlier in the week--drops that surprise rate rises from central banks have been powerless to reverse in the short term.

But the forint recovered its early losses against the euro, as some analysts said the broad weakness in emerging markets looked exaggerated.

"The market appears to be treating tapering as actual tightening, which is an overreaction. Tactically, emerging markets look oversold," said George Iwanicki, global emerging markets strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

"As painful as it may be in the short term, it is actually very positive that the brunt of the pain from tapering is being felt through currency adjustments; this is making emerging markets more competitive as a whole. Encouragingly, we are seeing central banks responding with orthodox moves like rate hikes."

Turkey and South Africa--among a group of emerging markets that have struggled to defend their currencies as investors adjust to more restrictive monetary policy in big economies--also benefited from the more optimistic tone.

The Turkish lira bounced from earlier lows to strengthen 0.8% to 224.34 lira to the dollar. Despite the recovery, it remains at a similar level to where it traded before the Turkish central bank raised rates.

The South African rand added 1.6% against the buck, having earlier traded close to a five-year low.

The Russian ruble, which hit a near-five-year low earlier Thursday, clawed back 0.5% against the dollar. The currency was given an added boost after the head of Russia's central bank said there were no plans to stop foreign-exchange interventions after 2014.

Hungary and Russia have moved into the market's cross hairs as the recent spate of emerging-market rate increases-- India also bumped up rates earlier this week--ramped up the pressure on countries that haven't followed suit.

"When Turkey got bullied into hiking rates by the market, there were two next: South Africa and Russia, neither of which had hiked and had become low yielders. The Hungarian forint is next," said Bartosz Pawlowski, global head of emerging-market strategy at BNP Paribas.

Hungary's central bank still has room to continue cutting interest rates, its governor said Wednesday, despite the recent weakness in the forint. The central bank has been trimming rates in small increments for several months.

But Hungary's large reserves of foreign exchange give it greater room for a fightback than many emerging-market nations.

"If officials get uncomfortable with the slide in the forint, I think they will intervene. They have the artillery to do that," Mr. Pawlowski said.

European equities picked up after the U.S. data, having earlier been dragged down by the tension surrounding emerging markets. The Stoxx Europe 600 index was 0.3% higher, while Germany's DAX added 0.4%. London's FTSE 100 lagged behind, paring losses to trade at 0.1% down.

In the U.S., the S&P 500 was up 0.7% in early trade.

Overnight, the Nikkei had dived 2.5%, wiping out most of Wednesday's gains, which came before the positive effects of the Turkish rate rise melted away.

In a further knock to global confidence, purchasing managers' data for January brought more evidence that manufacturing in China is slowing.

Elsewhere in currency markets, the New Zealand dollar remained lower after the country's central bank left interest rates on hold. Citigroup reported widespread selling of the New Zealand dollar against its Australian counterpart, with funds, companies and banks all joining the fray.

Brad Frischkorn contributed to this article.

title: *Hungary  Central Bank  Has No Foreign  Currency  Rate Target-Gerhardt
text:
30 Jan 2014 10:38 EDT *Hungary Central Bank Deputy Governor Gerhardt Reacts to HUF Weakness

30 Jan 2014 10:39 EDT *Hungary Central Banker Gerhardt Made Comment to Portfolio.hu

30 Jan 2014 10:41 EDT *Hungary Gerhardt: Hasn't Made In-Depth Calculations on Impact of Current HUF Levels

30 Jan 2014 11:00 EDT  Hungary Central Bank Has No Exchange Rate Target-Gerhardt


 
   By Veronika Gulyas 
 

BUDAPEST--The National Bank of Hungary has no exchange rate target, Ferenc Gerhardt, one of the two deputy governors of the bank told business website Portfolio.hu on Thursday, in a reaction to the forints easing against the euro.

"Processes are relatively new, there's too little information; we haven't made in-depth calculations based on the actual facts yet," Mr. Gerhardt said.

He also noted he cannot add much to central bank Governor Gyorgy Matolcsy's comments on Wednesday when he said there was ample room for further rate cuts in Hungary.

The forint weakened to a two-year low versus the euro earlier on Thursday. The euro-forint traded at HUF309.71 at 1547 GMT versus 312.42 at around 1000 GMT.

Analysts at BudaCash said market participants expect Mr. Matolcsy to verbally intervene and halt the forint from further weakening; and also to prove its independence from the government.

Investors have drawn a parallel with Turkey, suspecting that due to the political considerations of the government, Hungary's central bank would be just as unwilling as its Turkish counterpart to increase rates, BudaCash analysts said.

The euro-forint rate may rise further even to the HUF320 level until the National Bank of Hungary verbally intervenes, a local trader who preferred to remain anonymous said.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Forint falls on CPI plunge, yield curves steepen
text:
* Hungarian forint weakens as inflation nears 40-year low


    * Hungarian central bank chief sees more rate cuts
    * Zloty regains some losses in technical trade
    * Government debt yield curves steepen, showing long-term
uncertainty
    By Karolina Slowikowska and Sandor Peto
    WARSAW/BUDAPEST, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The forint eased on


Tuesday as Hungary's inflation fell to near 40-year lows, strengthening expectations that its central bank will cut interest rates even more, while other central European markets consolidated after falls. Government bond yield curves in the region, however, continued to steepen, indicating that worries over liquidity trends in global markets have not passed. Assets in the region fell on Monday in the aftermath of U.S. economic data that suggested the Federal Reserve may start to cut back its stimulus earlier than expected. Cheap funds from the Fed fuelled capital flows in emerging economies in the past two years, also allowing them to cut interest rates significantly to help their economies recover. Hungary said its headline inflation rate dropped to 0.9 percent in October from 1.4 percent in September, surprising analysts, whose consensus forecast was for no change. The forint weakened 0.3 percent against the euro by 1538 GMT, to 298.88. Hungarian central bank governor Gyorgy Matolcsy said the bank could further reduce its 3.4 percent base rate, which it has already more than halved since August last year, to counter falling inflation. "The rate cuts are not under threat from the inflation side, and the reductions slowly erode the forint's strength," one Budapest-based currency dealer said. "Foreign markets are not very supportive now, but there is no scare either." Poland's zloty, meanwhile, rebounded after Monday's fall and was bid at 4.207, firmer by 0.2 percent. Long-term government bond yields edged up in both countries, indicating uncertainty over long-term trends. Poland's 10-year yield rose 7 basis points to 4.42 percent, while Hungary's corresponding yield rose 19 basis points to 6.08 percent. "The Polish market is reacting today to events on foreign markets, where after Friday's (U.S.) data there is pressure on prices," said Maciej Popiel, a fixed income trader at PKO BP. Hungarian 10-year yields have risen by about 70 basis points in two weeks, while expectations for rate cuts keep short-term yields near 3 percent. That steepening in the yield curve can continue, one Budapest-based fixed income trader said. "If U.S. data meet expectations, 10-year yields there could still continue to weaken, and then we (Hungarian long-term bonds) can also weaken further," the trader said. Elsewhere, the Czech crown was bid weaker by 0.1 percent against the euro at 27.012, still sticking to the 27 level which it eased to in a 5 percent plunge last week as the Czech central bank started to sell it to help exports. Hungary's central bank chief ruled out similar intervention. But the Czech measure contributes to uncertainty in the region's markets, dealers said. Elsewhere in central Europe, Romania's leu was flat at 4.452 against the euro.

title: Hungarian  central bank  chief raises prospect of rate cuts
text:
* Inflation fell in October close to 40-year low

* Matolcsy rules out Czech-style FX intervention

* Says stimulus fund could help meet inflation target

By Leigh Thomas

PARIS, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Hungary could cut interest rates to counter falling inflation, its central bank governor told Reuters on Tuesday, ruling out Czech-style currency intervention.

Hungarian inflation dropped close to a 40-year low of 0.9 percent last month, well below economists' average forecast of 1.4 percent, official data showed on Tuesday.

Inflation is falling across the region and the Czech central bank launched currency interventions last week for the first time in more than a decade to counter the risk of a debt-deflation spiral.

Hungarian central bank Governor Gyorgy Matolcsy said in an interview that while falling inflation presented a policy "challenge", intervention was not the right option for Hungary because the economy was too small and debt levels - especially in the hands of foreigners - were high.

"We have to be very cautious," he said on the sidelines of a conference in Paris. "We don't have a policy to intervene, that means very, very small steps can be used."

He said such steps could include interest rate cuts, though he added this would be up to the central bank's monetary policy committee to decide.

Matolcsy, a former economy minister, added that another option was to strengthen the central bank's $12.5 billion stimulus plan.

"It might help to reach the inflation target" of 3 percent, he said.

The Hungarian forint fell to six-week lows on Tuesday after the low inflation figure, which Matolcsy said was partly due to one-off influences such as a 20 percent reduction in energy prices.

"But there are longer-term trends (at play), meaning weak consumption, higher savings and very strong motivation on the part of Hungarian households to lower their debt levels," he said. (Reporting by Leigh Thomas; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

PRAGUE/BUCHAREST, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Central European emerging stock markets, led by Warsaw, rose on Tuesday on optimism that a U.S. debt default will be averted, while the Polish zloty resisted softening pressures from lower-than-expected inflation.

There were signs in Washington that a Senate deal will be clinched to prevent a potentially calamitous default on federal debt.

Warsaw's stocks rose 1.49 percent to a nine-month high followed by Budapest with 0.97 percent and Prague . Telefonica rose 3 percent on the possibility Spanish parent Telefonica may sell a majority stake in it.

However, electricity producer CEZ fell 1 percent after its chief executive told Reuters the group was in talks with auditors on potential asset writedowns.

Poland's consumer price inflation edged down to 1.0 percent year-on-year in September from 1.1 percent in August, the statistics office said on Tuesday.

Analysts polled by Reuters had expected last month's consumer prices to have risen 1.15 percent from a year ago.

Piotr Bujak of Nordea Bank Polska said the main reason for the low inflation print was a deep drop in costs of education. "The underlying trend remains unchanged. Inflationary pressures are gradually gaining strength, but still subdued."

"The figures confirm rates to be kept on hold for long."

Polish inflation expectations are well-anchored, and monetary policy is likely to remain neutral, Polish central bank Governor Marek Belka said on Monday during a visit to Mexico.

By 1300 GMT the zloty was flat at 4.178 and was off a four-week high one day after dealers said state-owned bank BGK had intervened to prop up the currency.

Both Hungary's forint and the Romanian leu edged up 0.2 percent while the Czech crown was a touch softer at 25.6 per euro.

title: CEE MARKETS 2- Currencies  weaker, Czech crown drops after inflation data
text:
(Adds Hungary cbank, updates prices)


    * Czech CPI fell more than expected, intervention fears loom
    * Hungarian cbank minutes show room for further rate cuts
    BUDAPEST/BUCHAREST, Oct 9 (Reuters) - The Czech crown led
losses among emerging European currencies on Wednesday after
lower-than-expected inflation data raised the likelihood that
the central bank could intervene to weaken the currency.
    Czech inflation ran at annual rate of 1.0 percent in
September and consumer prices fell 0.4 percent month-on-month, a
bigger drop than analysts had expected. 
    The central bank said the data pointed to stronger downside
risks to its inflation outlook. With interest rates already
close to zero policymakers have been mulling intervention to
weaken the crown as a way to help lift inflation back to the
bank's target.  
    "(The crown's weakening) was an immediate reaction to the
inflation data," said Ivo Prokop, FX dealer at Raiffeisenbank.
    "Should it get confirmed (by future numbers) that the
inflation trend will be going this way, the crown will not
appreciate, as everyone will be afraid of the central bank."
    By 1250 GMT, the crown was down 0.5 percent versus
the euro at 26.6, extending losses from earlier in the session
and hitting a one-week low. On Tuesday, it had touched a
four-month high of 25.485.
    The Polish zloty and the Hungarian forint
 were each down 0.1 percent to the euro.
    Hungarian central bank minutes released on Wednesday showed


that all but one of the rate setters voted to cut the benchmark interest rate by 20 basis points last month to a record low of 3.6 percent and that further cuts might follow. In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk denied he was planning to dismiss Finance Minister Jacek Rostowski. The Romanian leu was down 0.5 percent at 4.465 per euro, its weakest level since Sept. 30. "We see this ... as a retrenchment from the leu's stronger gains after the (U.S. Federal Reserve) decision in mid- September (not to withdraw stimulus), which we warned were vulnerable to a correction since they also occurred in such small volumes," ING said in a note. title: CEE MARKETS 2-MOL hits 16-month low, crown tests  intervention  threat
text:
* Hungary's MOL shares down on Croatian INA stake deal worries * Czech Sept. 26 meeting minutes: intervention chances remain high 


    By Radu Marinas and Sandor Peto
    BUCHAREST/BUDAPEST, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Shares in Hungarian
oil and gas group MOL fell to a 16-month low on Friday
as a spat between Budapest and Zagreb over its stake in Croatian
peer INA escalated.
    The Czech crown held near a four-month peak against the


euro, testing the central bank's threats to intervene, while other Central European currencies were mixed. Stock markets in the region fell, including a 1.2 percent decline for MOL that led the Budapest bourse lower. Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban said on Friday that Croatia should consider buying MOL's stake in INA to prevent damage to bilateral relations. Relations between MOL and Croatia have been strained ever since MOL, which has a nearly 50 percent stake in INA, tried and failed to take majority control in early 2011. The row escalated this week after Croatia issued an Interpol and European arrest warrant for MOL chief Zsolt Hernadi in a bribery case. MOL has denied all the accusations. "It is weighed down by the continued uncertainty (over INA) that has been hanging over the shares for days," a Budapest-based equity dealer said. On currency markets, the crown was a little volatile during the day, before steadying after minutes from the Czech central bank's Sept. 26 meeting showed a majority of board members agreed currency interventions remained likely. With interest rates at near zero, the bank has been mulling using this tool to ease monetary conditions further. But the board has voted against the measure at the last two meetings. The Czech economy is starting to recover from a record recession, although inflation has been running below-target all year and crown strength remains a concern. Weakening the crown would help prop up price growth by making imports more expensive, in theory encouraging people to spend now. But the measure could also potentially backfire by further depressing consumer demand. Dealers and analysts say the crown is testing levels that might prompt the central bank into action. "The market might test how far it can push (the crown)," Raiffeisen said in a weekly note. "But given the current circumstances, i.e. still very fragile recovery and slowing inflation, significant crown appreciation would be exactly the case when most of the central bankers would decide to sell crown on the market, despite the uncertainties about the effect and future operations." Other currencies were mixed, with Romania's leu firming 0.2 percent to the euro, while the Polish zloty was flat. The forint eased 0.2 percent to 297 in what one dealer said was a likely option expiry at midday. "If the dollar is weakish next week, the forint could firm, but it will stay between 295 and 300," the dealer said.

Monetary policy remains the central theme in central Europe Thursday, as the Czech central bank may vote to launch a foreign exchange intervention to loosen monetary conditions, hot on the heels of Hungary slashing interest rates this week.

In Prague analysts expect no change to the central bank's benchmark interest rate, which is at a historic low of 0.05%.

But if the monetary policy board deems it necessary to ease monetary conditions in the country that is emerging from recession, it will come via large-scale koruna sales.

"The central bank is [now] the closest [it's been] to start foreign-exchange interventions after a year of contemplation," said Miroslav Plojhar, economist and currency strategist at Erste Bank.

Mr. Plojhar said its a 50-50 chance the bank votes for the move. However, the bank is not obliged to hold such a vote.

The central bank board hasn't found the need to launch an intervention yet, but governor Miroslav Singer recently said a koruna-sale is likely while the country's inflation rate continues to undershoot the central bank's 2% target.

That comes as the Hungarian central bank Tuesday cut its main rate to 3.60% from 3.80%, citing a slow economy and tame inflation as drivers.

In Sofia, Bulgaria's parliament has its last chance to hold a no-confidence vote in the left-leaning, Socialist Party-led coalition.

Opposition party Citizens for European Development of Bulgaria, or GERB, put forth the motion.

However, the party's lawmakers skipped a chance to hold the vote on Wednesday and it remains likely that GERB members will again fail to register in parliament for the vote Thursday, the last day the motion can be brought to a vote.

title: HEARD ON THE STREET: Among Emerging Markets, Central Europe Offering Stability
text:
(FROM THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 9/3/13)

By Richard Barley

[Financial Analysis and Commentary]

Not all emerging markets are created equal.

Countries such as Turkey, Indonesia and India have seen their currencies plummet as shifting expectations of U.S. monetary policy have sent hot-money flows into reverse. But the picture looks very different in Central Europe.

The Czech koruna strengthened in August, while the Hungarian forint and Polish zloty were only marginally weaker. Central European markets can't be entirely immune to global jitters about the Federal Reserve and conflict in Syria, but the region should continue to offer investors greater stability.

The big advantage for Central European countries is that they aren't dependent on the massive capital flows spurred by easy U.S. monetary policy, so don't fear their reversal.

While Turkey had a yawning current-account deficit of 6.5% of gross domestic product at the end of June, Hungary has swung to a surplus from a deficit of 7.2% of GDP in 2008. Poland has recorded its best current-account figures of the past decade in the past two months, Nomura notes.

On the growth front, Central Europe is accelerating -- albeit modestly and after extended weakness. The Czech Republic emerged from recession in the second quarter, growing 0.7% on the quarter, while Hungary's economy expanded 0.5% and Poland's 0.4%. Stronger growth in the euro zone -- particularly in Germany, a key trade partner -- should help the recovery continue.

Oddly, Central Europe may owe its current safe-haven status partially to the turmoil that has plagued Europe in recent years, as well as to European institutions much criticized for failing to prevent that crisis. The European Union's Excessive Deficit Procedure has forced countries to fix their fiscal problems.

Poland has a constitutional limit on debt set at 60% of GDP -- the Maastricht criteria for euro entry. Hungary has reduced its budget deficit to 1.9% of GDP in 2012 from 9.4% in 2006. The euro-zone crisis and bank deleveraging mean there has been no credit boom in Central Europe, unlike in Asia and Latin America.

There are still vulnerabilities. Czech politics are messy. In many other ways, though, the Czech Republic looks like the Central European equivalent of Switzerland -- its central bank is even thinking of intervening to weaken its currency.

In Hungary, the government has pursued unorthodox fiscal policies including heavy windfall taxes on industry that may deter investment. The country is still grappling with the problem that large amounts of residential mortgages are denominated in Swiss francs, making a weaker forint a real problem.

In Poland, some worry about bond-market stability -- nonresidents owned 37% of domestic government bonds as of April -- and the government has seen its budget deficit for 2013 widen due to weak growth.

But if growth picks up in the euro zone, then Central Europe could offer investors opportunities. It may yet be a bumpy ride, but their stronger fundamentals should win out. [ September 02, 2013 18:46 ET (22:46 GMT) ] [ (END) Dow Jones Newswires ] [ 04-09-13 0610GMT ]

    The government in Budapest, which faces an election next

phase out foreign currency mortgages, seeking to help struggling
households but hurting banks in the process. 
    Since Hungary's government announced its mortgage plan on


July 16, OTP shares have fallen by roughly 17 percent, wiping about 200 billion forints ($890.64 million) off the bank's market capitalization. The bank took another hit when its chairman and CEO sold a big chunk of shares to finance his agricultural business. At 1405 GMT, OTP shares were down 5.1 percent from the previous session at 4,307 forints, helping knock Budapest's blue-chip index down 2 percent. text:

    * Budapest's new FX loan push has weighed on assets
    * Crown weak on central bank intervention risk
    WARSAW/PRAGUE, July 26 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint led


gains in central European currencies on Friday, lifted by optimism over the government's foreign currency loan plan, while the Czech crown weakened ahead of a central bank meeting next weak. Hungary's Prime Minister Victor Orban said he aimed to resolve the country's foreign currency mortgage problem without wrecking the financial system. The forint was up by 0.35 percent to 296.68 against the euro by 1311 GMT, easing slightly from the day's high of 295.94, and recovering from a one-month low of 298.1 hit on Thursday in shallow trade. "Concerns about the programme to help FX borrowers have to a certain extent abated and the forint has somewhat rebounded due to that," a Budapest-based currency dealer said. The market reacted nervously after the cabinet issued a statement on Wednesday saying it planned to talk to banks about a solution to help the many Hungarian households who took out foreign currency loans when the forint was stronger and are now struggling to repay them. Orban's administration has passed a swathe of controversial laws since coming to power three years ago that have unnerved investors, including nationalising pension assets and imposing the highest tax on banks in Europe. The Czech crown eased 0.17 percent to 25.934 a euro ahead of a central bank policy meeting next Thursday at which policymakers are seen discussing whether to intervene to weaken the currency now that interest rates are effectively at zero. All 16 analysts who responded to questions on interventions in a Reuters poll said the bank would hold fire but the board is split and minutes from the previous session in June showed several bankers called for immediately launching crown sales. News on Thursday that all board member would attend the meeting mean it could be more difficult for the dovish camp on the board to push through sales of the currency, analysts said. The Czech economy is trapped in almost a two-year long recession hit by austerity measures and weak demand for its exports. Some policymakers are concerned a recovery expected in the latter half of 2013 is not materialising. Elsewhere, the Polish zloty, the region's most liquid currency, inched up 0.17 percent to 4.238, but the move was well within Thursday's trading range. The zloty shrugged off news that parliament has approved a draft bill allowing for higher deficits to aid the sharply slowing economy.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-China leads stocks lower,  fx  loan plan rattles Hungarian assets
text:
LONDON, July 19 (Reuters) - Emerging market equities dipped on Friday, led by losses in Chinese property and financial stocks while Hungarian shares fell sharply on concern about government plans to modify the terms of private foreign currency loans.

Emerging markets have begun to stabilise after weeks of outflows and losses suffered on concern about an end to the U.S. monetary stimulus which has boosted demand for high-yielding assets.

In a much anticipated speech to Congress on Thursday, Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said it was too soon to make a call on dialling back quantitative easing in September.

Despite Friday's losses, stocks were heading for their second week of gains.

"We are in a strong dollar but low interest rates environment which will take some pressure off from emerging markets in the short term and we have indeed seen a bit of index recovery but the issues around China and corporate governance mean we probably have more underperformance to come," said John-Paul Smith, global emerging equities analyst at Deutsche Bank.

Chinese stocks fell for a third straight day due to declines in financial and property firms.

After the market close China announced it was relaxing controls on bank deposit rates, part of long-awaited interest rate reforms.

India's central bank likely stepped in via state-run banks again, dealers said, to prop up the rupee, which has fallen back to levels seen before the central bank moved on Monday to drain liquidity and push up short-term interest rates to defend the currency. A government bond auction on Friday would be a key test of the central bank strategy, with investors betting the sale would be a struggle.

Emerging equities dropped 0.5 percent, with Hungarian stocks falling more than 2 percent to their lowest in more than two weeks.

Hungary's OTP Bank Chief Executive Sandor Csanyi sold a big chunk of his shares in the bank on Thursday, driving OTP shares lower after two days of steep falls on government plans to intervene on foreign currency loan contracts.

Hungary's forint hit two-week lows against the euro .

Emerging market debt spreads widened by 1 basis point to 321 bps over U.S. Treasuries. Emerging debt spreads have been tightening in recent days after widening as much as 100 bps in June.

In the week leading to July 17, emerging market outflows continued. Equity funds saw $0.04 billion in outflows, while bond funds suffered $1.3 billion of outflows, according to banks citing EPFR data.

BUCHAREST/WARSAW, July 11 (Reuters) - Most emerging European currencies firmed against the euro on Thursday after the U.S. Federal Reserve said it will stick to an easy monetary policy for now, while the prospect of central bank intervention kept the Czech crown weak.

In Hungary, the state debt management agency sold 47 billion forints worth of bonds, with yields around 60 basis points lower compared to yields accepted at the previous tender.

Romania also successfully placed bonds on Thursday with healthy demand supported by the comments from the Fed that its stimulus programme would continue for a while yet.

Hungary's June inflation inched up to an annual rate of 1.9 percent, still not far off a 38-year low hit earlier this year. Central bank policymakers have signalled they had room to cut interest rates further, a move priced in by markets.

"The bank's room for manoeuvre will continue to be defined by the external environment and the extremely loose monetary policy pursued by major central banks," said Erste Bank's Orsolya Nyeste.

"There is no particular obstacle to a July rate cut as external market conditions have turned for the better since last month."

Central and eastern European assets have plunged since May when the Fed signalled it would begin to taper its monetary stimulus that had sent a flood of money into emerging Europe. But Fed chief Ben Bernanke said on Wednesday the stimulus would continue as inflation remained low and the unemployment rate high.

By 1416 GMT, the Hungarian forint was up 0.7 percent against the euro at 292.040. The Polish zloty and Romanian leu were each 0.2 percent up.

In Romania, where the leftist government is set to start talks next week on a new aid deal with the IMF and the central bank has started cutting interest rates, traders said there was renewed interest for longer-dated debt on the secondary market.

The Czech crown was 0.2 percent weaker. With rates at a record low 0.05 percent, the Czech central bank has said it could intervene in the market to weaken the crown if it needs to ease monetary policy further.

"While (the crown) has strengthened in recent weeks (because of the EUR/USD), the space for further crown gains is limited because of threats of central bank intervention," CSOB said.

Elsewhere in the region, Serbia's central bank kept its benchmark interest rate at 11 percent on Thursday, bucking market expectations for a third consecutive cut.

Serbia is among markets which have struggled recently as investors pull out on the view that the Fed will start withdrawing stimulus, making rate cuts in these countries riskier. The dinar was flat.

title: DJ Monetary Easing to Continue in Central Europe Next Week
text:
PRAGUE--Further monetary easing is likely in Central Europe next week with an expected lowering of interest rates in Poland, following a cut in Hungary and dovish talk of foreign exchange interventions in the Czech Republic.

In Warsaw, Poland's central bank is expected to cut its benchmark interest rates 0.25 percentage point to a new all-time low of 2.5%, all 18 analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires said.

The aim is to help the slowing economy regain momentum and to bring slowing inflation closer to the central bank's target of 2.5%, which is the midpoint in the wider 1.5% to 3.5% tolerance range.

The rate council has lowered borrowing costs by two percentage points since November 2012 as the economy nearly stagnated in the first quarter with annual growth of 0.5%, while inflation eased to 0.5% in May.

Originally some market participants saw a risk of a deeper interest rate cut but the recently weakening zloty has shifted expectations.

Since the rate council's early June meeting the zloty has weakened from 4.25 against the euro to 4.32 midday Friday.

"If you asked me a few weeks ago I would have said there is a risk of a 0.5 percentage point rate cut," Raiffeisen Bank economist Marta Petka-Zagajewska said. "However, with the zloty where it is I see a risk there will be no cut at all."

The cut in Poland would follow a similar move in Hungary, where the central bank cut the policy rate 25 basis points to 4.25% on June 25 amid an easing cycle that began in August 2012 in a bid to liven up its lackluster economy.

And would come as the Czech central bank, which has its benchmark rate at the historic low of 0.05%, on Thursday said the likelihood of launching an intervention to weaken the koruna is increasing as it foresees "no tangible inflationary risks."

As it has no more room to lower interest rates, the next available tool is the exchange rate.

"Risks to [the economy] are generally disinflationary; they are pointing towards the need for looser monetary conditions than is expected in [the bank's] forecasts," the central bank said without adding when a move may come.

In Prague, households are slowing returning to shops and spending, but the annual increase in retail sales posted in April is likely to be offset by a minor decrease in May.

The data will follow the early-Friday release of revised Czech gross domestic product data that showed household consumption contracted by a mild 0.5% annually in the first quarter and it actually increased by 1.7% on a quarterly basis in the period.

Households are spending more in step with the government increasing its spending by 1.2% on year and 1% on a quarterly basis in the first three months of this year.

text:
* Warsaw stocks lead decline with 3.1 pct drop


    * FX stabilises after sharp selloff on Wed
    * Hungary seen cutting rates on Tuesday
    * Serbian cbank intervening to stabilise dinar - FX dealers
    By Jason Hovet and Marcin Goettig
    PRAGUE/WARSAW, June 21 (Reuters) - The sell-off in central


European stocks continued on Friday as investors cut their exposure to riskier markets after the U.S. Federal Reserve signalled a gradual end to its monetary stimulus programme, while currencies and bonds mostly stabilised. Poland's benchmark index led the losses, dropping over 3 percent as it was dragged lower by deep falls in local heavyweight stocks such as KGHM, Europe's second biggest copper miner, and coal miner JSW KGHM fell a further 7 percent on Friday to 123 zlotys, bringing its drop over the week to 22 percent after the stock suffered from a slide in copper prices and a lower than expected dividend. Currencies were mostly steady, but Hungary's forint remained under pressure ahead of an expected rate cut next week. The region's most liquid currency, Poland's zloty , shed 0.3 percent, holding around Wednesday's levels. The Czech crown eased 0.1 percent. Dealers said the Serbian central bank sold about 20 million euros on Friday to stabilise the dinar. On Thursday the bank intervened in the market to sell about 30 million euros, dealers said. "Generally it is the Fed," said a Budapest-based dealer. "Positions are re-shaken, and that's normal. But people will continue to sit on cash and they will realize that they need to use it for something." Hungary's forint weakened by 0.7 percent, but held within Wednesday's range. Hungary's central bank is expected to cut rates again on Tuesday but may express concerns that the emerging markets sell-off has hit forint assets and signal that the bank's easing cycle could end soon, a Reuters poll showed. The currency dealer said the rate cuts could undermine the forint in the longer term, reducing the profits of investors holding the currency. "Of course the lower carry can be a problem to the forint in the longer term," the dealer said. Bond yields stabilised in Poland, but continued to rise in Hungary after the jump the previous day triggered by the Federal Reserve news, which also drove central European currencies down as much as 2 percent.

4 Apr 2013 06:58 EDT DJ  Hungary Central Bank to Ease SME Lending in Bid to Boost Growth

By Margit Feher and Veronika Gulyas

The Hungarian central bank Thursday announced measures to ease lending to small and medium-size companies in a bid to support economic recovery while not putting the bank's price stability mandate at risk, new Governor Gyorgy Matolcsy said Thursday.

"Central banks are actively taking part these days in jump-starting growth, just look at the European Central Bank. I have informed the European Union of the nature of the program," Matolcsy said at a press conference, his first since he was appointed to the post by Prime Minister Viktor Orban in early March.

The program may boost gross domestic product growth up to 0.7 percentage point, the central bank projects. The bank forecasts this year's growth at 0.5% and the government, which is facing parliamentary elections next year, targets 0.9% growth.

Financial markets will "find that the program is precisely targeted to support growth and limited in its size and duration. It's a growth-promoting program," Mr. Matolcsy said.

Mr. Matolcsy, a close political ally of Mr. Orban, previously was economy minister and the architect of Hungary's much criticized unorthodox economic policies since 2010.

The central bank program, if implemented fully, will reduce Hungary's mounting foreign-currency reserves, which totaled EUR35.89 billion ($46.02 billion) at the end of February, by up to EUR3 billion, he added. It will also increase the central bank's balance sheet by up to 500 billion forints ($2.12 billion), he said.

The first part of the lending program is a HUF250 billion facility to be offered to small and medium-size enterprises to provide them with relatively cheap loans. Under the facility, the central bank offers retail banks loans at an interest rate of 0%, while banks are allowed to charge a 2% interest rate to lend the funds on to the SMEs and are required to speed up the evaluation process of applicants.

The second part involves a HUF250 billion refinancing facility that allows SMEs to convert their foreign-currency denominated loans into forint loans at the prevailing forint exchange rate on financial markets.

The refinancing facility is also offered to retail banks at a 0% interest rate. The program will be finalized April 30 after discussions with the country's eight biggest banks, analysts and the country's chamber of commerce and industry.

Both loan measures are planned to run for a three-month test period, starting June 1, Mr. Matolcsy said.

The third part of the program is a cap on retail banks' stock of two-week loans from the central bank. The central bank's key policy rate is the interest it pays to retail banks on their two-week bonds. Retail banks buy the central bank's two-week bonds, which is the central bank's main tool to increase or reduce liquidity in the financial system, with their excess cash. The policy rate is currently at a record low of 5%, after March's 25-basis-point rate cut, the eighth successive monthly cut.

The central bank will cap the stock, which currently stands at a record high of HUF4.5 trillion, to HUF3.6 trillion, by offering foreign-exchange swaps to retail banks, using its foreign-currency reserves Mr. Matolcsy said. The measure is aimed at reducing Hungary's vulnerability, he added.

The top decision-making body of the central bank, the Monetary Policy Council, approved at an extraordinary meeting Thursday the economic policy of the government in "a unified view," Mr. Matolcsy said.

Having met the inflation goal and with financial stability in place, the National Bank of Hungary may now support the government's economic policy, in line with the Central Bank Act, Mr. Matolcsy said.

Inflation will be below or close to the central bank's 3% inflation target throughout the next two years, said MPC member Andrea Bartfai-Mager, who was also present at the briefing.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Czech crown eases before cbank meets, forint firms
text:
* Crown eases on renewed worry that cbank could intervene

* Forint extends gain as cbank did not announce radical measures

By Jason Hovet and Sandor Peto

PRAGUE/BUDAPEST, March 27 (Reuters) - The Czech crown lost ground on Wednesday amid some worries before Thursday's central bank meeting that the bank could give new signals of market interventions to weaken the currency.

Hungary's forint firmed, going against the direction of other assets in the European Union's emerging markets which fell as the euro was knocked by Italy's disappointing bond auction and bailout plans for Cyprus.

Central European equity markets were lower, led by Bucharest's main stock index .BETI> which dropped 1.1 percent.

Hungary's currency and bonds were resilient after the country's central bank refrained on Tuesday from radical easing measures that had been anticipated by some investors.

The forint extended gains posted after Tuesday's central bank meeting, at which the bank cut its base rate by a quarter point to a record low of 5 percent. It was bid at 303.65 to the euro at 1537 GMT, 0.2 percent firmer from Tuesday.

"Positioning helps the forint," one Budapest-based currency dealer said.

"Some investors had expected the central bank to announce some unorthodox ideas (to help the recession-hit economy), and that has not happened, and the statement was quite moderate," the dealer said, projecting a 303-305 range for the next days.

Early this month Prime Minister Viktor Orban picked close ally and former Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy to head the bank with a mandate to help the economy, sparking fears the bank

may implement unconventional measures that would hit the forint.

Central banks in the region have been cutting their interest rates in the past year to help economies hit by economic slowdown in their main export markets in the euro zone.

With Czech interest rates already at "technical zero", the central bank there has said interventions could be its next easing tool to help the contracting economy.

The weakening of the crown to a nine-month low in the past month reduced those chances, but concerns ahead of Thursday's policy meeting weighed on the currency again.

It eased by 0.1 percent to 25.75 against the euro.

"We still see global names buying EUR/CZK from 25.700 up to now. Central bank could be one reason for nerves," one Prague-based dealer said. "We are also going into the Easter holiday weekend."

Market participants said the crown could rebound, just as it did after the bank's meeting last month, if the bank does not give clear signals of market interventions to come.

Elsewhere, Poland's zloty was flat at 4.181 against the euro, while Romania's leu eased 0.2 percent to 4.417.

All three of central Europe's bigger former communist economies have been cutting rates steadily in a bid to bolster growth as most of the euro zone falters.

Only Romania, which meets on Thursday, has stayed on hold due to inflation pressures. Analysts do not expect loosening there until later in 2013.

title: CEE MARKETS 2-Hungarian forint slips after rate cut
text:
(Recasts, adds Hungarian rates, Czech intervention)

* Hungary cuts rates 25 bps, market awaits new cbank head

* Italy vote knocks other regional assets

* Crown eases after cbanker says more easing may be needed

By Marcin Goettig and Sam Cage

WARSAW/SOFIA, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint slipped on Tuesday after the central bank cut interest rates for the seventh meeting running, ahead of the appointment of a new governor expected to further expand stimulus for the economy.

An inconclusive Italian election result that hit the euro and a raft of European stock and bond markets, put broad pressure on currencies across the developing economies of the European Union's eastern wing.

Hungary, the region's most-indebted economy, has now hacked 175 basis points off base interest rates since August, when the divided Monetary Council began an easing cycle to aid the recession-hit economy.

Hit by expectations the bank will do more, and worries over a policy mix which has put off international investors, the forint has shed more than 1 percent so far this year. It was bid 0.2 percent lower at 294.65 per euro by 1500 GMT.

"We would not be surprised to see the currency weakening past 300 in the coming weeks," said Equilor analyst Gergely Gabler in Budapest.

The cut to 5.25 percent - a record low - had been largely priced in and markets already expect the premium for holding the forint to be cut to about 4.5 percent. But there is lingering concern that riskier monetary policy measures cooked up in government workshops could hit the forint if the central bank implements them.

The forint has been stable at 290-295 in recent weeks, but previously it fell on fears that the bank could limit commercial banks' access to its two-week bills, the main tool that drains liquidity from interbank markets.

Regional stock markets followed western European peers sharply lower, with the Budapest bourse leading losses with a 1.8 percent fall. Poland's zloty was the biggest foreign exchange loser, dropping 0.5 percent.

Dealers all blamed the turnaround in expectations for the Italian elections from more positive initial polls on Monday.

"The market is on a roller-coaster," said Bartlomiej Rostek, a currency trader at ING Bank Slaski. "Yesterday it seemed that we are in for further zloty gains and now we have a complete risk-off."

The Czech crown dipped to a day's low of 25.58 per euro after a board member said the central bank may still need to ease monetary policy further and foreign exchange would be the likely way to go. The currency later recovered some ground and was 0.2 percent lower on the day.

title: CEE MARKETS 3- Currencies  gain after EU clinches budget deal
text:
(Updates throughout)

* Deal means more EU funds to support region's investment

* CZK near 1-mth high as intervention risk seen lower

* Broad euro weakness also supports CEE currencies

By Sam Cage and Marcin Goettig

BUCHAREST/WARSAW, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Central European currencies gained on Friday, lifted by news that European leaders had reached a deal on the long-term budget, and the Czech crown hovered near a one-month high after the central bank sounded softer on currency interventions.

Stock markets were mixed, with Hungary's main stock index

dragged lower by a more than 4 percent drop in oil and gas group MOL after an Abu Dhabi energy firm sold shares.

There was relief that EU leaders had struck a budget deal as countries in central Europe rely on European Union structural funds to support public investments in infrastructure like roads, bridges and airports.

An impasse on the EU budget could stall the long-term investments, needed to spur growth in the region's weak economies.

Poland is the largest recipient of the funds, which have helped it avoid recession since 2008, the only country in the European Union to do so.

"The currencies gained somewhat after the news about the deal," said a Warsaw-based dealer.

The zloty gained 0.3 percent to 4.15 versus the euro by 1551 GMT. Hungary's forint rose 0.7 percent, while the Romanian leu added 0.1 percent.

Analysts said that a temporary reversal of the usual correlation between the euro/dollar rate and regional currencies could provide further support for the zloty.

"We are in an interesting period when the EUR/PLN rate is moving in lock step with the EUR/USD rate," said Miroslaw Budzicki, a strategist at Poland's largest lender PKO BP.

Most often a fall in the euro versus the dollar, usually driven by higher risk aversion, means losses for regional currencies versus the euro.

But currently the 30-day correlation between the EUR/PLN and the EUR/USD was the highest in 22 months, Reuters data showed, inverting the usual relationship.

Budzicki said that a likely continuation of the euro's slide, which was triggered by comments from ECB chief Mario Draghi on Thursday, meant that the zloty could gain more in the short term.

Draghi's comments that the exchange rate was important for growth and price stability were perceived by investors as a sign the bank could be willing to cut interest rates if euro appreciation continues.

"Additionally Polish rate cut expectations have been scaled back," Budzicki added.

The Polish central bank dropped the wording on further possible "monetary easing" from its statement after it cut rates on Wednesday for a fourth successive month, signaling that a pause in the easing cycle may be near.

CROWN FIRMS

The Czech crown rose 0.1 percent to 25.23 per euro, close to a one-month high hit the previous day after the central bank said interventions to weaken the currency looked "less urgent".

Analysts said the central bank could tolerate some strengthening but any strong firming beyond 25.20 or 25.00 could prompt it to step into the market to weaken the currency.

Polish bonds were stable, while their Hungarian counterparts gained following the forint's gains.

Societe Generale analysts recommended buying the Romanian leu, after its slide over the last three weeks from a one-year high against the euro hit in mid-January. The currency was flat on Friday.

title: ECB Weidmann: Condemns Political  Intervention  in Monetary Policy
text:
Governments across the world are intruding in the realm of monetary policy, risking the inflation-fighting achievements of past years and endangering economic stability, European Central Bank Governing Council member Jens Weidmann said Monday.

Mr. Weidmann, who also serves as the president of the German central bank, the Bundesbank, took aim specifically at the governments of Japan and Hungary, who in his words had "encroached" on the activity of their central bank.

Mr. Weidmann further warned against countries turning to the exchange rate as a political tool. He said a consequence of politicians meddling with central bankers, "whether intended or not, could lead to an increasingly politicized exchange rate. Until now, the international monetary system has come through the crisis without a race to devaluation, and I really hope that it stays that way."

"Questionable encroachments are already visible, for example in Hungary or Japan, where the governments are intervening heavily in the duties of the central banks, pressuring for a more aggressive monetary policy that threatens the end of central bank autonomy," said Mr. Weidmann according to the text of a speech to be delivered Monday evening at the headquarters of Deutsche Boerse AG (DB1.XE) and provided by the Bundesbank in advance.

Mr. Weidmann's remarks are also significant as it is relatively unusual for a central bank official to take issue publicly with the policies of other countries. The head of the Bundesbank also took a small swipe at activities on the other side of the Atlantic.

He said the recently agreed budget compromise in the United States to avoid the "fiscal cliff" is "not a sustainable solution to the fiscal problems." He added that raising the debt ceiling or delayed expenditure cuts "could indeed quickly lead to the next showdown. What is necessary here is more determined action in the common interest."

The Bundesbank--founded from the ashes of the Second World War--is widely viewed as an anchor of stability in Germany, an institution that citizens believe will maintain the value of hard-earned savings.

European policy makers have also increased pressure on the central bank to take on new tasks. For example, they are aiming to give the ECB some banking supervisory powers as part of a "banking union" on the continent. German observers are, however, worried that this will blur the banks' primary goal of keeping inflation just below 2% over the medium term. In his speech, Mr. Weidmann stressed that the creation of a banking union "shouldn't create new conflicts of interest that distract monetary policy from its primary goal of monetary stability."

There is also concern in Germany that European politicians have relied too heavily on central banks to solve the financial crisis at the expense of necessary fiscal reform. Mr. Weidmann said in a recent interview that monetary policy is like a drug in the sense that it "attacks the symptoms but does not solve the origins and also comes with risks and side effects."

Both Japan and Hungary have come under international scrutiny for alleged political meddling in monetary policy. In Japan, the country's central bank has come under pressure from newly-elected Prime Minister Shinzo Abe to ramp up money printing.

In Hungary, markets are worried that a new central bank governor, due to replace outgoing head Andras Simor, will follow the wishes of Prime Minister Viktor Orban and print money as a way to spark growth but the consequence of which is to weaken the currency.

title: CEE MARKETS 3-Foreign debt issue plan supports Hungary assets
text:
* Could be first Hungarian forex issue since 2011

* Currencies shrug off inflation, verbal interventions

(Releads, adds detail on Hungary and Poland inflation)

By Dagmara Leszkowicz and Sam Cage

WARSAW/BUCHAREST, Jan 15 (Reuters) - The prospect of a Hungarian foreign currency debt issue underpinned the country's assets on Tuesday and the forint and zloty shrugged off slowing inflation and efforts by officials to weaken currencies.

Emerging European currencies were mostly a touch higher despite inflation data that was bearish for Polish and Hungarian interest rates and a chorus of verbal intervention aimed at pressuring currencies to help export-driven economies.

Hungary mandated banks to arrange meetings with investors, which may lead to the first foreign currency issue of the junk-rated country since 2011, lending some support to the forint and local debt markets.

The forint rose 0.2 percent to 294.3 per euro by 1428 GMT and debt yields fell along the curve, with five-year paper trading at 5.75 percent.

"The government didn't say it in so many words but this will definitely be a new issue," one Budapest-based fixed income dealer said.

"We'll see what demand there will be but we can see there is both an opportunity and a need for an issuance here."

Lower inflation and the prospect of interest rate cuts have also pressured currencies, and the zloty and forint have both lost about 1 percent in 2013 after hefty gains last year.

In Hungary, inflation slowed to a one-year low of 5.0 percent in December, below analysts' average forecast, and a central banker said it could be close to its 3 percent target in the next two years due to government cuts in household energy prices.

PAUSE IN POLISH CUTS

Poland's inflation eased below the central bank's target for the first time in more than two years in December, strengthening the case for more interest rate cuts from the current 4 percent.

But last week's signal from Poland's central bank that it will pause its easing campaign to evaluate the state of the economy following three interest rate cuts is still underpinning the zloty and Polish bonds.

"We stick to our expectations of the main rate falling to 3 percent," said ING Bank Slaski economist Rafal Benecki. "The data is positive for the short end of the yield curve."

The zloty was a touch higher at 4.117 per euro. Elsewhere, the Czech crown lost 0.1 percent and Romania's leu was flat, though still close to a nine-month high hit last week due to the prospect of clinching a new International Monetary Fund deal.

title: INSIGHT-Orban to use Hungary  central bank  in battle for growth
text:
* New governor to bring riskier new policies -sources

* More rate cuts, unorthodox tools to boost growth likely

* Radical new measures could risk forint selloff

* Govt, central bank have been at odds over policy

By Krisztina Than and Sandor Peto

BUDAPEST, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has an ace up his sleeve as he tries to revive a recession-bound economy and secure his political future: soon he can take full control of a central bank which has long resisted his will.

By March Orban will pick a new National Bank governor who is likely to flood the economy with cheap credit using unconventional tools - the kind of measures that are controversial enough in giants such as the United States, let alone in a small emerging economy like Hungary's.

With Hungarians still feeling the effects of crisis and commercial banks reluctant to lend, central Europe's most indebted economy badly needs a boost and Orban has little time to lose. He faces parliamentary elections in 2014 and support for his right-wing Fidesz party is crumbling.

Orban is used to getting his way. Since coming to power in 2010, he has filled top public posts with Fidesz loyalists but the central bank has proved a tougher nut to crack.

Last year he tried to curb the bank's independence with new legislation, but had to backtrack on parts of the law under pressure from the European Union and European Central Bank.

Now Orban, whose unorthodox and sometimes unpredictable measures to lower the budget deficit have already drawn fire, has another chance to get his way at the central bank: Governor Andras Simor completes his six-year term on March 2.

Orban has yet to name a successor. However, several sources in central banking and politics told Reuters that the new governor is expected to be close to Fidesz and someone willing to pursue the kind of policies Simor has largely resisted: risky unconventional ideas on stimulating the economy which have been hammered out in government workshops.

Investors, worried that such action could upset Hungary's often volatile forint currency, want to know who will take the helm.

However, a central bank source expected the government to make the real decisions in future. "Markets assign too much significance to the person of the new governor. Monetary policy will not be decided here, but via remote control," the source said on condition of anonymity.

The new governor will serve for six years, well beyond the next elections. Fidesz still leads in opinion polls, but its support has dived to about 20 percent among all voters from over 50 percent of votes secured at the last election.

Sources told Reuters that whoever gets the job, the bank will embark on new measures to push more money into the economy. Options include channeling more funds to the banking sector to boost lending, buying government bonds on the secondary market and even reducing foreign currency reserves.

Orban's office declined comment. "The Prime Minister will make his nomination in appropriate time to allow a smooth transition at the governor's post," his press chief said in an emailed response to Reuters questions.

However, Economy Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy, one of Orban's closest allies, has made clear the new governor must cooperate more on turning recession into growth.

"The real turnaround will come because the central bank's leadership will be the number one strategic partner of the government," he wrote in the weekly Heti Valasz last month.

Matolcsy, the architect of the unorthodox budget policies such as Europe's highest bank tax and the effective nationalisation of private pension funds, is himself seen as a frontrunner to head the bank.

OFFSHORE KNIGHTS

Simor, a former commercial banker and local head of the international accountancy firm Deloitte, was appointed by a previous Socialist government in 2007. He came under fire from Fidesz for keeping interest rates high and doing too little to support growth.

The attacks have become personal, with Fidesz criticising Simor over investments he made in a Cyprus-based firm. Right after his landslide election victory in 2010, Orban said the central bank was "not a shelter for offshore knights".

Simor has withstood pressure to resign. Last month he said he had made policy suggestions to the government in the past two years but "received no answer". The government had asked Simor to consider tools used by major central banks in developed countries to boost growth.

So far the bank has taken only limited action. Last year it began offering two-year loans in exchange for collateral and buying mortgage bonds. However, this achieved little as demand for credit from Hungarian firms is very weak due to the state of the economy, and commercial banks have been holding onto the funds rather than lending them out.

Much larger, wealthier economies have suffered similar problems and central banks in some, notably the United States and Britain, have taken radical action to flood the banking system with funds in the hope of stimulating growth.

The Bank of Japan is also considering a major new wave of monetary easing, sources say, under heavy pressure from a new right-wing government.

However, such tactics are controversial. The ECB has refused to do anything that might push up euro zone inflation and some Federal Reserve policymakers have expressed concern about the longer-term effects of U.S. "quantitative easing".

In Hungary, a country of 10 million people, the central bank has said quantitative easing other than using liquidity-boosting instruments is risky in a vulnerable emerging economy.

Last year the forint was one of the best performing emerging market currencies but it has suffered a number of sharp drops since the global crisis of 2008 as investors took fright about government economic policies.

The central bank fears that radical measures could hurt the currency again. "Tools involving greater risk-taking by the central bank and government bond buying could further erode investor confidence and trigger a capital flight," it said in a 2012 study on the use of unconventional monetary policy tools.

Such objections are likely to be overruled once Simor leaves the bank, which has experienced political meddling from Hungarian governments of both the right and left in the past two decades, even though its independence is enshrined in law.

The question is how fast and deep the policy changes will be, and wobbles in the forint in the past few weeks signal growing uneasiness among investors.

"The strategic cooperation envisaged by Matolcsy means that the bank will have to support growth with all kinds of monetary stimulus measures," said Eszter Gargyan, an economist at Citigroup in Budapest.

"I don't think this has been fully priced in by markets and in case of aggressive measures we could see a bigger selloff in the forint in 2013. The question is how far they will go."

SLOW SPORTS

Orban, an avid soccer player, has likened monetary policy to a slow sport and he seems to have used the same tactics in gradually increasing his influence over the bank.

"Monetary policy belongs to the world of slow sports. If someone makes hasty moves there, that could create a situation in markets which has very serious consequences," he said in February 2011.

Later, Fidesz used its large parliamentary majority to appoint four new dovish policymakers who can outvote Simor and his two deputies on the Monetary Council.

One central bank source said dialogue between the two groups on the seven-member council was sparse, sayin [20130110 143839 GMT]

g that policy meetings more resembled "parallel monologues". The Governor and his deputies had found themselves isolated, with the new members calling the shots, especially in the past five months.

In August last year the four pushed through their first interest rate cut to support the economy, outvoting Simor and his deputies who wanted no change due to inflation and the risk of a forint fall. The newcomers have consistently rejected accusations of acting under government influence.

Four more rate cuts quickly followed, taking the bank's base rate to a two-year low of 5.75 percent by the end of last year without substantially weakening the currency, as a global hunt for higher yields boosted appetite for Hungarian assets.

With foreigners' Hungarian government bond holdings near record highs at 5 trillion forints ($22.49 billion), yields are now the lowest in years and markets expect further rate cuts.

However, Hungary's main interest rate remains the highest in the EU and the economy is barely clambering out of recession. GDP contracted 1.5 percent in annual terms in the third quarter of 2012 and economists forecast stagnation this year.

The government officially projects growth in 2013 but unemployment is at 10.6 percent, and negotiations with the IMF and EU on an international loan have collapsed. This weak growth outlook is likely to encourage Orban to take some policy risks.

Orban has said the main problem is that Hungarian businesses have no access to cheap credit. "We must hope that with good economic policy we'll be able to achieve a steady decrease in rates," he told public radio last month.

A second central bank insider said a wider array of economy-boosting policy measures were likely under the new governor. "I think the bank should adopt a much more liberal approach to helping corporate lending," the source said.

NEW IDEAS

Several sources familiar with the central bank's operations described a menu of new measures possible after Simor and one of his deputies, Ferenc Karvalits, leave their posts in March.

The bank will probably boost long-term financing to allow commercial banks to provide cheaper credit, possibly using state-owned banks, they say.

"There is no chapter in textbooks about what to do in small, open economies; the task at hand is to write that chapter," a third central bank source said, adding: "Anything that could help boost lending will be on the table."

Gyorgy Barcza, an analyst at Szazadveg think tank which is close to the government, said he believed Orban's administration understood the risks of a sharp currency fall.

"The central bank has some limited room to move, either by providing preferential refinancing loans to banks similar to the earlier 2-year loans, or by lending out parts of its foreign currency reserves to commercial banks," he said.

Barcza said this way banks could have access to cheaper foreign currency funding. This in turn could allow them to ease the payments of households which took out mortgage loans in euros and Swiss francs due to their lower interest rates, but have since struggled with repayments when the forint fell.

The central bank could also stop paying interest on commercial banks' mandatory reserves, sources and analysts said. Several sources said it might take a more active role in buying government bonds on the secondary market.

In the short term this could drive down yields but the measure could easily backfire if markets perceive it as monetary financing - under which a central bank effectively prints money to fund government spending.

So far the bank has used this tool only to ease market turbulence, the last time being during the 2008 crisis. "We see no disturbances on the fixed income market, hence no need to cure it," said Concorde Securities analyst Janos Samu.

One of the four dovish rate setters, Ferenc Gerhardt, has kept open this possibility. "It's not the National Bank of Hungary's task to intervene in the fixed income market and the need for this has not strengthened. But the possibility is there," he told the daily Magyar Nemzet last month.

Other ideas that came up in Hungarian media are a reduction in foreign currency reserves, and limiting funds that commercial banks can hold in two-week bills, the main tool the central bank uses to drain extra liquidity from interbank markets. Rumours of the bills idea pushed the forint to a five-month low versus the euro in late December, even though central bankers denied it.

Analysts have warned that if banks' access to the bills were

limited - in the hope that they would boost lending instead - they could opt to buy government bonds or move cash abroad, creating the risk of capital flight.

A relatively small reduction in the central bank's foreign currency reserves, which stood at 33.9 billion euros at the end of 2012, is conceivable through financing expiring debt from forint issues and then converting these funds at the bank.

But any deeper cut in the reserves, the main buffer to fend off forint falls, could provoke market turmoil. A source familiar with central bank matters said candidates for the governorship would experience reality if they got the job.

"They may have ideas like that on their minds, but as soon as they get there it will be clear that this cannot be done," the source said. ($1 = 222.3606 Hungarian forints)

title: DJ PMIs in Focus in First Week of New Year in Central Europe
text:
(This item will be published next Jan. 4, 2013.) 


 
   By Veronika Gulyas and Sean Carney 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BUDAPEST--Little macroeconomic data are scheduled for release in central Europe after Christmas and before New Year's Eve, but purchasing managers indexes for the manufacturing sector will be watched closely by investors in the first week of 2013.

PMI figures have been below the threshold level of 50 in Poland, the Czech republic and Hungary in recent months, indicating a contraction in activity, mainly a result of a slowing euro-zone economic growth.

In Prague, on the last day of 2012, the Czech central bank will release minutes from its Dec. 19 monetary policy meeting, when the central bank unanimously voted to keep interest rates at historic lows, with the benchmark rate at 0.05%. After the rate decision, the bank's governor, Miroslav Singer, said monetary policy easing was likely to take place in mid-2013 through intervention on foreign exchange markets.

Hungary's current account is expected to post a large surplus in the third quarter, up significantly from the previous quarter.

"The positive current-account balance is favorable for the currency, but the interest differential has been melting away since the summer, and thus the forint cannot really benefit from the improving external sentiment," Erste Bank economist Zoltan Arokszallasi said.

title: Hold RA CEE MARKETS 3-Leu highest since end-Aug as rally holds ground
text:
* Leu rally slows, hits highest since Aug 31

* Chances of Romanian political limbo ending cheer London

* Other FX little changed in illiquid trade

(Updates throughout)

By Jason Hovet and Dagmara Leszkowicz

PRAGUE/WARSAW, Dec 14 (Reuters) - The Romanian leu hit a 3-1/2-month high on Friday on rising hopes that an overwhelming victory for Prime Minister Victor Ponta in an election last weekend will stabilise policymaking.

Other currencies were little changed in a traditionally illiquid December trade, with investors abstaining from opening fresh positions ahead of the end of the year, traders say.

In Romania, Ponta has been locked in a bitter dispute with President Traian Basescu, who is reluctant to reappoint his leftist rival as prime minister. But he has limited options after Ponta's decisive win in Sunday's parliamentary poll.

With Basescu in Brussels for an EU summit, his absence is delaying talks on forming a new government, helping keep the country in limbo at a time when it is due to start negotiating a new International Monetary Fund deal.

The leu gained almost 1 percent on Thursday thanks to the hopes that political uncertainty will ease. The rally slowed on Friday, with the unit up 0.04 percent to 4.474 per euro by 1425 GMT, after hitting its highest level since Aug. 31 at 4.468.

"The expectation is for political stability and a new IMF deal," said a Bucharest-based trader.

The leu's gains came as other emerging European currencies stayed weak on prospects of looser monetary policy to stimulate economies suffering under austerity at home and a slowdown in trade with the crisis-hit euro zone.

In Romania, a spike in inflation and the political uncertainty caused by the feud between its president and prime minister has prevented rate setters from cutting interest rates to help an economy on the edge of recession.

Ponta's party won a two-thirds majority in Sunday's election. The party tried unsuccessfully in the summer to remove Basescu from office, a move criticised by the European Union.

Basescu said at the time he would never again appoint Ponta as prime minister and he has given no clear signal since the election. Analysts say he may try to split Ponta's alliance of leftists, liberals and conservatives.

"More positive price action could come in the near term but the longer-term picture remains murky," ING analyst Vlad Muscalu said in a note.

Societe Generale, in a regular weekly emerging markets note, said it was more positive on the leu, the only unit in the region to have lost ground this year. The French bank said it had closed a long euro position against the leu.

RATE CUTS NEARER

The Polish zloty and Hungarian forint are among the best-performing currencies in the world this year with gains of around 9 and 11 percent, respectively.

But the two currencies are down up to 3 percent since a rally sparked by yield-chasers taking advantage of liquidity measures from global central banks started to fizzle in August, when expectations of easier monetary policy gained ground.

The forint, and Czech crown were mostly steady on Friday while Poland's zloty edged some 0.1 percent higher.

"The market is very illiquid now and a higher volatility - if such one appears - is not related with currencies' fundamentals," said Piotr Kalisz, head of CEE Economics at Citibank Handlowy.

"But prospects of a sharper slowdown will probably push currencies lower as soon as the first quarter of next year and we expect the zloty to weaken to around 4.3," he added.

Hungary's central bank meets next week, while Czech rate setters are also due to meet on policy. But with rates already near zero in the latter, markets are looking for signals on when they might opt for currency intervention as a next easing tool.

"The CZK will underperform on the back of the weak growth outlook and risks of central bank FX intervention," Societe Generale said.

Most are counting on Hungary's central bank (NBH) to continue an easing cycle by reducing its base rate a quarter of a percentage point to 5.75 percent.

"It seems apparent that the doves on the MPC are more or less in full control of monetary policy," Danske Bank said.

In Poland, the central bank has started its easing cycle last month, cutting borrowing costs twice since then to 4.25 percent and the market widely expect another interest rate cut as soon as next month.

text:
TODAY'S CALENDAR 
Local/GMT 
1200/1400 Hungary central bank minutes 
 

Hungary's central bank Wednesday will publish the minutes of its September rate-settting meeting at which the monetary policy board surprised markets and eased monetary policy.

Ahead of the vote, analysts mostly expected no change to policy, but the central bank made its second consecutive 25 basis-points interest-rate cut that brought the benchmark rate to 6.50%.

Rate setters have already revealed that the vote, just as the previous vote in August, passed by a four to three majority. In the previous vote, the newer, dovish members outvoted the central bank's governor and his two deputies who then opted to keep the rate unchanged.

The minutes can nonetheless provide further indication about the short-term outlook for monetary policy in Hungary and may show whether Hungary will join the Czech central bank in verbally intervening on markets to ease recent currency gains.

Final readings of first quarter gross domestic product data in the Czech Republic and Hungary are due Friday, along with Czech May jobless reading and Hungary's foreign trade balance in April.

In Prague, the revised GDP reading is expected to be little changed from the preliminary first-quarter reading, which came in worse-than-expected with contractions of 1% in both annual and quarterly terms.

Dalimil Vyskovsky, a fixed-income trader at Komercni Banka in Prague, said the sharp decline in the flash reading was puzzling and said the bond market will be closely watching Friday for any revisions.

The economic growth data is likely to play a larger-than-normal role in the Czech central bank's monetary policy decision later this month, Mr. Vyskovsky said.

Any upswing in Czech May unemployment, which is expected at 8.2% from April's 8.4%, will add to pressure for the central bank to cut interest rates on June 28, which would be the first change to monetary policy in more than two years, analysts said.

In Budapest, investors are eying Hungary's detailed gross domestic product data to capture which factor pulled Hungary's economy into recession in early 2012.

Preliminary GDP data showed a 0.7% contraction in unadjusted terms, mainly due to a plunge in construction in February and March, as well as on further declining consumption and investments, Takarekbank said.

title: RESEARCH ALERT-Wider Hungary forint band unlikely.
text:
BUDAPEST, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Hungary will leave the forint's 4.5-percent-wide intervention band unchanged in the short-term, brokerage Bankar said on Tuesday, taking issue with a country update by investment bank Warburg Dillon Read. 

 Warburg said earlier on Tuesday that it expected the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) to widen the flotation band to 10 or 15 percent in an unforced move at the beginning of 1999. 

 Such a measure would give the NBH more flexibility in its daily operations and reduce the vulnerability of the forint to speculative attacks, London-based Warburg analysts said in the report. 

 Laszlo Makay, analyst at Hungarian brokerage Bankar, said a widening of the band would not be reasonable in the near term and could be much smaller than 10-15 percent. 

 "The Hungarian currency is currently strengthening within the band due to the renewed confidence in Hungary by foreign investors, so there is no need for any change," he said. 

 The forint ended at a new 10-week high at 0.2 percent below parity on Tuesday, boosted by a slow but steady capital inflow after heavy withdrawals in the wake of Russia's financial crisis. 

 Makay said the central bank had suggested in its monetary policy guidelines that the forint band might be widened only if inflation drops below 10 percent and stays there. 

 Inflation ran at 12.5 percent in September.
