title: Hungary weathers Russia storm, finance troika says.
text:
BUDAPEST, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The troika of officials running Hungary's economy said on Friday the country has had to adjust to the Russian crisis but will weather the storm. 

 "I think the most critical part of the process is over," National Bank of Hungary President Gyorgy Suranyi told an economic forum in Budapest, referring to the bank's decision earlier this week to reverse a longterm downward trend and hike key repo interest rates by 100 basis points each. 

 The bank acted to prop up the forint after foreign investors cashed in their holdings on the Budapest bourse, partly to cover losses in Russia, and bond yields rose to some two or three percentage points above the NBH's own issues. 

 But Suranyi, joined by Finance Minister Zsigmond Jarai and Economics Minister Attila Chikan, said the bank's foreign exchange holdings had been barely dented, standing now at $8.8 billion, and he had detected an easing on the bonds market. 

 "Yesterday in the market we saw even a slight decrease in bonds that mature in more than one year," Suranyi said. 

 Jarai said the impact of the Russian crisis was having an effect on Hungary's economy but he still expected a GDP growth rate of five percent this year. 

 "Russia will influence the Hungarian economy, but we still believe five percent growth is a real expectation for Hungary because of its dependence on the European Union market," Jarai said. 

 "Two months ago we were talking about five to six percent growth, but now we are talking about five percent - so we go down a bit," Jarai told the forum sponsored by Fortune Magazine. 

 He added that the government was determined to maintain budget discipline and would not spend beyond already forecast budget deficits. 

 He also said Hungary's bourse, which dropped more than 40 percent this year, had been hurt because "unfortunately, in the mind of investors Hungary is still part of the Russian empire". 

 "But this is not the case: we are almost part of the European Union and not dependent on Russia," he said. 

 Suranyi said there was no immediate need for any widening in the intervention band or any change in Hungary's crawling peg devaluation system, which combats inflation by ratcheting down the currency at a rate of 0.7 percent a month. 

 "There is no pressure at all on the forint, which means that the forint exchange rate system is not only in line with expectations of market players, but is also in line with our sustainability objectives," he said. 

 He added that a cut in U.S. interest rates, which is widely anticipated in global markets following Senate testimony this week by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, should be beneficial for Hungary. 

 "If it has any direct impact, then it would rather bring down Hungarian rates or at least would leave them unchanged, but in no way does it mean an upward pressure," Suranyi said. 

 "So I do not think it would have any unfavourable impact, on the contrary I think if it has any effect it would be favourable." 

 Suranyi showed no sympathy for anyone who had speculated against the forint, saying a shortage of forints in the market should be relieved after speculators close out futures positions. 

 "There are no real signs of speculation against the forint ...and those who did are closing out their positions," he said. 

 "...This temporary liquidity shortage is due to the fact that speculators have to close their futures positions, but we do not think the National Bank should help speculators reduce their losses," he said. 

 "I do not think that it would make sense for the central bank to pump extra liquidity into the system, even temporarily, although there are several tools in the hands of the National Bank for such a step."

 budapest.newsroom@reuter.com)).

title: Hungary  forex  reserves $8.8 bln - c.bank.

title: Hungary NBH says economy weathering Russian crisis.
text:
BUDAPEST, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Central bank governor Gyorgy Suranyi said on Tuesday that Hungary's economy was weathering the Russian storm without the need for any major adjustments. 

 Suranyi, in a news conference and separate interview with Reuters Television, said no major actions were needed to protect the forint from outflows of investor capital and said Hungary might beat year-end inflation targets, though next year's GDP performance could suffer if global trends continue. 

 Analysts mostly applauded his statements as helping to dispel some negative speculation about the state of the Hungarian economy in the midst of global market turmoil. 

 "It's not so much news as a psychological announcement," said Norbert Toth, analyst at ING Barings in Budapest. 

 Suranyi quashed recent market speculation that the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) might widen its currency intervention band, which allows the forint to float in a 4.5 percent range against a basket of dollars and marks. 

 "I rule out the possibility of widening of the band because for the time being it might create depreciation in a wider band and any depreciation is not reasonable for the time being," Suranyi said. 

 He said a "nominal" hike in interest rates was a more likely option to prop up the forint, hit by a wave of foreign investors liquidating their Hungarian share portfolios. 

 He acknowledged there was pressure on the forint but denied that the amount withdrawn had caused a significant dent in the NBH's foreign exchange reserves of more than $9 billion. 

 "We would speak about a couple of tens of millions of dollars (spent on active intervention)," he said. 

 Suranyi said the Hungarian economy remained on target for reducing inflation, one of Hungary's persistent problems. He said the bank might be able to lower its year-end CPI target to 13 percent year on year for December, from the current forecast of between 13 and 14 percent. 

 "We cannot exclude a downward modification of the inflation target for the current year," he said. 

 He also lent his support to the government's moves to cut the crawling peg currency devaluator, which ratchets down the value of the forint on a monthly basis. 

 The government has announced that the peg will be reduced to 0.7 percent from 0.8 percent on October 1 and has mooted a further cut to 0.6 percent is likely for January. 

 "We have a good chance for a (further) cut in the crawl from the beginning of next year," Suranyi said, noting the prerequisite for doing so was "responsible, tight fiscal policy". 

 Suranyi said Hungary might have to cut its 1999 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth target by one percentage point to 4.5 percent if negative global trends emanating from Russia, Asia and Latin American continue. 

 But he said that it was time for the investment community to stop lumping Poland, Hungary and Czech Republic, all three of which will enter NATO this year and are expected to join the EU early next century, with other emerging market countries. 

 "I would like to challenge this categorisation," he said, adding that the economic performance and the institutional and legal structures of the three countries were "entirely different from so-called emerging markets". 

 Istvan Racz, analyst for Credit Suisse/First Boston, said that the NBH seemed to be handling the capital outflows without too much difficult and agreed with Suranyi that Hungary was only moderately affected by the Russian crisis. 

 "What he said on the general state of the economy I would fully agree to," Racz said. 

 ((Michael Roddy, Budapest newsroom ++ 36 1 327 4040 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Hungary  will not widen  currency intervention  band.

 "I rule out the possibility of widening of the band because for the time being it might create depreciation in a wider band and any depreciation is not reasonable for the time being," Suranyi told Reuters Television in a telephone interview. 

 There has been widespread speculation in recent weeks that the bank might widen the band, which allows the forint to float against a basket of marks and dollars, in response to foreign investors cashing in their Hungarian shares and withdrawing from the Hungarian market. 

 Suranyi said depreciating the currency was "really not required by any economic indicator and it would create a pressure on inflation as well". 

 "If there is a need for adjustment it is rather the interest rate and - if it is a longer term development, I mean if the outlook has to be revised on the medium and long term - then there is a need rather for a fiscal than an exchange rate adjustment," Suranyi said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Hungary, Poland swim vs  FX  tide.
text:
LONDON, Sept 10 (Reuters) - Two central European countries are swimming against the tide of devaluation, rumour and currency collapse sweeping the emerging markets. 

 Analysts say by cutting their crawling devaluation rates, the pace of currency depreciation which compensates for domestic inflation, Poland and Hungary are keeping a firm eye on their own economic fundamentals - especially slowing inflation. 

 "If you look at these countries in terms of fundamentals, they are several leagues higher than Russia and most of the Asian countries," said Nigel Rendell, emerging markets strategist at Santander Investment Bank in London. 

 But such confident gestures could backfire if they are aimed purely at countering market bearishness, the analysts added. 

 "Trying to outwit the market is a dangerous game to play for a central bank or finance ministry," Rendell said. 

 Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban said this week the decision to ease the pace of the forint's monthly crawling devaluation to 0.7 percent from 0.8 percent from October 1 was aimed partly at fending off adverse market speculation. 

 But analysts said emerging market sentiment was currently so jittery that any mention of devaluation, even if accompanied by concrete moves to the contrary, risked attracting exactly the kind of speculative attention it sought to avoid. 

 "As a statement, it's not the one they should have made," said Andrew Kenningham, an emerging markets analyst at Merrill Lynch in London. 

 The announcement lent little support to the forint, which continues to languish at the weakest end of Hungary's 4.5 percent wide intervention band. On Thursday morning it stood 2.22 percent below its target central parity. 

 Analysts said the central bank might be forced to widen the trading band, although it was unlikely to go back on its decision to slow the devaluation rate of the target parity because of the negative signal that would give. 

 News on Wednesday that Poland's Monetary Policy Council (RPP) was slowing the zloty devaluation rate to 0.5 percent a month from 0.65 percent, and cutting a key interest rate by one percentage point, also had a defiant ring. 

 "It is high time that foreign capital adjusts to what is happening in Poland," RPP member Boguslav Grabowski told reporters. 

 The Polish moves, the latest in a series of steps in recent months to slow the zloty's downward crawl and cut rates, have won broad market approval and followed indications that consumer prices fell for a second consecutive month in August. 

 The zloty surged nearly one percentage point on Thursday to 4.71 percent above its parity, set daily by the central bank against a basket of five Western currencies. 

 Analysts said Poland was particularly insulated from the risk of sudden outflows of investment capital. 

 Only about $4 billion of foreign "hot money" was left in Poland - $1.5 billion in the Treasuries market and $2.5 billion in equities - against foreign exchange reserves of $27 billion, Kenningham said. 

 In contrast, hot money equalled 60 percent of reserves in Hungary. But Hungary's balance of payments was relatively strong, with a current-account deficit only half the size of foreign direct investment in the country, Kenningham added. 

 Analysts say Poland and Hungary are at or near the top of the emerging markets pile where fundamentals are concerned. 

 Both countries have seen big falls in inflation in the past few years, and have sensible and stable fiscal policies. Both also have relatively limited formal trade exposure to Russia. 

 Tim Ash, an economist at West Merchant bank in London, said Poland's current account remained vulnerable to Russian fallout because of previously high levels of informal "suitcase trade" - Russians buying cheap Polish goods for resale at home. 

 "There was definitely scope for interest rate cuts, but the loss of the suitcase trade makes cutting the crawl rather strange," he said. 

 Sluggish second-quarter growth in Germany, a more important trading partner for both countries, could also weigh on the Polish and Hungarian economies, Ash added. Germany's annual gross domestic product grew in the quarter by just 1.7 percent year-on-year. 

 Analysts said another major risk remained - the possibility that devaluations elsewhere could spark a further round of emerging market currency sell-offs in which rational fundamentals took a back seat. 

 "If we see another swipe at emerging market currencies I think all bets for Central Europe would probably be off," Rendell said. ((London Newsroom +44 171 542 6414, fax 583 7239, uk.emergingmarkets.news@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Hungary minister says economy sound amid chaos.
text:
BUDAPEST, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Hungarian Minister of Economy Attila Chikan said on Thursday that the economy remained sound amid global turmoil and urged investors to distinguish among emerging market countries. 

 "Investors still tend to lump us together too much," Chikan said at a news conference. "They must learn to differentiate." 

 Chikan said that despite some pressure on the forint, which has been hit by investors withdrawing money from the stock market to cover losses elsewhere, the central bank had ample reserves. 

 "The National Bank is sticking on its exchange policy and they are ready to intervene if necessary," Chikan said. 

 "Hungary has ample foreign currency reserves," he added, referring to central bank reserves estimated at some $9 billion. 

 The central bank was in the foreign exchange market on two days last week as the Hungarian bourse slipped to near 17-month lows, but traders have said the bank's total dollar outlay was not more than about $100 million. 

 Despite the forint being buffeted by the Russian crisis, Hungary plans to go ahead with further cuts in the crawling peg devaluation system that reduces the value of the forint on a monthly basis, Chikan said. 

 "We would like to continue the decrease of the devalution rate of the forint," Chikan said. "Our plan is, if nothing dramatic happens, then the first of January will see another 0.1 percent decrease." 

 Hungary introduced a monthly crawling peg devaluator in 1995 designed to ratchet down then-rampant inflation. The devaluator stands at 0.8 percent but the government has already announced that it will be cut to 0.7 percent on October 1. 

 Chikan said he saw no immediate reason to revise downwards government Gross Domestic Product growth projections of five to 5.5 percent in 1999. 

 The government's forecast had been based on the assumption of three percent growth in Western Europe, he said. 

 Only if the growth projections for Western Europe, which consumes almost 80 percent of Hungarian exports, changed substantially would Hungary have to revise its forecasts, he said. 

 "However, I have to say that when we talked privately...five percent was the lower limit of the growth projection," Chikan said. "Maybe it won't be higher, but we hope that it will not be lower." 

 Earlier, Credit Suisse First Boston said it expected Hungarian GDP growth may be slightly below the government target of at least five percent in 1999 due to the Russian crisis. 

 "The growth target is probably too optimistic - growth is more likely to be 4-4.5 percent in view of the Russian crisis," CSFB said in a weekly update on European emerging markets.

title: Hungary move to boost confidence in forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, Aug 31 (Reuters) - Hungary's decision to slow the devaluation of its forint amid capital outflows caused by the Russian crisis was unexpected but supported by economic fundamentals, analysts said on Monday. 

 The cabinet decided on Saturday to cut to 0.7 percent from 0.8 percent the forint's monthly devaluation rate - a regime in place since 1995 to curb runaway inflation at that time. The change will take effect on October 1. 

 Analysts said the measure could boost confidence in the forint, which has taken a beating in the Russian crisis, prompting the National Bank of Hungary to intervene for an unprecedented three times in one day last week. 

 "I had not expected this measure, but it has not surprised me and I think it is a very good move," said Attila Torok of Postabank Securities. 

 The forint depreciated more than two percent in the past few weeks as foreign investors sold Hungarian shares and bonds and withdrew the proceeds to cover losses suffered in Russia. 

 The forint approached the weakest point of the 4.5-percent-wide intervention band several times last week but was turned back by NBH interventions. 

 On Monday, the forint opened stronger against the NBH currency basket, at 1.5 percent below parity, up from Friday's close of 1.7 percent below midline. 

 Analysts said the NBH interventions were successful, although they had a mostly psychological impact because the total amount spent was estimated at only $100 million. 

 They said the joint decision by the government and the central bank to cut the depreciation rate would help to undercut widespread speculation of higher interest rates or a widening of the forint's flotation band. 

 The latter measures could decrease pressure on the forint temporarily, but would seriously undermine confidence in the exchange rate regime and monetary policy, analysts said. 

 "It would have been a serious mistake to widen the flotation band or devalue the forint as it would have seemed to justify speculation (against the forint)," Torok said. 

 Hungary introduced its crawling peg devaluation regime in March 1995, reducing speculation against the forint and keeping it at the strong end of of the intervention band for most of the past three years. 

 The monthly devalution rate has been reduced incrementally to 0.8 percent from the original 1.9 percent. 

 The decision on a further cut in the rate would strengthen confidence in the forint, analysts said. 

 "On the one hand, this measure increases real interest rate yields (on government securities) to foreigners," said Gergely Forian Szabo of K&H Brokerhaz. 

 "On the other hand, it strengthens confidence." 

 Analysts said the move was justified by strong economic fundamentals and a high level of foreign currency reserves, which amount to $9 billion. 

 "The move will obviously have a reassuring impact on investors and make them think whether it is worth mixing Hungary with Russia," Torok said. 

 Torok estimated that foreigners held Hungarian bonds worth $1.5 billion and shares worth about $2 billion, with the total figure remaining well below foreign currency reserves. 

 In the longer term, the forint was expected to regain some ground, but analysts said it was unlikely to return to the central bank's resistance level at the strong end of the band.

text:
BUDAPEST, Aug 28 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) intervention to support the forint on Friday was an inexpensive way to show investors that it will defend the Hungarian currency, analysts said. 

 "This is the best strategy possible right now," said Zoltan Kurali, analyst at BNP-Dresdner Securities in Budapest, estimating the intervention had cost $50 million. 

 He said the moves protected the forint against outflows of speculative money from Hungary. 

 "It is not huge in the greater scheme of things," said John Lomax, analyst at HSBC Investment Services, referring to the size of the intervention. "Hungary clearly has plenty of reserves to cope with that." 

 Dealers said the central bank intervened three times in morning trade when the forint fell to about 2.0 percent below parity, still within the central bank's 4.5-percent-wide intervention band. 

 The NBH stepped in again in the afternoon. 

 The measures bolstered the forint to finish at 1.7 percent below parity, compared with Thursday's close of two percent below midline. 

 "They didn't want to wait until it would be too late or too costly to protect the currency," said Peter Bihari, analyst at Budapest Bank. 

 Dealers estimated the day's currency sales by the central bank at up to $100 million. 

 The moves may not be enough, however, to prevent a forint currency crisis, analysts said. 

 "A lot depends on how the situation in Russia develops," said Lomax. "If events get materially worse, then there is a very real chance of a currency crisis in Hungary." 

 The forint was among the currencies which suffered from Russia's financial crisis although the government and analysts have said Hungarian business was not closely tied to Russia. 

 The forint fell to record lows this week as foreign investors withdrew funds from Hungarian stocks and bonds to cover losses they suffered amid Russia's crisis. 

 The Budapest Stock Exchange's BUX index closed at 5,167.71 points on Friday, down by 300.25 points from Thursday and by 42.7 percent below its all-time high reached on April 23. 

 Government securities yields have been rising this month and continued to do so on Friday, with the Government Debt Management Agency's benchmark yields rising by between 58 and 112 basis points. 

 Traders said the NBH declared the result of its one-year bonds' auction unvalid on Friday, probably to avoid an excessive rise in yields on the securities.

title: WRAP/Emerging Mkts Fall -2: Russia Rebound Unconvincing
text:
Russian stocks rebounded slightly Friday from dramatic falls earlier in the week, but traders cautioned that the move was exaggerated by the fact that volume has dried up to a trickle. 

 The Russian Trading System index closed up 5.6% at 66.77 points from Thursday's 63.2 points. But overall volume was less than $2.2 million, and market participants said the overall mood remained grim. 

 The ruble (RUR) also rebounded slightly, and traders said interbank quotes for the dollar ranged from RUR10 to RUR13, compared with quotes of RUR12 to RUR14 on Thursday. However, the central bank later announced its official rate for the currency was RUR7.905 per dollar. 

 The bounce in Russia didn't spill over to most other emerging markets. Polish shares plummeted to their lowest level for more than two years as foreign investors continued to flee the market. Most stocks fell by the daily allowable maximum of 10%. Market participants said the market has room to fall further. 

 "We haven't reached the lowest levels yet," said Andreas Roithner, salesman at Raiffeisen Capital & Investment Polska. "There are no support levels anymore, there is free fall. At the moment, everybody is trying to get out." 

 The zloty (PLN) closed sharply lower, with the dollar fixed at PLN3.8150, up from Thursday's fixing of PLN3.7950. However, volumes on both the share and foreign exchange markets were low. 

 That was in contrast to Hungary, where volume on the stock market remained heavy at 21 billion forints (HUF) as the Budapest Stock Exchange's BUX index closed at 5167.71, 5.5% down on the day.

title: WRAP: Emerging Mkts Shares,  Currencies  Tumble On Russia
text:
LONDON (Dow Jones)--With no end to Russia's economic crisis in sight, Eastern European and African stock markets look set to continue to fall after sustaining more heavy losses Friday. Currencies are also falling, with central banks intervening to limit the damage. 

 As shares on the Budapest Stock Exchange fell 12% at the opening following declines of 14% Thursday, the National Bank of Hungaryintervened twice in the foreign exchange market to stabilize the forint (HUF). 

 "It's complete panic selling," said John Barnett, equities analyst at Raiffeisen Securities & Investment in Budapest. Asked how far the market could drop, he said, "It's impossible to say at this point." 

 The Turkish central bank intervened on three occasions to support the lira (TRL) as shares fell 5.5% following Thursday's 13% decline. The country's financial markets weren't comforted by assurances from Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz that the government will stick to monetary policy targets agreed to with the International Monetary Fund, and won't go on a spending spree ahead of elections in April. 

 Russia's share market was relatively stable, down just 1.25%, or 0.79 of a point, to 62.41 points following a string of heavy declines in recent sessions. 

 However, concerns over the future of the country's economy mounted as details of Prime Minister-Designate Victor Chernomyrdin's economic policy began to emerge. As part of a plan to be presented to parliament Monday, the prime minister is likely to propose printing rubles to meet wage arrears and shore up the country's banks, as well as re-nationalization of strategic industries.

text:

title: FOCUS-Hungarian c.bank acts, East  currencies  lurch.
text:
PRAGUE, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The Hungarian central bank intervened to support the forint as eastern European currencies battled a wave of volatility and investor nerves triggered by uncertainty over Russia's debt restructuring deal. 

 The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said it intervened on the foreign exchange market to reduce forint fluctuations that it said were unjustified by domestic economic fundamentals. 

 "The main reason for the current intervention was to soothe the exaggerated exchange rate movements unjustified by macroeconomic indicators," NBH managing director Adam Farkas told Reuters. 

 Dealers said the intervention came when the forint traded at around 1.5 to 1.6 percent below parity, a safe distance from the weaker end of the intervention band. At the time of the intervention the forint traded at between 226.30 and 226.50 to the dollar, and the move pushed it up to around 226.00. 

 The forint closed at 226.30/80, compared to Tuesday's close at 225.20/40, while against the basket it finished at around 1.40 percent below parity as compared to Tuesday's close at 1.15 percent under the midrange. 

 Ukraine's hryvnia was also hit hard closing at 2.2491 per dollar on the republic's Interbank Currency Exchange, down from 2.2485 on Tuesday and just under its trade band ceiling. 

 The Polish zloty and the Czech and Slovak crowns also lost ground throughout the day, but traders said that while market sentiment overall was bearish, the central European currencies should weather the storm in the end on strong fundamentals. 

 "The debt deal is fairly bad, but this was expected. Confirmation the deal is going through caused a slight correction in eastern European currencies, but now markets such as Poland and the Czech Republic should concentrate on their own fundamentals," said Rob Taylor, a trader at Nomura. 

 "I can see further weakening ahead, but I can't see any more contagion unless we have a huge devaluation of the rouble, which is likely to be the fear at the moment due to MICEX trading being suspended today," he added. 

 Late on Tuesday Russia announced details of a plan to restructure $40 billion of short-term domestic debt into longer-term paper. The plan aims to cut the cost of servicing the state's domestic debt. 

 Analysts said the plan was an effective default and left unanswered many crucial questions that could hit investor confidence in Russia for years to come. 

 "As far as the weakening (in eastern Europe) today, that has been on the back of the default in Russia and just a confirmation of it, we shouldn't expect things to spiral out of control from here unless things get worse on the devaluation side on Russia," said another London-based currency trader. 

 The rouble slumped against the German mark on the main currency exchange after the central bank voided dollar trades and said it would not set a dollar rate for the day. It was fixed at 7.6 marks per dollar versus 4.4995 the previous day. 

 The zloty closed at 0.94/0.23 percent, stronger than parity, against Tuesday's 2.83/2.56 and the opening 0.40/-0.40 percent. The Czech crown also eased to around 18.64 against the mark from an opening around 18.345. 

 "The crown is following the zloty and rouble lower, but on a much smaller scale. There are still questions over the Russia deal but it doesn't effect the Czech crown that directly," said Breta Tichanek, a trader at ING Barings . 

 The Slovak crown eased slightly against its mark/dollar basket but dealers said the move came on local selling rather than on negative sentiment from Russia. 

 However, the continued uncertainty sparked by the Russian financial crisis once again affected the Slovak money market where interest rates shot up in nervous trade. One-day interbank rates rose to 26/27 percent, bid/offer, on Wednesday from Tuesday's 16/16.5 percent. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: INSTANT VIEW -  Hungary  c.bank forint  intervention .
text:
BUDAPEST, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) intervened repeatedly on Wednesday to protect the national currency from what it said were swings "unjustified by macroeconomic indicators. 

 Following are analysts' comments. 

 PETER BIHARI, BUDAPEST BANK, BUDAPEST 

 "I think it has less of a financial explanation, and it was more to calm investors' minds and to demonstrate the central bank's commitment (towards the forint)." 

 "The central bank governor stated repeatedly during the last few days that if the need arises, the NBH would intervene to protect the forint. The move was probably (intended to) demonstrate that these were not just words." 

 NIGEL RENDELL, SANTANDER INVESTMENT BANK, LONDON 

 "I think it's a direct result of what's going on in Russia and other emerging markets. All emerging currencies seemed to be under pressure and several central banks have been intervening to protect their currencies." 

 "I think Hungary intervened largely just to try to keep things on an even keel. I don't think there is anything more sort of sinister than that."

 "I have heard that it was only a small amount. The central bank wanted to reassure the market that it is there and is ready to protect the forint. 

 "There is no attack against the forint, it is only that foreigners reallocating their portfolio withdraw funds, partly due to the Russian events. 

 "The NBH could reassure the market more easily if it declared it would not widen the (4.5 percent wide) intervention band until December. Fears that the band would be widened hinder speculation (in favour of the forint) return to the market." ((Budapest newsroom +36 1 327-4047 budapest.newsoom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS- Hungary  c.bank  intervenes  to calm markets.
text:
BUDAPEST, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) intervened repeatedly on the interbank currency market on Wednesday, in a step which analysts said was aimed at reassuring investors hit by emerging market jitters. 

 "I think it has less of a financial explanation and it was more to calm investors' minds and to demonstrate the central bank's commitment (towards the forint)," said Budapest Bank analyst Peter Bihari. 

 The NBH said it intervened to cut forint fluctuations that it said were unjustified by domestic economic fundamentals. 

 "The main reason for the current intervention was to soothe the exaggerated exchange rate movements unjustified by macroeconomic indicators," NBH Managing Director Adam Farkas told Reuters. 

 "On the other hand, we wanted to lend confidence to the market," he said, adding the forint was still within its 4.5 percent wide intervention band when the NBH entered the market. 

 It was the second time that the NBH had intervened on the currency market since Hungary's crawling peg devaluation regime was launched in March 1995, dealers said. 

 The NBH declined to disclose how much foreign currency it spent on supporting the forint, but market participants said it was a small amount. 

 Dealers said the intervention came when the forint traded at 1.5 to 1.6 percent below parity, weaker than its all-time low of 2.05 percent below midrange reached earlier this week. 

 The forint has been jittery since May due to the spillover impact of Asian and Russian market turbulence. It has been repeatedly breaking through earlier record lows since last week as foreign investors covered losses suffered in Russia. 

 The forint finished at 1.4 percent below parity after the intervention, and at 226.30/80 against the dollar, down from Tuesday's close of 225.20/40. 

 An analyst said the NBH took pre-emptive action within the intervention band because it feared the forint could fall to the bottom of the range. 

 "We believe the main reason for the central bank to intervene inside the band was that it expected the forint exchange rate to further fall during the day, eventually reaching the (weak) frontier of the band," said Takarek Broker's Tamas David. 

 Market participants said the intervention came after Hungarian shares and government bonds extended recent losses mainly caused by foreign investors' sales. 

 The Budapest Stock Exchange's BUX index closed at 6,386.36 points, down by 384.10 points or 5.67 percent, 29.22 percent below its all-time high of 9,022.95 points reaced on April 23. 

 Hungarian government bond yields rose. 

 "The yield on one-year paper was 16.4 percent yesterday, but they were sold even at 16.85 percent today, while two-year bonds went up to 15.35/40 from 16.2 percent," said CA IB Securities trader Tamas Puskas. 

 Market participants agreed with the central bank that Hungary's economic fundamentals were strong, but said the country's markets could not avoid the contagion started by Russia, at least in the short run. 

 "We can expect a bad and changeable market, depending on what happens in Russia," Puskas said. He said funds withdrawn from Hungarian government securities were much below the capital which flowed out from Polish bonds. 

 The NBH did not rule out the possibility that it would intervene again if Wednesday's move does not calm the market. 

 Some analysts said the forint's weakening showed that capital was flowing out from the country through an illiquid currency market, rather than indicating that the currency was attacked by speculators. 

 "The NBH could reassure the market more easily if it declared it would not widen the intervention band until December," said Budapest Fund Management Peter Duronelly. 

 "Fears that the band would be widened hinder speculation (in favour of the forint) return to the market," he added. 

 ((Budapest newsroom +36 1 327 4044 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Central European  Currencies  Face Weakness On Russia News
text:
WARSAW (Dow Jones)--Central European currencies were further buffeted on Wednesday by ill economic winds blowing from Russia, and analysts said more volatility can be expected. 

 In Hungary, the central bank intervened for the first time since early 1995 to sell dollars in support of the flagging forint. Poland's zloty and the Czech koruna both weakened in response to the plunging Russian ruble. 

 Central European currencies will remain acutely sensitive to movements of the ruble, analysts said, but they added that sound economies and limited trade and financial links with Russia should shield them from severe damage. 

 "We are looking at continued weakness and volatility" said Anthony Thomas, an economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "But to turn central Europe into a full blown crisis we would have to see not just Russia but China and Latin America go as well." 

 All three currencies reacted quickly to news of Russia's plan to restructure ruble-denominated debt, which analysts worried could result in huge losses for foreign investors. The currencies took another hit later in the day amid news of the ruble's 69% plunge against the Deutsche mark. 

 Under the deal, announced late Tuesday, holders of Russian treasury debt maturing before the end of 1999 must trade in their securities for a variety of new ones that mature much later and yield less. 

 The National Bank of Hungary intervened to sell dollars when the forint dropped to 1.7% weaker than the midpoint of its trading band, down from 1.18% at the close of trading Tuesday. The forint is allowed to fluctuate by a maximum of 2.25% from the midpoint.

title: Hungary  c.bank says ready for  forex intervention .

BUDAPEST, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said on Monday it was ready to enter the interbank forex market to protect the forint, which has fluctuated wildly within the intervention band in the past few days. 

 "According to the NBH, the direction and size of currency movements within the forint's intervention band exceed the desired level and results in an unjustified uncertainty on the currency market," the NBH said. 

 "Therefore, if it becomes necessary, the NBH is ready to act against movements within the band, unjustifiable by economic trends," the NBH said.

 It said any steps would be temporary and would not signal a change in Hungary's monetary policy.

title: Europe Focus -2:  Currencies  Were Ripe For Profit-Taking
text:
The Czech koruna floats freely, although the central bank intervenes occasionally to reduce volatility. Hungary and Poland have managed exchange-rate regimes, a factor that makes them less vulnerable to outside shocks. 

 The Polish zloty is fixed to a basket of five Western currencies and is devalued at a rate of 0.65% per month. It is allowed to fluctuate within plus or minus 10% of the central parity rate. 

 Hungary's central bank allows the forint to move a maximum 2.25% from the midpoint, which is fixed using a basket of 30% dollar and 70% Deutsche mark. The bank devalues the forint by 0.8% each month against the basket. 

 Russia and Asia aside, local factors were also at work on Tuesday. The soaring zloty and koruna were vulnerable to profit-taking, analysts said. And the Polish and Czech currencies were also weakened by expectations of interest rate cuts in both countries. 

 To varying degrees in all three countries, the currencies have strengthened as investors buy Treasury bills and bonds in search of higher yields than are available in Western Europe. 

 These investors see central Europe as a "convergence play." As Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic move toward European Union membership in a few years, economic policies will become more restrictive and interest rates will decline to Western European levels. 

 "We have seen something of a euphoric period for central European markets over the past several weeks," said David Simmonds, an economist at Citibank in London. "These investors are looking at these markets as the new Spain or Greece," he said.

title: Hungarian Forint Plunges -3: Investors Ignore Fundamentals

By the close at 1300 GMT, the currency appeared to have stabilized, hovering within a few basis points around the midpoint on the band. At one point the forint slipped to about 0.2% on the weak side of the band. 

 At the time of the forint's last steep fall, just after Hungary's parliamentary elections in May, the National Bank of Hungary said it wouldn't intervene on the market other as long as the forint remains with the 4.5% trading band. 

 "Today is a terrible day market-wise," said Istvan Racz, director at Credit Suisse First Boston in Budapest, pointing to the 7.8% drop the Budapest Stock Exchange's BUX index suffered Tuesday. "Basically, it's about Russia. I think we are severely affected by this." 

 Racz also said that the market may also be unclear about the central bank's intentions regarding monetary policy, following the announcement Monday of a relatively steep cut in interest rates. 

 As reported, the bank said that effective Aug. 15 it will cut its overnight reverse repo rate to 13.5% from 14.5%, while cutting the overnight active repo rate to 20.5% from 22.5%, also effective Aug. 15. 

 The repo rates are the central bank's tools for adding and draining liquidity from the interbank money market. 

 As investors run for the exits, they appear to be ignoring fundamentals, evidenced by the market's disregard for a string of positive data Tuesday on Hungary's inflation, trade balance and budget deficit, Racz said. 

 "Unfortunately, there is a lack of appreciation of the fact that Hungary's external viability is still at a pretty high level," Racz said.

 "There is some profit repatriation, mainly on the fixed income market," said Norbert Toth of ING Barings, adding that it was the spill-over effect of speculation with the Russian rouble. 

 Kurali added that the weakening of the forint in the past few weeks over uncertainty around Hungary's elections held on Sunday had caused losses to foreign investors. 

 Centre-right Fidesz Hungarian Civic Party won the elections over the ruling Socialists and is expected to form a government with two other rightist parties in the next few weeks. 

 "There is some uncertainty," said Kurali. "They (the parties) may not get to an agreement quickly." 

 Kurali said the central bank was unlikely to raise its interest rates to stabilise the market as it would contradict its 25 basis point cuts in four repo rates on Monday, which was underpinned with positive macroeconomic figures. 

 He said the central bank may prevent an excessive weakening of the forint by selling dollar on the market, which would not cause any problem to the NBH as Hungary's foreign currency reserves were high. 

 He added the NBH may also reintroduce fixing the yield on its one-year bonds so as to offer attractive yield levels to investors. 

 ((Budapest newsroom +36 1 327 4044 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Hungary  forint rebounds,c.bank denies  intervention .
text:
BUDAPEST, May 28 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint fell more than one percent to an historic low against its parity basket before partly recovering on Thursday prompting the national bank to deny reports it had intervened to prop up the currency. 

 The forint closed at one percent above parity within the 4.5 percent wide intervention range, rebounding from an all-time low of 0.3 percent above midrange. 

 Against the dollar, the forint ended at 213.82/214.20, down from Wednesday's close of 211.50/60. 

 Traders said the National Bank of Hungary intervened by selling dollars to support the Hungarian unit but the NBH denied it taken any such action. 

 "The National Bank of Hungary denies that it intervened on the foreign exchange market to support the forint," the NBH said in a statement. 

 Some traders said the NBH was on the market for a short period at around 1100 GMT, selling foreign currency. 

 All traders agreed the forint rebounded due to a foreign currency selling deal, which was relatively small but had a strong impact as the market had been illiquid. 

 "In our estimate, (the deal) was not larger than $20 million," one dealer said. 

 The NBH said it had no reason for intervening as the forint stopped falling without reaching midrange, while economic factors did not justify a weakening of the currency. 

 "The improvement of the external balance, the trend (of decline) in inflation and interest rates and the country's economic performance do not justify that the NBH should intervene within the flotation band," the NBH said. 

 It said the forint traded in an illiquid market on Wednesday and its movement was temporary. 

 "The movement off the end of the band is in relation with the market atmosphere and the payment of a larger import bill, and can be regarded as temporary," the central bank said. 

 Participants said the fall was due to market uncertainty caused by Russia's current economic woes and financial problems in other emerging markets. 

 Also the market has been concerned about possible changes in economic policy in Hungary, where a centre-right coalition will take over from the outgoing Socialists as soon as official election results are published, probably next week.

title: Edgy post-poll Hungary markets eye foreigners.
text:
BUDAPEST, May 25 (Reuters) - Hungary's edgy markets are waiting to see how foreigners will react on Tuesday to the Socialist government's toppling by a rightist party in weekend elections. 

 The forint weakened on Monday and the Budapest Stock Exchange BUX index fell 8.7 percent on sales by local investors after the centre-right Fidesz Hungarian Civic Party beat the ruling ex-communist Socialist Party in Sunday's polls, but public holidays in Britain and the United States limited foreign interest. 

 "Tomorrow will be critical," said CAIB Securities analyst Csaba Ludanyi. "Foreigners are not so discouraged that they would get rid of their securities at any price...but we will see what happens to the forint." 

 The forint closed at 1.55 to 1.60 percent above parity in the National Bank of Hungary (NBH)'s 4.5-percent-wide intervention range, compared to Friday's close of 1.95 percent above midrange. 

 Traders said the currency, which has usually traded at 2.25 percent above parity for the past two years, weakened in modest trade as domestic dealers speculated on uncertainty over the composition of the new government. 

 Analysts said the central bank might intervene later this week if the forint continued to weaken on jitters over the new government's economic policy, increased by expectations that Fidesz will form a coalition with the agrarian-based Smallholders. 

 They said Hungary's economic fundamentals remained strong and a central bank intervention could successfully prevent excessive securities sales triggered by political uncertainty. 

 "There may be a panic-triggered selling wave, and in this case it would make sense to intervene," said Csaba Ludanyi of CAIB Securities. 

 Analysts said a key issue was how foreign investors would react to the post-election nervousness. 

 "Uncertainty may last for a while and it's a question of how long the patience of foreigners endures and how long they bear losses," said Zoltan Bakonyi of K&H Securities. "I think that they are still patient." 

 But some analysts said the forint might suffer a substantial further weakening if the central bank did not intervene, and this might discourage many foreign investors even though the forint was expected to remain well within the intervention band. 

 BNP-Dresdner Securities analyst Zoltan Kurali said the forint might fall to the middle of the intervention range. 

 In that case the National Bank (NBH) might return to fixing the yield on its one-year bonds instead of letting it float freely, so as to support a yield curve which would ensure acceptable yields to investors. 

 Other analysts said the NBH might prevent an excessive weakening of the forint by buying foreign currency. 

 Ludanyi said some investors who had sold currency futures in proportion to the central bank's basket - 30 percent dollar and 70 percent mark - might begin to buy foreign currency to prevent further losses if the forint fell excessively. 

 Domestic investors who had bought stocks on credits might continue to sell their shares, he added. 

 Most analysts said the forint could face substantial pressure until the new government clarified its intentions on economic policy, but sound fundamentals would prevent a crisis. 

 "Macroeconomic figures are still positive," Kurali said. 

 Some investors recalled that the Polish economy had performed well after the centre-right ousted a government led by the ex-communist party late last year, another analyst added. 

 Analysts said the stock exchange was likely to remain the market most vulnerable to uncertainty. The government securities market, where benchmark yields hardly changed on Monday, was expected to remain quiet. 

 Cuts in four of the NBH's five repo rates earlier on Monday had contributed to confidence that government securities remained unaffected by election uncertainty, analysts added. 

 The NBH said it had reduced both the overnight and one-week repo rates to 23.875 percent from 24.125 percent, the one-week reverse repo rate to 17.875 percent from 18.125 percent and the one-month reverse repo rate to 18.375 percent from 18.625 percent. 

 "The repo cut may be a step to prevent a rise in 

  yields...and it also follows a fall in year-on-year inflation to 

  16 percent in April from 16.4 percent in March," Ludanyi said.

title: Hungary may widen HUF band on cap inflow - Salomon.
text:
BUDAPEST, April 29 (Reuters) - Hungary is likely to widen the 4.5 percent intervention band of its forint if the recent strong portfolio capital inflow continues, Salomon Smith Barney said in a report on the currency on Wednesday. 

 "In many respects, the Hungarian economy is displaying those characteristics that led the Polish authorities to repeatedly widen the exchange rate bands for the Polish zloty over the past few years," analyst Wike Groenenberg said in the report. 

 Salomon said it expected Hungary's gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by almost five percent this year against a backdrop of strong domestic demand and exports. 

 Hungary's solid economic fundamentals are encouraging a sharp increase in portfolio capital inflows, the analyst said. 

 She said the strong foreign interest was due to expectations that the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary - all of them European Union member candidates - implement economic policies aimed at achieving convergence with the European Monetary Union's requirements. 

 The collapse of Italian, Spanish and Swedish bond yield spreads over Germany are prompting investors to look for a yield pick-up elsewhere and central Europe is the key beneficiary. 

 "However, following the substantial currency and bond rallies in those (the Czech and the Polish) markets, attention has more recently focused on Hungary," she said. 

 Domestic demand growth and a keenness to cut inflation levels from 16.4 percent in March argue against Hungarian authorities allowing real interest rates to decline, she added. 

 Finance Ministry Peter Medgyessy said that, together with central bank governor Gyorgy Suranyi, he had proposed that the government decide on Thursday to cut the forint's monthly 0.9 percent devaluator to 0.8 percent. 

 But Medgyessy stressed in an interview to Reuters on Tuesday that he had agreed with Suranyi that they would not propose a widening of the forint's band. The 10 basis point cut in the devaluation rate would be a small change and investors would still be rewarded by more than LIBOR, Salomon said. 

 It added that, in the next few weeks, the central bank was unlikely to alter its monetary policy stance significantly in light of the two rounds of general elections on May 10 and 24. 

 But a continued strong portfolio capital inflow later may prompt a decision on widening the forint's trading band, although such a decision would not be easy as the small width of the band has served Hungary well by increasing exchange rate predictability, Salomon added.

 "Many speculators, including corporates, sold (forex futures) hoping that this will improve their positions next year," said Balazs Benczedi of WestLB Hungaria. "They expect the forint to firm and also the monthly (one percent) devaluator will be cut (to 0.9 percent on January 1.)" 

 "December futures positions were turned into next year positions," he added. 

 The forint finished at 2.2 percent above parity within the National Bank of Hungary's 4.5 percent wide floating intervention band, compared with the opening two percent, which was also Monday's closing level. 

 Against the dollar, however, it ended lower, at 201.44/49, compared with Monday's close of 201.01/11, reflecting the dollar's strength against the mark, dealers said. 

 They said Tuesday's firming against the basket, comprising 30 percent dollars and 70 percent marks, brought the forint close to levels where it usually traded before the recent uncertainty on Asian markets weakened it. 

 The forint has lingered at levels around two percent above parity in the past two weeks. 

 According to market talk, several players had seen the forint weakening further because they expected a large-scale forex buying for the days before the maturing of December forex futures on the Budapest Commodity Exchange on Wednesday. 

 They bought forex when the forint was two percent above parity, hoping to sell it when the forint eased versus the basket, dealers said. 

 But the forint did not weaken as players closing December futures immediately reinvested their funds in 1998 maturities such as March and June, and this also triggered closings of earlier loss-making speculative long positions, traders said. 

 "This means (market players) are maximally optimistic over the forint's future," Benczedi said.

title: Hungary forint seen steady at current level.
text:
BUDAPEST, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint is likely to remain at current levels in the next few months after falling on recent turmoil on emerging markets, analysts said on Thursday. 

 "I think the forint is weaker due to the turmoil which began in Asia and overspilled to the U.S. and Europe," said Gabor Oblath of economic think-tank Kopint-Datorg. 

 "Quite a few foreign investors withdrew money from eastern Europe and the consequences spread to Hungary, although it was quite unjustified by the state of the economy." 

 The forint fell to its lowest point in two years on October 28 to 194.50 against the dollar, in reaction to Asia's economic problems. This represented a level of 1.24 percent above parity, the mid-point of the National Bank of Hungary's 4.5 per cent intervention range for the currency. Since then the currency has risen to two percent above parity, closing on Thursday at 200.40 to the dollar. 

 Before its late-October fall, the forint was usually trading at the National Bank's resistance level, or 2.25 percent above parity, against a basket comprising 30 percent dollars and 70 percent marks. 

 The forint's record fall came on the same day as the Budapest Stock Exchange, depressed by a previous collapse on the Hong Kong bourse, suffered its largest ever daily drop. The BUX index dived 1,294.54 points or 16.5 percent to 6,540.74 points. 

 Since then, the BUX has climbed to a closing 7,126.56 points on Thursday but has remained volatile at levels well below its record 8,627.95 points reached on August 7. 

 Peter Bihari of Budapest Bank said foreign investors are estimated to have withdrawn about 50 to 60 billion forints from Hungary, fearing an overspill affect of financial problems in Asian countries, including South Korea and Japan. 

 "There is an uncertainty factor on international markets now and this has an unfavourable impact on emerging markets in general," he said. 

 "Foreign investors burned themselves and now they are licking their wounds," he added. "The forint's movement is likely to remain hectic in the next few months and it won't stick to the top of the (4.5 percent wide) intervention range." 

 However, analysts agreed that the state of the Hungarian economy did not justify the weakening of the forint. 

 "The current account is so good and other economic indicators are improving in such a way as to make a weak forint unjustified," Oblath said. "This is simply a psychosis." 

 However, most analysts did not regard a weaker forint as a threat to the economy and some of them even said it was a positive factor as it scared away hot money from the country. 

 "I don't think it would be bad if the forint remains unchanged and short-term capital inflow is at a low level," Oblath said, adding that the National Bank of Hungary's losses offsetting the inflationary impact of direct investment and other capital inflow have been high this year. 

 While a forint trading below the intervention level makes the currency more risky for foreign speculators, analysts said the forint was unlikely to ease substantially further unless the tension on world markets increases. 

 "I don't think a substantial weakening is likely," Oblath said. 

 He added that the forint's strength will also depend on the monetary policy the central bank follows from January 1, when the monthly crawling peg devaluator will be cut to 0.9 percent from one percent. 

 "If it offers a high real yield compared with inflation and the devaluation rate is reduced, the forint may move back towards the National Bank's resistance level," he said.

title: Asia-Induced Volatility Seen Persisting In Hungary's Markets
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- If Hungary's equities market was an airliner, the "fasten seat belts" sign would be blinking, and analysts who have watched the market slide 17% in the last month say turbulence in global financial markets is here to stay for at least a few weeks. 

 In addition, a "guilt-by-association" perception of emerging-market economies among investors means that events in Asia are likely to have deeper and longer-lasting repercussions in eastern European markets such as Hungary than in nations to the west. 

 The mood grew more uncertain this week as it became increasingly evident that South Korea is the latest victim of the financial tumult gripping a number of Asian nations. That means investors holding Hungarian assets who have positioned themselves defensively probably will sit tight, perhaps until year end, onlookers say. "The word is 'caution'," said an emerging-markets sales executive at a European investment bank in London. 

 "We are trying to find something to follow," said Gabriella Bor, equities analyst at New York Brokerhaz in Budapest. "For the next few weeks, the volatility should continue, but then I think the market will stabilize." 

 "The short-term developments are still hard to predict. People (in Hungary) will have both eyes on Asia," said Spencer Jakab, head of Hungarian equities research at Credit Suisse First Boston in London. "Korea is the real litmus test. If that stays together, I think things will be okay." 

 Jakab said that based on its cash flow, shares of oil-and-gas company MOL Rt. would be fairly valued around 5,600 forints ($28.55), 33% above Thursday's closing price of 4,210 forints. Another of Jakab's picks is tile maker Zalakeramia Rt. Based on its earnings and capacity growth, the stock should trade at around 12,000 forints, up 39% from 8,650 forints at Thursday's close, according to the analyst. 

 Also supporting the market is the resilient forint, which the National Bank of Hungary devalues 1.0% monthly against a basket composed 30% of dollars and 70% of German marks. The forint weakened moderately after equities began to slide in late October, but has since stabilized well on the strong side of the central bank's intervention band. 

 The devaluations, along with Hungary's fast-growing exports and strong investment inflows, mean the forint is among the least risky of Eastern Europe's currencies, according to a recent report by brokerage firm Merrill Lynch. On the negative side, buying interest may be depressed over the rest of 1997 by the defensive, cash-heavy positions in which emerging-market investment funds now find themselves, particularly open-ended funds that could face large redemptions by investors. 

 Also unclear is the extent to which domestic investors' local holdings are still leveraged with "Lombard loans" from Budapest securities firms. Such loans, collateralized with securities, allowed domestic investors to leverage their way into ever-riskier positions earlier this year, when the BUX peaked at nearly 8500 points. But when the market started to fall, securities firms seeking to minimize their losses sold the shares collateralizing the loans, pushing the market further downward. 

 A broker at a Budapest securities firm cited isolated stories of investors forced to sell possessions such as cars to meet cash calls. But the deleveraging makes the market healthier, he added. More evidence that investors are pulling in their horns came this week, when the Budapest Stock Exchange said it had suspended the per-investor limit on BUX futures because the number of net open positions had fallen below 50,000. The limits, designed to protect against surges of short-term funds flooding the futures market, took effect in September. 

 And with Asia's problems "not over by a long shot," Eastern Europe's worries remain, Jakab said. "Unfortunately, there's not only more turbulence ahead, but more bad times as well," he added.

title: Hungary economy seen sound despite forint, shares.
text:
BUDAPEST, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint weakened relatively little due to the recent turbulence on world markets and economic fundamentals are still showing an improving picture, analysts said on Thursday. 

 "I do not see any fundamental reasons for a weakness of the forint," said Peter Muszely of Concorde Securities. 

 Hungary's forint closed at its weakest point for two and a half years on Tuesday at 1.25 percent above parity due to foreign currency buying triggered by a slump of share prices on the Budapest bourse on a global trend. 

 The forint firmed to two percent above parity on Wednesday, but renewed global uncertainty started by a new fall on the Hong Kong stock exchange pushed the forint down to 1.7 percent above parity on Thursday and traders said it might continue to ease. 

 Analysts said the forint would ease further within the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) 4.5 percent wide intervention band only if global share markets continued to decline. 

 "The Hungarian economy is improving and also the latest figures, August current account data, showed a positive picture," said Istvan Racz of Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 He added that problems on Far Eastern emerging markets, urging structural changes there, would not have a direct impact on Hungary. 

 "Economically, we are linked with Western Europe, and financially with Western Europe and the U.S. (and not the Far East)," Racz said. 

 Analysts said the developing stock exchange as a financing resource still had a relatively small importance for Hungarian companies and international events would affect the Hungarian bond market little as foreigners were minor players there. 

 They added a large-scale NBH intervention to protect the forint was unlikely even if international events weaken the Hungarian currency further. 

 But if the forint eases to levels around parity on any particular day, the central bank may decide to demonstrate the seriousness of its anti-inflation stance and may intervene, Racz said. 

 "A substantial intra-day devaluation could mean certain inflationary pressure on a psychological basis," he said, adding, however, that the current weakness of the forint was even positive for the NBH. 

 "It is not good for a central bank if its currency is always at the resistance level, putting it under a continuous pressure to intervene."

BUDAPEST (AP-Dow Jones)--The Hungarian forint is little changed against the dollar Friday, with dealers keeping their eyes riveted on changes in the dollar's levels against the Deutsche mark. 

 At 952 GMT, traders quoted the dollar at 197.28 to 197.33 forints, down slightly from 197.38 to 197.43 forints in mid-session trading Thursday. They quoted the mark at 108.67 to 108.70 forints, up from 108.57 to 108.62 forints. 

 'It's been exciting Friday,' said a foreign exchange dealer at a major Hungarian bank in Budapest. 'The dollar-mark (ranges) have been moving around quite a bit, and the forint's been following those.' 

 As the forint has moved, it's weakened slightly from Thursday on the National Bank of Hungary's intervention band of 4.5%, which allows the forint to move 2.25% either way. The central bank uses a fixing basket made up of 30% dollar and 70% mark to establish the band. 

 At around 930 GMT, the forint was seen at 2.21% from the band's midpoint, on the forint's strong side of the band. In mid-session trading Thursday the forint was 2.25% from the midpoint.

title: Hungary Forint Up Vs Basket; No Effect Seen From Rate Cut
text:

 The forint has strengthened to 2.25% below the central's bank's midpoint from about 2.20% in mid-session trading Wednesday. 

 Traders had expected the forint to strengthen due to cyclical factors at the beginning of each month and to demand for the currency sparked by gains in the Hungarian stock market earlier this week.

 'The forint has strengthened since yesterday (Wednesday), but there's no clear direction on the market,' said a foreign exchange trader at the Budapest subsidiary of a European bank.

title: FORINT STEADY VS BASKET, COULD EASE AFTER BUX FALL.
text:
BUDAPEST, Aug 11 (Reuter) - The Hungarian forint finished steady against the central bank's dollar/mark currency basket but firmer against the dollar in slack Monday trade, dealers said. 

 The Hungarian unit finished steady against the dollar at 198.60/65, compared with a midday level of 198.65/70 and an opening of 198.09/13. 

 "It was a slack day with the forint at the central bank's resistance level and tracking the dollar/mark," said Attila Behan of ING Bank. 

 Behan said there could be some hard currency buying on Tuesday if the BUX Index of the Budapest Stock Exchange continues Monday's falls which saw it lose 5.82 percent of its value, the second highest daily fall ever. 

 "Some investors may expatriate funds, although we haven't seen any sign of it yet," he said. 

 If such a trend was sizeable it would move the forint substantially below its accustomed level at the resistance level of the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) intervention range. 

 The forint floats in a 4.5 percent wide range against a currency basket made up 30 percent of the dollar and 70 percent of the mark.

title: Hungary  central bank  assets, profit drop in 1996.
text:
BUDAPEST, April 18 (Reuter) - The balance sheet total of the National Bank of Hungary fell to 5,119.3 billion forints in 1996 from 5,420.4 billion, while its pre-tax profits dropped to 2.46 billion from 6.6 billion in 1995, the NBH said on Friday. 

 The NBH said in a statement that its balance sheet total dropped mainly due to the spending of Hungary's privatisation revenues for reducing the country's foreign debt. 

 The NBH's foreign currency and gold reserves dropped to $9.7 billion by December 31, 1996, from 12 billion at the end of 1995 as soaring privatisation revenues at end-1995 and early 1996 were parked In the reserve account before being spent on debt repayment, the NBH said. 

 The NBH's net foreign currency debt dropped by $4.5 billion in 1996 to $12.87 billion. 

 Relatively high forint interest rates and the creation of convertibility for the forint on January 1 for current account transactions encouraged a drop in foreign currency deposits of banks with the NBH and boosted forint deposits, the NBH said. 

 These foreign currency deposits fell by 161.2 billion forints in 1996, while the forint deposits rose by 232.3 billion, with forint funds kept in the reverse repo facilities rising substantially, the NBH said. 

 Throughout 1996, the forint was usually pinned to the resistance level of the NBH's 4.5 percent wide floating intervention range and the NBH increased Hungary's forint liquidity by buying substantial amounts of foreign currencies. 

 However, the NBH ensured a balanced market by taking up deposits in the reverse repo facilities, thus counteracting the increase in forint liquidity, the central bank said. 

 Due to the increase in funds kept in the reverse repo facilities, the NBH's interest expenditures rose by 39 billion forints in 1996, the NBH said.

title: Hungary  Central Bank /Rate Cuts -3: A Strong Forint Feared
text:
Analysts also said if external balance figures keep worsening, then the government might move to adjust the forint's 'crawling peg' devaluation schedule. 

 Pegging is when a government stabilizes the price of a currency by intervening the market. Hungary's 'crawling peg' devalues the forint by 1.2% each month, a level which is intended to mirror reductions in inflation. 

 If inflation doesn't fall as expected, then the gap between the inflation rate and the forint's annual devaluation rate might go as wide as 10%. The annual compounded devaluation rate of the forint is 15.4%. 

 That gap would allow room for the forint to appreciate sharply, weakening exports and worsening the trade balance, analysts said. 

 However, the government has said it has no plans to reduce the crawling peg schedule in the second half.

BUDAPEST, April 25 (Reuter) - A spate of panic-buying of dollars in afternoon trade on the interbank market weakened the Hungarian currency to 30 pips inside the central bank's intervention range, dealers said on Thursday. 

 The forint ended at 147.30/35 to one dollar, compared with its opening 146.85/90 and a midday level of 146.95/147.00. The central bank bid stood at 147.05 at the close. 

 "The panic started after dealers started selling dollars as it strengthened in the morning but were then caught short in the afternoon," ING Bank's Attila Behan explained. "The buying back snowballed." 

 Behan expected the forint to stay at least 30 pips inside the intervention range tomorrow. Further weakening could lead to National Bank of Hungary (NBH) intervention, he said. 

 "The NBH is already sniffing around. If (the forint) weakens another 30 pips I expect them to test the market."

BUDAPEST (AP-Dow Jones)--Hungary's central bank will not widen its foreign exchange intervention band of 4.5%, according to the vice president of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB), the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) reported Thursday. 

 The vice president, Laszlo Csirjak, said he was acting to quell rumors that the bank might widen the band. 

 'I think it's good news,' said Geza Pollanyi, a foreign exchange dealer at OTP Bank in Budapest. 'The market has been stabilizing since March and this decision promotes stability.' 

 Csirjak said that a wider band could lead to an 'undesired revaluation' of the Hungarian forint. Csirjak also said that a wide intervention band was incompatible with Hungary's 'crawling peg' devaluation policy. That policy in effect amounts to a fixed foreign exchange rate, Czirjak said. 

 An instrument of monetary policy, pegging is stabilizing the price of a currency by intervening in a market. At present, Hungary's 'crawling peg' policy, which was adopted in March, limits the maximum monthly intervention rate to 1.2% a month.

title: Hungary central bank intervenes  to help forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, Aug 29 (Reuter) - The central bank, the National Bank of Hungary, has intervened in the interbank foreign exchange market to help the forint, which had been undercut by falling interest rates, dealers said. 

 The forint rose to 129.85/95 to the dollar after the intervention against 130.55 before the midsession break, they added. 

 Gabor Butor of Unicbank said the intervention was relatively small, somewhere between $10 million and $20 million, but was effective because the afternoon is usually slow on the market. 

Central bank officials declined to confirm or deny that intervention had taken place. 

 The forint had been pinned to the resistance level of its 4.5 percent wide trading range for months because its high interest rates, coupled with relatively slow, pre-announced, crawling-peg devaluations, offer attractive rates of return. 

 But the key overnight rates fell today to 26.125/25 percent against 28.25/50 percent yesterday and 30.5 percent a week ago. Some trades were conducted near 20 percent today. 

 The central bank ensures that the forint stays within its trading range through selling or buying unlimited amounts of hard currencies at the support and resistance levels, respectively. title: Banks unload  currencies  after forint devaluation.
text:
BUDAPEST, March 13 (Reuter) - After a nine percent devaluation announced Sunday and effective today, the Hungarian forint closed at the central bank's new bid rate as banks unloaded their long currency positions following a forint devaluation, dealers said. But there was no clear picture of rate movements this morning as banks were barely able to make a market amongst themselves as almost of them were intent on selling currencies, and the only buyer was the central bank. 

 The forint ended midsession at 117.38/45 to the dollar, against Friday's 112.15/20 close. 

 That put the forint slightly weaker than today's 117.25/35 open, but that did not reflect the trend of speuclators cashing in profits on the long-anticipated devaluation. 

 "Everybody tried to get out of their positions, resulting sales (of currencies) to National Bank of Hungary," MBFB dealer Zita Verner said. 

 "The NBH's price was better than the market rate," she added. 

 By the midsession break the central bank's bid rate stood at 117.42. Shortly later the National Bank of Hungary set the midpoint of its 4.5 percent-wide intervention range at 120.03. 

 Last Friday the midrate was 109.63. 

 The market is expected to stay where it is now for the rest of the week, she said. "We'll stay here. Everybody touched the floor, and now it will be interesting to see where forint rates would go," Verner said. 

 The impact of currency sales will be felt on the money market only from Thursday, but dealers differed whether tax payments and reserve accumulation requirements would then help bring rates down.

title: Hungary's forint reverses some losses, eyes CPI.
text:
BUDAPEST, March 10 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint reversed some of the heavy losses suffered earlier on Thursday due to the zloty's fall and government bond prices stabilised around the lows reached in early trade, dealers said.  

At 1615 GMT the forint was quoted at 243.20/60 to the euro, down sharply from 241.61/242.11 late on Wednesday, but firmer from the intraday peak of around 244.50.  

"The forint firmed back a little after the zloty calmed down around 3.95 (to the euro)," one dealer said.  

In early trade the forint had dropped almost one percent and yields had risen by up to 12 basis points, tracking drastic losses in Polish markets. Hungary also cut its auction of 12-month Treasury bill auction on Thursday due to low demand.  

Most traders said the falls were caused by a regional trend rather than any market intervention by the National Bank of Hungary (NBH). The central bank declined to comment.  

Bond yields stabilised in the afternoon after initial rises. Dealers expected them to be flat at the higher levels reached on Thursday or even move further up in the coming days if U.S. and euro zone government papers do not recover from recent losses.  

"Longer papers will stay at this level or weaken further and shorter ones will probably not change much," one dealer said.  

The forint reversed some of the losses in vibrant trade in the afternoon, but its retreat calmed some fears of an attack on the edge of its trading band.  

"The danger that someone will use the two-day holiday to move the forint out of its trading band is now a little bit more mooted," one dealer said.  

Some analysts had expected foreign banks to use the national holiday in Hungary on March 14 and 15 to push the currency above the edge of its trading band at 240.01.  

With those fears temporarily subdued, the publication of February CPI data on Friday, forecast at 3.8 percent, could still cause a strong market reaction.  

Finance Minister Tibor Draskovics said earlier on Thursday that inflation was declining too fast and that the central bank kept higher rates than needed for its own inflation targets.  

Lower-than-expected inflation may fuel expectations of sharp interest rate cuts at the end of March and a new forint strengthening towards the top of its trading band at 240.01.  

Traders said the forint's retreat reduced the chance that the currency firms to the top of the band in illiquid international trade on Monday and Tuesday.  

While the NBH probably has the means to intervene in the international market through its agents even if the local market is closed, most traders said it was unlikely to step in before Wednesday's local reopening.

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary cuts 12-month T-bill auction, yields rise.
text:
BUDAPEST, March 10 (Reuters) - Hungary cut its 12-month Treasury bill offer at an auction on Thursday after a forint slide caused a jump in market yields and curbed appetite for the bills, traders said.  

The Government Debt Management Agency (AKK) said it sold 24 billion forints ($133 million) worth of the 12-month paper, cutting its offer by six billion forints.  

Bids totalled only 30.2 billion forints, compared with a 1.5 bid cover at the previous auction of the 12-month bills held two weeks ago.  

The bills were sold at an average yield of 7.05 percent - while the bids accepted spread in an unusually wide range between 6.80 and 7.10 - lower than the previous auction's 7.26 but well above Wednesday's fixing levels at 6.85.  

"Looking at the forint levels at the time of the auction, only the particularly courageous went into the auction," one trader said.  

The forint fell one percent in early trade to about 244.50 to the euro, sharply reversing earlier gains as foreign investors cut overweight positions in Central Europe's domestic fixed income markets, hitting currencies.  

By 1132 GMT it recovered to 243.25/45.  

In Hungary's local market some dealer said it was possible that the central bank (NBH) stepped in before the fall to curb the earlier forint rises towards to top of the currency's band at 240.01, but others said intervention was unlikely.  

Traders said Hungary's 12-month Treasury bills usually received less attention than shorter papers. Demand at the auction was even lower than usual, but the reduction in the offer was neither a big surprise nor an upset to the government's financing plans.  

"At the earlier auctions this week the AKK raised its offers," one trader said.  

The AKK sold 30 billion forints worth of 3-month bills and the same amount of six-month bills this week. It increased its original offers by five billion forints at both auctions.
