title: Hungarian Forint Strength May Force Rate Cuts - Agency
text:
BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Hungary may be forced to intervene in the market over the coming days as the forint strengthens, a survey of 17 analysts by online economic news agency Portfolio.hu showed Tuesday.  

The forint has drifted within 1% of the strong end of its trading band against the euro in the past week, and is currently at HUF241.80 to the euro. The upper limit of the trading band is HUF240.01 to the euro.  

Slowing inflation and a series of expected rate cuts won't cause the forint to weaken more than a few points before summer, the analysts said.  

Inflation slowed to 4.1% on the year in January, down from 5.3% in December. The bank's key interest rate is currently 8.25%.  

The central bank has come under increasing pressure to cut its key rate, but has been reluctant - some analysts say too reluctant - to cut rates sharply.  

"(The central bank) let this run a bit too long. They should have kept the currency around HUF245 (to the euro). The verbal intervention that they would defend the strong end of the band surprises me," Olivier Desbarres of CSFB told Portfolio.hu.  

Emergency rate cuts and direct foreign exchange intervention are the central bank's most likely tools for weakening the currency, the analysts said.  

If the central bank is forced into cutting rates before the next meeting of the monetary policy council, it cannot cut them by less than 100 basis points, Concorde Securities analyst Janos Samu said.  

"If we get an attack on the intervention band (trading band against the euro) we would expect the (central bank) to intervene strongly in the FX market. We could (also) see a rate cut of 200 basis points. In such a speculative environment we do not think a rate cut of 50 or 100 basis points would be enough to kill the attack," Lars Christensen of Danske Bank said.  

Regular monthly rate cuts will continue, the analysts agreed. A minimum 50 basis point cut is expected at the next rate meeting March 29.  

The market is nervous, dealers say, and an attack on the band could come at any time. If that happens, drastic measures may cause a temporary correction, but such a correction would be short-lived, ING Bank's Gyorgy Barcza said.  

"Even if there is a major correction in the forint, it will be only transitional," Barcza said.  

Raiffeisen Bank's Bence Lanyi thinks the pressure will ease as the trend of disinflation turns around in the summer and the problem of budget balances jump to the fore. The Hungarian government is expected to create an election budget ahead of the general elections in 2006.  

-By Marton Dunai, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0623; marton.dunai@dowjones.com [ 01-03-05 1406GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Emerging  FX -Forint dips further after rate cut.
text:
LONDON, Feb 21 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint added to earlier losses on Monday after the central bank cut interest rates by a larger than expected 75 basis points while the Slovak central bank intervened to weaken the crown.  

Hungary's Monetary Council said a favourable inflation outlook had allowed them to lower key rates to 8.25 percent, but added it would toe a cautious line going forward given the country's sizeable current account and budget deficits.  

The forint fell as low as 243.85 after the decision, but by 1454 GMT had recovered somewhat to trade around 243.40 per euro .  

Most analysts had expected the bank to cut by 50 basis points, but said surprisingly benign January inflation data and last week's forint strength had probably tipped the scales in favour of a bigger move.  

Some said the central bank may be disappointed if it hoped that in moving more aggressively it would help take some of the steam out of the forint's rally - it struck near two-year highs against the euro last week.  

"You can read it in two ways. A big easing now may persuade people to reduce long positions, on other hand you could take it as very bullish for bonds," said Zsolt Papp, emerging markets analyst at ABN AMRO.  

"The market might be inclined to go for the second reading."  

Foreign inflows into the bond market have driven the forint higher in recent weeks as investors bet on an accelerating pace of rate cuts boosting prices.  

Four new Monetary Council members, hand-picked by Prime Minister Ferenc Gyurcsany, are expected to give the rate-setting body a more dovish bias in future meetings.  

The forint is not far off the strong limit of its trading bands against the euro, which comes in around 240, though Governor Zsigmond Jarai said on Monday he was not concerned.  

The market was awash with rumours last week of sizeable positions being taken in the options market betting that the limit would be breached.  

SLOVAK CROWN DOWN AFTER INTERVENTION

The Slovak central bank confirmed it had intervened to weaken the crown on Monday, after the currency had earlier risen to a fresh record high of 37.95 per euro , in its fourth market intervention in the past two weeks.  

"We are intervening because we are still not satisfied with the pace of the crown firming," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.  

Analysts said with foreign investment inflows continuing to pour into the country, the best the bank could hope for was to hold the crown steady.  

"Including today, they've probably now intervened to the tune of over $1 bln in recent weeks, and only succeeded in keeping the crown flat," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at CSFB.  

The Slovak crown traded a shade down at 38.03 per euro.  

It was a less bullish picture for the neighbouring Czech crown, which retreated from 2 1/2 year highs against the euro as the pressure was cranked up on Prime Minister Stanislav Gross to resign. Gross vowed to fight on after a weekend meeting with President Vaclav Klaus following calls for him to quit from junior coalition partners, the Christian Democrats, over questions about the funding of his flat and his wife's business.  

The crown eased off its highs, but losses were fairly limited. It was down 0.2 percent to the euro at 29.91 .  

If the Christian Democrats leave the coalition, the government would lose its one-vote parliamentary majority, though analysts said they would probably not want to trigger early elections.  

Shares in the country's leading phone company Cesky Telecom (SPTTsp.PR) dipped on concerns the political spat was a threat to the firm's upcoming $3 billion privatisation.  

The crown's strong gains so far this year have, in part, been built on expectations of strong foreign inflows arising from the Cesky sale.

title: ANALYSIS-Hungary's Draskovics lays credibilty on the line.
text:
BUDAPEST, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Hungary's Finance Minister Tibor Draskovics has put his credibility on the line over the 2004 budget, but analysts question whether the man who promised so much will deliver any more than his predecessors.   

Draskovics has said repeatedly that government revenues will pick up towards the end of the year, allowing Hungary to patch over holes in the budget and deliver a deficit no bigger than 4.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).   

But revenues have continued to be weaker than forecast, and were 23 billion forints less than planned in August. This has prompted a rethink of methodology used to forecast value added tax receipts, and unnerved investors who are banking on Hungary cutting the deficit so it can join the euro in 2010.   

"The outcome of this year's deficit is important not only because markets regard it as a test of credibility, but also because this is the basis for next year's calculations," said Tamas Vojnits, economic analyst at Hungary's biggest bank, OTP.   

The problem is that it is deja vu, all over again.   

Draskovics could become the victim of the political pressure which claimed the scalp of predecessor Csaba Laszlo, if there is a hat trick of missed budgets with a deficit overshoot in 2004.   

No one in financial markets really expects Draskovics to achieve his promised deficit of 4.6 percent and analysts say investors will tolerate any number under five percent.   

Only an overshoot of five percent or more will provoke a market selloff, they say, or if Draskovics makes creeping upward revisions to the deficit like those made by Laszlo in 2003.   

Laszlo, an able technocrat, presided over a rise in the budget deficit to 6.0 percent of GDP in 2003 from an original target of 4.5 percent.   

He could not withstand pressure to spend more from the ruling Socialist Party and a mismatch between central bank policy and the fiscal side triggered three forint crises in 2003.   

BACK TO 1996, NEW FACE IN 2004   

The Socialists have a bad record on budget discipline. In 1996 then-prime minister Gyula Horn baulked at the radical reforms of finance minister Lajos Bokros and kicked him out of office - yet he still managed to lose a 1998 election.   

In 2004, there is a political unknown in the form of Ferenc Gyurcsany, a popular politician who is set to become prime minister later this month. He wants to make Hungary a fairer society and to rebuild support for the Socialist Party.   

Gyurcsany has so far talked the kind of language markets like, stressing continuity, but no specifics.   

If Hungary wants to come on target with a 4.6 percent deficit, spending cuts in the region of 160 billion forints or around 0.8 percentage points would be needed, based on an overshoot in line with the central bank's forecast of a deficit of 5.4 percent of GDP.   

There is some wriggle-room.   

"Spending items pencilled in for November-December could also be delayed until January 2005, a 'trick' which has been used before," CSFB analyst Olivier Desbarres said.   

Neither Gyurcsany nor Draskovics will talk numbers, although analysts said Draskovics gave his clearest hint there would be an overshoot when he told Reuters on Wednesday that the finance ministry would look at VAT revenue projections.   

But other politicians have at least started to talk about a potential overshoot, among them Gabor Kuncze, head of the smaller party in the ruling Socialist-led coalition, the Free Democrats, which has four ministerial posts.   

"If there is around a 0.3/0.4 percentage point difference, it seems that this has already been priced in by markets," Kuncze told public service TV on Thursday. "However if the difference turns out to be significantly bigger, which I do not believe it will, then there is need for intervention."   

That leaves investors wondering if the 11 percent Hungary pays in official interest rates is enough to reflect the risk.   

For the moment it is. "The key to the forint's stability remains the high carry versus the euro zone, which attracts large foreign exchange inflows that in turn finance the 9 percent of GDP current account deficit," said CSFB's Desbarres.   

The forint is also underpinned by Hungarian companies and individuals borrowing cheaply in euros and then converting those euros into forints, and barring a massive external shock, there is no sign that will change.   

"The last time the Hungarian private sector significantly unwound its foreign exchange shorts/forint long positions was in 1998, following the Russian debt default," Desbarres noted. FOR FACTBOX ON BUDGET PLEASE DOUBLE CLICK.

title: Hungary's Jarai: Exchange Rate Regime To Remain In Place
text:
BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Hungary will maintain a currency preference range of 250 to 260 forints ($1=HUF22.97) against the euro, but it will be more flexible about this range than previously, Governor Zsigmond Jarai said Friday.  

"We'll treat the HUF250 to HUF260 range with more flexibility since we've already agreed on the 2005 inflation goal and the inflation target is our chief goal," Jarai told a press conference.  

"It's possible that in three or six months a different exchange rate will be needed for this inflation goal," Jarai said.  

However, in the short term, the bank will allow little deviation from this preference range and will adjust rate policy to keep the forint at this level.  

At around 1000 GMT, the forint was trading at between 264 and 265 against the euro after the bank raised its key deposit rate to 12.5% from 9.5% to prevent further weakening.  

But for now, the central bank will only tolerate small and temporary deviations from the preference range, but the current currency weakening isn't small and temporary, but reflects a radical change in investor sentiment, Jarai said.  

"The past few days prove that there's a systematic change in investor sentiment toward Hungary. Not only short-term hedge funds are behind the current weakening, but portfolio investors as well," Jarai said.  

The forint weakened to around HUF269 against the euro early Friday after tumbling earlier this week from HUF261.50 last week as portfolio investors have lost confidence in Hungary.  

"They have become insecure about Hungary's economic fundamentals... and we can only reinstate their trust by this high interest rate level," Jarai said.  

Hungary's current account deficit this year will be higher than the bank expected at the start of this year, and the budget deficit, while on a narrowing path, will also be high. Furthermore, Hungary finances its current account deficit mostly via foreign portfolio investments so portfolio investors' confidence in Hungary is vital.  

"Because of the imbalances, currency depreciation expectations increased among portfolio investors. That's why we need to hike rates this much," Jarai said.  

The current interest rate provides a 6% forward-looking return adjusted for 2004 inflation, a level "considerably high but not unprecedented" for Hungary, Jarai said.  

The current exchange rate of the forint will remain in place until the country joins ERMII, the exchange rate regime that serves as the ante-room to euro-zone membership.  

Hungary's target date to adopt the euro of Jan. 1, 2008, was a consideration for the central bank when it decided about Friday's rate hike, Jarai said.  

The central bank considers the target date for euro membership is a realistic goal and Hungary could still achieve it. Despite its current economic woes, an improvement in its fundamentals is on the cards from next year, Jarai said.  

"We can still enter the euro zone Jan. 1 2008," Jarai said.  

Hungary will join the European Union in May 2004 and the central bank wants to enter ERMII as soon as possible after that, he added.  

"A tight economic policy is needed for that and we'll pursue a tight monetary policy to reach our euro goals," Jarai said.  

High inflation and a wide budget deficit are Hungary's main hurdles on its road to adopting the euro. Reducing inflation is a chief goal of the central bank.  

When deciding about the Friday's hefty rate hike, "the central bank considered whether a weaker currency or higher interest rates lead to greater economic tensions, and we decided that a weaker forint would, as it would pose a threat to the inflation goals," Jarai said.  

"The exchange rate is the chief tool in Hungary for reducing inflation," Jarai added.  

Jarai rejected central bank intervention on the open markets as a possible way of stemming the forint's weakness, saying that intervention can only control temporary swings in the currency.  

Minister of Finance Laszlo Csaba was present at the central bank's rate meeting as usual, Jarai said, although the bank didn't seek government approval for the rate hike because it is independent he added.  

The central bank expects the economy to start improving next year on a recovery in the European Union and especially Germany, Hungary's most significant export market. Even if economic growth doesn't accelerate from this year's level of about 3.5%, it is expected to become more balanced. Exports are expected to drive growth, rather than domestic demand and household consumption which have led the economy in the past two years.  

If the forint and bond markets recover, the central bank will reduce interest rates, Jarai said. The amount of Hungarian government bonds denominated in forints in foreign hands is worth about EUR8 billion, he said.  

"It's not impossible to cut rates if investor confidence returns," Jarai said.  

-By Margit Feher, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0622; margit.feher@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary c.bank, finmin try to talk up weak forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, Nov 25 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank and finance minister attempted to talk up the sliding forint on Tuesday, saying the weakness of the currency and bonds was temporary and not justified by the economy's fundamentals.   

By 1501 GMT the forint firmed to 260.95/261.45 to the euro, from below 262 earlier on Tuesday, but remained highly volatile, still trading outside the bank's preferred range of 250-260.   

The forint started falling on Monday on a sell-off in government bonds and extended losses on Tuesday, as bond sales continued, with yields surging over 100 basis points in two days and expectations for an interest rate hike lingering.   

The central bank (NBH) said the forint should trade at 250-260 to the euro for its four percent end-2005 inflation target to be achievable, adding that it believed the currency's present falls were "temporary."   

The NBH said it would not react to temporary and small fluctuations of the currency, but "would take the necessary steps if it believes market developments jeopardise the achievability of the inflation target".   

Traders said the sell-off in Hungarian bonds was mainly due to a spillover of jitters from Poland where the zloty and bonds eased after last week's poorly-bid auction.   

But they added the risk appetite of big foreign investors or end users - key holders of Hungary's bonds and thus financiers of the country's wide current account deficit - was very low and markets would remain highly vulnerable to contagion in the region, mainly from Poland, and shifts in sentiment.   

Finance Minister Csaba Laszlo also said the markets' weakness was temporary and not due to fundamental reasons.   

He told Reuters the budget vote in Parliament was progressing as planned and the government's plan to cut the public sector deficit to 3.8 percent of GDP next year, from five percent this year, would be approved later on Tuesday.   

YIELDS SURGE, MARKETS ON EDGE   

The yield on Hungary's 2008/C bond was up 60 basis points at 9.80/10.00 percent, while the 2006/G was quoted at 10.30/50 percent, up 55 basis points.   

Traders said sentiment in the next few days will be key to auctions of five-year 2009/C and ten-year 2014/C bonds on Thursday, which will be closely watched by markets.   

Poor demand at the auctions may trigger a further sell-off and forint weakness and may eventually force the central bank to raise key interest rates when its Monetary Council holds its next regular meeting next Monday.   

"I believe the forint will remain very volatile in the next few days...but the bank must avoid hiking rates as that would only fuel expectations for further rate hikes," one trader said.   

This week's is the second mini-crisis in Hungary's financial markets this month. Early in November a sell-off in bonds weakened the forint and forced the NBH to steady the markets by buying bonds in an unorthodox form of intervention.   

Foreign investors have been burnt in Hungary's volatile financial markets three times this year, as the forint has gyrated between levels of 234 and 270 to the euro.   

Hungary will auction 30 billion forints ($134.7 million) worth of five-year and 20 billion worth of 10-year bonds on Thursday, down from the usual offer of 40 and 30 billion. The the government has said it will reduce supply until January to boost demand and improve liquidity.   

In January Hungary will issue one billion euros worth of eurobonds.

title: ANALYSIS-Forint swings add new twist to ERM2 debate.
text:
LONDON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Market turbulence in Hungary may raise fresh doubts in the European Union about the ability of the future member state to hold its forint within the required bands against the euro before adopting the single currency.   

However, some analysts say the turbulence only underlines the advantages of joining the exchange rate mechanism (ERM2), the anteroom for euro zone membership.   

The forint and Hungarian government bonds slid sharply on Monday, forcing the Hungarian National Bank to buy bonds in an unorthodox open market intervention.   

Hungary wants to join ERM2 soon after becoming a full EU member in May 2004 and last month began informal talks with the European Central Bank (ECB) to discuss that aim and its ultimate goal of euro accession in 2008.   

ERM2 locks a currency into a central parity rate against the euro and sets 15 percent fluctuation limits above and below that rate.   

However, the ECB and EU Commission have said they would prefer the original narrow 2.25 percent bands to be applied for two years when assessing a country's fitness to adopt the euro.   

For the original euro founders, the Maastricht treaty stated that a country must observe ERM fluctuation margins for at least two years prior to joining the euro.   

"It's important to note that for Hungary the narrow band concept doesn't have any meaning until 2006. So unless you think the 15 percent bands are going to be a problem, there's not necessarily a reason to think ERM2 will be a problem," said Jeff Gable, emerging markets analyst at Deutsche Bank.   

FORINT SWINGS   

It's not clear whether the idea of early ERM2 entry with a view to waiting several years before joining the euro will be acceptable to euro zone officials.   

The Bundesbank in particular has questioned whether early membership of ERM2 is the best option, especially given the problem across eastern Europe of bloated budget deficits.   

"Against this background, you have to ask the question whether an early membership in ERM2 makes sense, or whether it it better to wait and reach a higher degree of nominal convergence," Bundesbank Vice President Juergen Stark said in August.   

The forint dropped around three percent against the euro in little over a day's trading this week as foreign investors liquidated positions in the local bond market on a spillover of negative sentiment from Poland and Russia.   

The central bank's credibility also took a knock when it exacerbated the bond market sell-off with a warning that it was prepared to hike interest rates if the currency failed to strengthen.   

However, it helped calm the market on Monday by intervening to buy government bonds and leaving interest rates on hold at its regular policy meeting, aiding a recovery in the forint.   

"There are probably one or two ECB members who are looking at the fiscal numbers and the currency volatility in Hungary and probably shaking their heads," said one London-based analyst.   

BETTER INSIDE THAN OUT   

In answer to the sceptics within the euro zone, some analysts say entering the ERM2 could be the best way to curb the kind of volatility seen in the forint and the Polish zloty recently.   

Ratings agency Fitch, in a report on the 10 EU accession countries on Tuesday, highlighted the potential positive impact of ERM2 membership.   

Fitch said ERM2 participants would benefit from the ECB's backing of the system, reducing vulnerability to episodes of financial contagion along the lines seen in Hungary in the past few days.   

It also said ERM2 membership would make it more likely that a country meets the euro zone entry criteria and hence joins the bloc on a three-to-four year time horizon.   

"The EU needs to ask how FX volatility and high long-term interest rates help long-term investment and growth...they don't, they're counter-productive," said Charles Robertson, emerging markets analyst at ING.   

"This volatility is only hurting Hungary's capacity to join the euro quickly and see real economic convergence...you could argue that it highlights the interests of joining," said Robertson.

title: Polish zloty, bonds claw back losses.

ground slowly on Monday, as buyers picked up bargains in the

markets were little affected by a nervous morning in Hungary,

title: Hungary Central Bank : To  Intervene  In Bond Market Soon

"From now on, we'll enter the market as buyers of bonds. The market is illiquid and the yields are high," Gabor Missura told Dow Jones Newswires.  

Missura declined to specify which maturity the central bank is targeting.  

Currency and bond traders said that, as of 0845 GMT, they hadn't seen the central bank in either the bond or the currency market. Bond yields were 20-30 basis points higher than late Friday, after a rise of more than 100 basis points last week on strong selling by nonresidents.  

The forint is trading at HUF263.50-.80 ($1=HUF261.95) against the euro, significantly weaker than the central bank's preferred range of HUF250-260.  

"The forint was pushed from HUF261.50 to HUF264.40 without a single deal struck in it. Bids are higher and higher but there are no offers," a dealer at a Hungarian commercial bank said.  

Bond traders also said deals are thin on the ground.  

"The (yields on) three- and five-year maturities are 20-30 basis points higher, but hardly any deals have been struck," a trader at Raiffeisen Bank said.  

The central bank said the country's economic fundamentals don't justify the past few days' rise in the long end of the yield curve. The government and the central bank remain committed to plans to adopt the euro Jan. 1, 2008, the bank said in a statement.  

"The central bank hopes that the current market disorder will correct shortly," the bank said, repeating its statement Friday that it considers the developments temporary.  

The central bank said the reason for the past two days' weakness is that some market participants needed to reshuffle their investment portfolios after falls in Polish and the Russian markets. Their selling led to stop-loss sell orders, which deepened the Hungarian market's losses, the bank added.  

The central bank's statement comes just hours before its Monetary Council is due to publish its interest rate decision, at 1300 GMT.  

Market expectations of a rate hike have strengthened on the recent weakness, whereas until Thursday, no-one had expected the bank to raise rates. While most economists and traders still say the central bank will probably leave its key rate at 9.50%, forecasts of a 50-100-basis-point rate hike are increasing.

title: ECB's Tumpel Gugerell:Euro Gains Ground In Ctrl, E Europe
text:
FRANKFURT (Dow Jones)--The euro is becoming increasingly important in Central and Eastern European countries that are applying to join the European Union, Gertrude Tumpel-Gugerell, a member of the European Central Bank's governing council, told a banking conference Monday.  

Candidate countries have issued euro-denominated bonds totaling more than EUR30 billion, and one country, Montenegro, has actually pegged its currency to the euro, she said.  

The share of the euro in accession countries' official reserves is around 50%, higher than in other regions.  

In Hungary and Romania the euro is the official intervention currency, Tumpel-Gugerell said.  

The use of the euro for invoicing sales of Russian oil in the region is also under discussion, she added.  

Montenegro adopted the euro peg unilaterally to boost the credibility of its own currency, she said in response to a question.

title: Hungary cbanker says no immediate forint target.
text:
BASEL, Switzerland, June 30 (Reuters) - Hungary has no immediate exchange rate target for the forint following its recent shift in the currency's fluctuation bands but would be satisifed to see it return to the previous target range, a top central banker said on Monday. 

 Peter Adamecz, deputy president of the National Bank of Hungary, told reporters that with hindsight the 2.26 percent lowering of the forint's parity band had not been well timed. 

 "With hindsight, we can safely say that it was not particularly good timing for the change in the frame for the exchange rate and intervention band. It was not meant to be an actual devaluation of the currency," he said on the sidelines of the annual meeting of the Bank for International Settlements. 

 Asked if the forint could return to the previous target range of 250-260 to the euro, Adamecz said: 

 "It might come back. We have not an immediate exchange rate target. 

 "We are just looking at certain ranges which would be more suitable from the point of view of the inflation target for 2004." 

 Asked if the bank had any other range, he said, "We don't have any other range in mind. We would be satisfied to have the currency in that range that you mentioned." 

 Adamecz said the shift in the intervention band was not related to any preparations by Hungary to join the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism prior to adopting the euro. 

 Hungary is one of 10 countries, mostly from central and eastern Europe, preparing to join the European Union next May. By treaty, the new members will be obliged eventually to join the single currency. 

 Under ERM-2, currencies may fluctuate by 15 percent either side of a central parity point. 

 EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Pedro Solbes recently indicated that countries in ERM2 would have to restrict fluctuations to 2.25 percent but later said this was just an assessment criterion for euro entry. 

 Asked whether exchange rate criteria had been discussed in last week's meeting in Frankfurt of the EU aspirant countries and the European Central Bank, Adamecz said," It was in fact a confirmation of what we already knew." 

 "It was already clear that the exchange rate fluctuation band in ERM-2 is similar to what we have already in Hungary but there is a narrower tolerance band for the definition of exchange rate stability." 

 Adamecz said Hungary currently had no timetable for ERM2 entry.

title: Hungary Jarai: Ready To Defend Euro HUF250 Exchange Rate
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- Hungary's central bank will bring the forint's exchange rate back up to 250 against the euro, even if it takes interest rate hikes or intervention, National Bank of Hungary President Zsigmond Jarai told Dow Jones Newswires Thursday. 

 Jarai was speaking after the authorities unexpectedly devalued the currency Wednesday, cutting the central rate in its trading band by 2.26%, a move which sent the currency into a tailspin. 

 It was trading between HUF268-269 to the euro Thursday morning, having weakened Wednesday from HUF255 to HUF270. 

 Jarai said in an interview, however, that the bank is ready to live with a weaker exchange rate for a few days and will stay on the sidelines for now to see how the market settles down. 

 The bank won't intervene or raise rates Thursday and will wait for the European Central Bank's rate decision Thursday before assessing its next move, Jarai said. 

 "We want to keep the exchange rate at 250 forints ($1=HUF230.80). We have the tools to keep it there and we're going to keep it there," Jarai said. 

 "If the market prices in a weaker forint, we will react. That could mean a rate hike or that we just won't cut rates after an ECB cut." 

 Jarai admitted that Wednesday's move confused the market and the reaction was more severe than the government had expected. But he stressed that the devaluation didn't mean the bank is ready to sacrifice its inflation targets. 

 "We agreed to the weaker currency because it doesn't threaten our inflation targets," he said. 

 "We're maintaining those targets and we'll do what it takes to meet them. 

 "The shift in the band limits our maneuvering abilities somewhat but we see that we won't need that room anyway. We can get to the inflation target with the new band just as well," Jarai said. 

 He added that the bank is ready to be more flexible with the target for end-2003 but won't compromise on the end-2004 goal. Jarai sees inflation at the end of this year between 4.5% and 5%, just above the 4.5% target. An exchange rate of HUF250 to the euro will allow end-2004 inflation to be under 4%, Jarai said. The bank's target for end-2004 inflation is between 2.5% and 4.5%. 

 "We won't allow inflation to accelerate as getting it back to lower levels would require too great a sacrifice," Jarai said, adding that the central bank and the government had made a verbal pact on the shift in the currency band. 

 "The central bank believes that the move was possible right now because the shift won't compromise our inflation goals," he declared. 

 "The move is a symbolic step on the government's part to exporters that the forint won't strengthen to below HUF240 again," he said. Hungarian exporters have long complained to the government that the strong forint was damaging competitiveness. 

 After the devaluation the forint's strongest spot in the band is now HUF240.01, from HUF234.69. 

 Part of the pact was that the government will reduce public spending this year by HUF74 billion and will remain committed to its 2003 budget deficit target of 4.5% of GDP, Jarai said. The budget deficit was a whopping 9.7% of GDP last year. 

 Analysts said, however, after Wednesday's announcement, that the spending cut isn't substantial and the government will exceed its deficit target regardless. They added that a spending cut in the range of HUF250 billion would have been more reassuring for investors. 

 Jarai stressed that he government needs to remain vigilant in its goal of cutting the budget deficit further and meeting its deficit targets set out in its Pre-Accession Economic Plan submitted to the European Union. 

 The HUF74 billion cut in 2003 spending "is a step in the right direction but further budget adjustments are needed, chiefly to achieve the 2004 budget deficit target," Jarai said. 

 The government aims to reduce the deficit to about 3.0% of GDP in 2004. 

 The verbal pact with the government doesn't include anything about further currency band shifts, Jarai pointed out. 

 But he saw no need for any more such moves, which the market interpreted as a de facto devaluation. They generated a high degree of instability and loss of credibility among investors that the central bank wanted to avoid, he said. 

 "I don't think more shifts will be necessary." 

 The timing of the move was unfortunate since the forint had already weakened to 253-256 against the euro by the time of the announcement, Jarai said. 

 "The decision for the shift wasn't based on the current forint exchange rate," Jarai said. 

 "We won't allow inflation to accelerate as getting it back to lower levels would require too great a sacrifice," Jarai said, adding that the central bank and the government had made a verbal pact on the shift in the currency band. 

 "The central bank believes that the move was possible right now because the shift won't compromise our inflation goals," he declared.

 After the devaluation the forint's strongest spot in the band is now HUF240.01, from HUF234.69.

 But he saw no need for any more such moves, which the market interpreted as a de facto devaluation. They generated a high degree of instability and loss of credibility among investors that the central bank wanted to avoid, he said. 

 "I don't think more shifts will be necessary." 

 The timing of the move was unfortunate since the forint had already weakened to 253-256 against the euro by the time of the announcement, Jarai said. 

 "The decision for the shift wasn't based on the current forint exchange rate," Jarai said. 

 "We incorporated into the verbal pact that the finance ministry supports ERM II entry as soon as possible," Jarai added. "Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy is inclined towards swift entry." 

 Exchange Rate Mechanism II is a trading band which countries have to join for at least two years prior to euro membership. Hungary plans to join the E.U. in May 2004. 

 "If the 2004 tightening in the budget really takes place as the government promises, the equilibrium exchange rate could be weaker than HUF250," Jarai said, referring to the rate at which the government plans to enter ERM II. 

 Jarai said he doesn't see wages rising more than 5% nominally next year, which is slightly above the bank's projection of 4.1% on average. 

 That fits with recent remarks from Prime Minister Medgyessy who has said public sector wages won't rise faster than inflation. 

 Wages last year rose 18.3% nominally and 13.6% when adjusted for inflation, including sharply steeper rises in the public sector. 

 "Until now we had to have a stronger currency (than HUF250) due to lax fiscal and wage policies...." said Jarai. 

 "But joining ERM II would be worthwhile with a rate close to the equilibrium rate. That rate should be weaker than the average rate of the past two years," Jarai said. 

 Based on the central bank's annual average exchange rate statistics, the average rate of the past two years is HUF249.83.

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary cbank not to prop up forint, but warns.
text:
(Updates with warning in c.bank statement in paras 3, 6, 7-10, analyst comment in 11-13.) 

 BUDAPEST, June 4 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank will not intervene to strengthen the forint after sharp falls as budget adjustments and improved competitiveness prospects help it meet inflation targets, Governor Zsigmond Jarai said on Wednesday. 

 "There is no need for intervention, the current exchange rate is far from the edge of the band and even further from the new edge," Jarai told a news conference. 

 But in a statement released by the Monetary Council later, the bank warned that after a devaluation of parity in the forint currency's band it still had the means to defend inflation targets. 

 The government and the central bank announced earlier on Wednesday that they were devaluing the forint's parity rate to 282.36 against the euro from a previous 276.10 to boost job creation and competitiveness ahead of EU accession next year. 

 Jarai said the forint should fluctuate around 250 to the euro, below earlier levels of around 245, to help achieve inflation targets. 

 When Jarai spoke, the forint traded slightly lower then 256 against the euro, but after the news conference its slide continued. 

 WARNING IN LATER STATEMENT 

 In a statement issued later the bank said the government's request to shift the central parity was acceptable because "under the present economic circumstances, considering the impacts of a disinflationary international environment, the inflation targets of around 4.5-5.0 percent for end-2003 and 2.5-4.5 percent for end-2004 were achievable provided that the forint's exchange rate stabilises at around 250 to the euro." 

 But the bank added that should this not happen, it still had the tools to tighten monetary policy if it sees its inflation targets at risk. 

 "The Monetary Council believes...that in the new exchange rate band it still has enough room of manoeuvre, in case there is a threat to the inflation targets, to help economic processes move in way which promote further successful disinflation," the bank added. 

 At 1555 GMT the forint was quoted at 267.65/268.15. 

 Some analysts said the bank will have to raise its key interest rates if the forint does not firm back to around 250 from its present low levels of 266, to which it plunged after the devaluation was announced. 

 "Should verbal intervention remain ineffective, the central bank will have to hike interest rates," DZ Bank said. 

 Hungary's key two-week deposit rate stands at 6.5 percent.

title: FACTBOX-Hungarian forint's bumpy road towards ERM-2.
text:
BUDAPEST, June 4 (Reuters) - Hungary on Wednesday devalued
central parity in its Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM 2)-type
forint band by 2.2 percent to 282.36 to the euro from 276.10.
Hungary is alone among 10 states due to join the European
Union next May to have already adopted an ERM-type band.
Hungary plans to adopt the single currency euro in 2007. A
key condition of that is for the forint to stay in a 30-percent
wide band for at least two years without adjustment.
Following is a chronology and facts about Hungary's road to
ERM-2.
FORINT BAND
May 4, 2001 - Flotation band changed for first time in over



six years. Forint swiftly gains over 10 percentage points to 245


 to the euro, boosted also by EU convergence inflows. 

 October 1, 2001 - Forint's crawling peg devaluations lifted 

 and parity rate set at 276.1 to the euro in +/-15 percent band. 

 Previous band had been +/-2.25 percent. 

 January, 2003 - Central bank (NBH) fends off hot money 

 attack against the top of the currency band, buying 5.2 billion 

 euros in the market and slashing interest rates. 

 May 23, 2003 - NBH says it resold 3.8 billion euros and 

 stopped currency market interventions. By June 4, forint falls 

 four percent to below 256 to the euro - lower than levels after 

 January's speculative attack. 

 June 4, 2003 - Government and NBH shift central parity to 

 282.36 against the euro - effectively devaluing forint by over 

 2.2 percent Forint falls to 265. 


INFLATION TARGETING
June 12, 2001 - NBH launches policy of implicit inflation



targeting to underline inflation-cutting impact of stronger



forint. Previously, the bank did not set inflation targets. The



new policy assumed Hungary would join euro zone in January,



2006, having trimmed inflation to about two percent for 2004-05.



July 12, 2002 - New pro-growth centre-left government and



NBH change euro zone entry target date to 2007 as inflation



targets rise. Official ERM-2 and euro zone target dates due to



be set in second half 2003.


CURRENCY LIBERALISATION
Jan 1, 1996 - Forint made convertible for current account
deals according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) criteria,
but short-term capital movements remain restricted.
June 15, 2001 - NBH and then ruling centre-right cabinet



lift restrictions on short-term cross-border capital movements,



saying liberalisation needed to allow domestic firms and foreign



investors to hedge currency risks boosted by wider forint band.



All major currency restrictions lifted, opening up new business



opportunities for foreign investors, including trade in forint



derivatives and Hungarian short-term debt. Flurry of forint



denominated Eurobonds shows international investors bet on


Hungary's future EU convergence.


INTERVENTION BAND WIDTH
1992, July 12     - 0.6 percent
1994, June 1      - 1.0 percent
1994, August 5    - 2.5 percent
1994, December 22 - 4.5 percent
2001, May 4       - 30 percent
FORINT DEVALUATIONS
Hungary devalued the forint in 23 one-off moves between



January 1, 1990 and March 13, 1995. The nine percentage point



devaluation on March 13, 1995 was the second largest move after



a 15 percent devaluation on January 7, 1991.



The pre-announced monthly crawling peg devaluation rate,



launched in March 1995 at 1.9 percent, was cut 14 times before



being lifted on October 1, 2001.



Central parity rate in the 30-percent-wide band launched in



2001 was devalued by 2.2 percent on June 4, 2003, to 282.36



against the euro from 276.10.

title: Hungary 's c.bank says ends market  intervention .
text:
BUDAPEST, May 26 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said on Monday that it had ended currency market intervention after selling billion of euros following an inflow of hot money that it fended off in January. 

 "The central bank has finished currency market operations and returns to its earlier practice, in which it influences the exchange rate mainly through its interest rates," the NBH said in a statement. 

 NBH Governor Zsigmond Jarai told a news conference that in January 5.3 billion euros in hot momey flowed into the country due to unjustified speculation that Hungary would lift central parity in the forint's 30-percent-wide band. 

 The NBH cracked down on speculation by buying the euro at the upper end of the band, slashing interest rates and narrowing foreign players' access to its deposit facilities, forcing them to sell their forints at lower exchange rates. 

 The NBH defended the band and has resold 3.8 billion euros through market operations since then, posting a profit of 43 billion forints ($206.7 million), Jarai said. 

 Hot money players lost altogether 240 million euros on winding up their speculative positions, the NBH said. 

 The bank said local investors also posted profits on the speculation as about 1.2 billion euros was rebought by foreign hot money investors from local banks. 

 Jarai said the speculative wave improved the credibility of the NBH's inflation targets instead of breaking the forint band. 

 "It has showed that the bank does everything by using all its tools so as to reach lower inflation levels," he said. 

 The NBH's international reserves fell to 11.562 billion euros by the end of April from January's peak at 14.2 billion.

title: ANALYSIS-EU votes,  fx  seen reviving C.Europe rate cut cycle.
text:
BUDAPEST, May 6 (Reuters) - Expectations of interest rate cuts in central Europe should continue to strengthen as several countries hold referendums on EU membership in the next few weeks, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 They said political, domestic and external economic factors and firming currencies would all point in that direction. 

 So would any continued drop in eurozone debt yields which would make the assets of countries which expect to join the EU next May more attractive. 

 "In most states, interest rate cut expectations have strengthened," said Zsolt Papp, analyst at ABN AMRO in London. 

 "We expect the European Central Bank (ECB) will cut later this year, and inflation rates are also lower than expected." 

 Central Europe's main currencies have rebounded in recent days, driven in part by a stronger euro and falling eurozone yields, while government bond auctions have seen strong demand. 

 Slovakia's stronger crown is seen prompting interest rate cuts after the central bank intervened on Monday, a Polish zloty rally could also trigger cuts, and that could eventually pull Hungary into the cycle as well, analysts said. 

 The Czech central bank, however, is seen stopping short of trimming interest rates as there are concerns that a deflation period could end soon and low interest rates would not be sufficient safeguard against inflationary pressure. 

CURRENCY RISES BACK 

 Lower world oil prices have helped EU candidates keep inflation, a major concern ahead of EU accession, in check, while recent falls in EU debt yields made their high-yielding fixed income assets increasingly attractive, analysts said. 

 "We see scope for all the regions' currencies to strengthen, all have had reasons for being held back recently," said Koon Chow, emerging market currency analyst at CSFB in London. 

 "We've had intervention in Slovakia, verbal intervention from Hungary's central bank and finance ministry, political uncertainty in Poland and a deteriorating trade and current account deficit in the Czech Republic." 

 Referendums on EU membership could add to currency strength in the region, risking a revival of surges late last year which governments feared would slow economic convergence with the wealthier EU. 

 Of 10 candidates, Malta, Slovenia and Hungary have already voted to join the expanding 15-nation EU. Lithuania votes this weekend, followed by Slovakia, Poland, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Latvia. Cyprus is not expected to hold a vote. 

 The June 7-8 referendum in Poland, by far the biggest EU candidate, may attract strong inflows if the result goes in favour of membership as the polls indicate is likely. 

 "Poland's case is a little more uncertain and, if there is a 'yes' vote, strong capital inflows may start, not only in Poland, but across the whole region," said ABN's Papp. 

 SLOVAKIA MAY CUT FIRST 

 Analysts said Slovakia may be the first to cut interest rates after the central bank bought 200 million euros in the market on Monday to curb the crown . 

 The bank may bring forward its end-month meeting to cut the 6.5 percent two-week repo rate, and may even cut market players' access to high-yield repos as Hungary's central bank did early this year to fend off speculation. 

 "They can intervene in the market, they can cut interest rates, and they could also not sterilise surplus market liquidity with their repo tenders," said CSOB's Marek Gabris. 

 In Poland, April food price data due on Wednesday is expected to encourage a further reduction in interest rates. 

 "The earlier fall of the zloty was caused purely by political risks, and now the markets return to fundamentals and focus on the EU referendum," said Jacek Wisniewski, analyst at Bank Pekao in Warsaw. 

 Hungarian Central Bank Governor Zsigmond Jarai said on Tuesday he saw no reason for interest rate cuts, adding the NBH could only follow other cuts in the region if they prompted inflows into Hungary and lifted markets. 

 "Hungary can potentially deliver a cut if the forint were to strengthen to 240-242 (from around 245 to the euro)," said Chow.

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary int'l reserves drop to 13.05 bln euros.
text:
BUDAPEST, March 7 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said on Friday that its international reserves dropped to 13.05 billion euros by the end of February from 14.19 billion euros at the end of January. 

 The bank published the figures on its official website www.mnb.hu("http://www.mnb.hu/"). 

 The drop in forex reserves is an important indication about the actual amount of euros offloaded on the markets by the NBH since its interventions in mid-January, when it had to fend off a massive foreign speculative attack against the strong end of the forint's 30 percent wide flotation band. 

 NBH Governor Zsigmond Jarai said last month the foreign exchange reserves dropped to 12-13 billion euros in February, adding that this lower figure already included proceeds from a eurobond worth one billion euros issued earlier this year. 

 Jarai said two-thirds of the speculative capital that came in January, had already left Hungary's markets. 

 But analysts said the data published on Friday showed there was still a significant amount of 'hot forints' in the markets, seeking a home. 

 "These data suggest that the problem is still there...that there is still some 2.8 billion euros worth of hot money around," said Istvan Zsoldos at CA IB in Budapest. 

 "It's not worrying but it shows that it's not quite true that two-thirds of the hot money has left," he added. 

 In January the NBH bought an estimated almost five billion euros during interventions to defend the limits of the forint's ERM-2 style trading bands. 

 Then the bank also slashed its key interest rates and imposed strict limits on its key two-week deposit facility, trying to force speculators' 'hot forints' to leave Hungary's financial markets, where the huge excess liquidity hindered their efficient operation. 

 Last month the NBH reversed these earlier emergency measures, hiking the overnight deposit rate by 200 basis points to 5.50 percent and bringing monetary policy back to normal. 

 The bank also abolished restrictions on its weekly two-week deposit tender, which currently yields 6.5 percent. 

 The bank said these steps could be made as two-thirds of the speculative capital which came in January had already left Hungary's markets, via the central bank's euro selling auctions, interventions or deals with local exporters. 

Hungary's international reserves jumped to 14.19 billion euros by the end of January, from 9.92 billion at end of 2002 as a result of the speculative attack on the band.

title: Hungary's forint bucks easier trend amid rate talk.
text:
BUDAPEST, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint bucked a central European trend for easing currencies on Thursday, closing flat against the euro amid market talk of a possible central bank (NBH) hike in the overnight deposit rate. 

 Short-term Treasury bill yields rose on the speculation, while government bond yields ticked up slightly amid uncertainty over monetary policy and political tensions over Iraq, shrugging off earlier over-subscribed auctions. 


At 1445 GMT, the forint           was quoted at 246.10/30, or 10.83
percent above parity in its 30 percent wide trading band, against
Wednesday's 246.15/30 close. It had earlier dipped to lows near
247.00.
Other central European currencies weakened on growing concern over
possible military action Iraq, with Poland's zloty         falling to
32-month lows against the euro.

title: Hungary forint down in thin trade, T-bills firm.
text:
BUDAPEST, Feb 14 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint fell in thin
trade on Friday on small-scale euro orders from commercial bank
clients, while short-term government paper yields continued to

    The forint                 closed at 245.60/80 against the
