title: Poland, Slovakia May Gain From Hungary's Forint Upheaval
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- Despite the currency turmoil in Hungary recently, analysts and fund managers say they haven't lost faith in the region. 

 They say that while Hungary - which had been one of the top euro-zone convergence plays of late - has lost some of its luster, other countries, notably Poland and Slovakia, remain attractive spots for those looking to park money in Central and Eastern Europe. 

 And, they say, Hungary shouldn't be written off just because some speculators got burned by central bank action last week. 

 "The fundamentals and the outlook haven't changed for Central and Eastern Europe, despite a rise in risk premiums for emerging countries," said Gyorgy Barcza, economist at ING Bank. "Polish, Slovak and even the Hungarian markets (can still) offer appreciating currencies and relatively high bond yields." 

 In Hungary and Poland, which are headed for European Union membership in 2004, long-term bonds are providing real yields of 13%-14%, Barcza added. 

 The Hungarian central bank's success at defending the forint's trading band last week with massive rate cuts and new restrictions on two-week deposits sent shock waves through markets, serving as a rude awakening to those who saw unlimited profits in the region's markets. 

 "Many leveraged speculators got severely burned (in Hungary)," said Callum Henderson, head of emerging EMEA research and strategy at Bank of America in London. "Until now, there was good money in Hungary." 

 Many managers responded by exiting Hungary and by winding up positions in other regional currencies. In knee-jerk reactions, speculators estimated to have lost EUR300 million on the forint attack closed positions elsewhere, which hit the Polish zloty, and the Czech and Slovak korunas. 

 "After last week, a number of investors are probably attaching a somewhat higher risk premium to (regional) exposure," said in a research note Thursday. "(However,) the normal thing would be to assume that this quickly unwinds." 


     Dedicated Emerging Market Funds To Remain In Region



Analysts agree that any real worries should be short term. They point
out that many dedicated emerging market funds see this area as the best
choice among global emerging economies, especially when viewed against
those in troubled Latin American countries.



Poland, the largest economy in the region, appears to be a top choice
for investors. Polish "inflation remains remarkably benign, and real
interest rates remain the highest in the region," Bank of America's
Henderson said.



"This (recent zloty weakness) is a classic case of regional contagion,
but the volatility's mainly technical," said Thomas Browne, vice
president for emerging market research at Deutsche Bank in London. "I
still believe we're in for a multiyear linear appreciation trend for the
zloty,"



That trend could see the zloty at 3.60 against the euro by year-end, a
15% appreciation, Browne said.



Slovakia, once the poor cousin of the Czech Republic, had been largely
overlooked by investors since its split with Czechoslovakia. Now,
however, prospects for a stronger currency - boosted by foreign direct
capital inflows and high interest rates compared with neighbor Hungary -
are helping to lure fund managers.



"Slovakia is very interesting," ING's Barcza said. "It has the most
undervalued currency. Its economy is on the way to restructure to a
market economy, and its productivity gains will lead to a currency
appreciation, while inflation is to remain low."



Barcza said he expects the Slovak koruna to strengthen to SKK40.5
against the euro by year-end from SKK42.35.



"We have decided to add to our allocation (in Slovak bonds) despite
underperformance year-to-date," said Bank of America's Henderson, who
raised Slovakia's weight to 10% from 5% in his model portfolio. He said
he favors the 7.8% bonds maturing January 2007 and the 9.00% bonds of
April 2005.



       Russia Might Also Gain From Hungary's Woes



Other winners of capital flows out of Hungary could be Russia and
Turkey, although Turkey's potential may be limited because of doubts
about reform and geopolitical worries over a U.S. war with Iraq.



"Russia has the highest weight in my portfolio," said Zoltan Cseko,
fund manager at CIB Fund Manager in Budapest. "High oil prices are
bond-negative, but for Russia, they provide fast economic growth."



Turkey is still in negotiations with the E.U. on getting a date to
open formal negotiations for membership, and investors remain cautious
despite its potential.



"Turkish bond markets are neither a convincing nor cheap enough
proposition to constitute an obvious convergence trade," UBS Warburg
said in a research note. "But dedicated convergence funds are itching
for new product. In this sense, 2003 will be the make or break year for
Turkey as a convergence trade."



Many analysts are quick to remind, though, that all is not lost in
Hungary, saying that last week's 200-basis-point rate cut weakened the
forint to an unsustainable level given central bank inflation goals.
That means the bank eventually will have to hike rates to push the
currency close to the strong edge of its trading band.



Even after the central bank's success last week at defending its
currency band, some analysts speculate that Hungary could be pushed to
eventually abandon it.



"Likely E.U accession in May 2004 suggests that fundamental pressure
for currency appreciation remains intact," said J.P. Morgan, the bank
that is suspected of being behind the attack on the forint.



"Most likely, local authorities eventually will revalue the forint's
parity or widen the fluctuation band or let the currency float freely,"
it added.



The bank allows the forint to trade in a plus-or-minus 15% band around
a midpoint set against the euro at HUF276.11 ($1=HUF231.45). Foreign
speculators, reportedly led by J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs, pushed the
forint out of its band on the strong side at HUF234.69 in an effort to
force Hungary to revalue its currency trading band.



The National Bank of Hungary intervened by selling forints worth an
estimated EUR5 billion to EUR7 billion over two days to weaken the
forint. The bank slashed its key, two-week deposit rate to 6.5% and
limited the amount for accepting deposits from commercial banks.



-By Margit Feher, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0622;
margit.feher@dowjones.com



(David McQuaid in Warsaw contributed to this story.)

title: Zloty at 31-mth low vs euro,hedge funds cut exposure.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty fell to a 31-month low versus the euro on Thursday as hedge funds cut exposure to the region's currencies after taking losses in neighbouring Hungary, but any further decline was seen limited, analysts said. 

 The zloty has tumbled nearly six percent since Hungary slashed interest rates and intervened on the forex market last week to keep the forint from breaching the upper end of its trading band. 

 "This is spillover from Hungary, hedge funds have taken losses there and are reducing positions elsewhere," said Wike Groenenberg, economist at Schroder Salomon Smith Barney in London. 

 The zloty traded at 4.2222 versus the euro and 3.923 against the dollar at 1302 GMT, down 1.3 and 1.0 percent respectively on the day. 

 "We will see further volatility as long as uncertainty in Hungary continues. But when it fades, there may be a buying opportunity," she said, adding that more zloty-bashing by Polish government officials could also unsettle the currency. 

 The zloty, forint and Czech crown have all benefited from so-called convergence trades, as investors mopped up the region's assets hoping yields would fall in the run-up to European Union entry in 2004 and euro zone membership later in the decade. 

 Negative global sentiment towards emerging markets amid growing uncertainty ahead of a possible U.S.-led war against Iraq has led investors to unwind some of the hefty gains made in the region's currencies over the past year. 

 "Once the global market situation stabilises for a bit, we should see the zloty return to its slow upward drift," said Mateusz Szczurek," chief economist at ING Bank Slaski in Warsaw. So far in 2003, the zloty has lost 4.9 percent versus the euro, the forint 5.3 percent and the Czech crown has remained flat, while the single currency strengthened nearly 2.5 percent versus the dollar during the same period. 

 VERBAL INTERVENTION

 The zloty, a free floating currency since 1999, also continued to be unsettled by recent comments from Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko. 

 Kolodko told Reuters in an interview in Madrid late on Wednesday that "the gradual yet limited depreciation of Polish zloty will continue" in the short-term. 

 Kolodko also reiterated his view that Poland should join the euro zone in four years at a zloty exchange rate of 4.35 to the euro. 

 That has set a target for the volatile market, which had in the past largely ignored government attempts to talk down the currency. 

 Some players also fretted that the finance ministry had or was on the verge of carrying out an earlier threat to directly intervene in the market and sell the zloty. But analysts said any such move, which would be the first by the ministry, would probably not take place until March or April at the earliest, if at all. 

 The ministry has in the past signalled it could go directly to the market to buy hard currencies to finance its foreign debt financing costs instead of dealing with the central bank. While some observers believe the government could carry out this form of intervention others say such a move is unlikely since it would probably boost costs at the spend-thrift ministry. 

 Poland's fixed income market also continued to edge lower on Thursday but selling appeared to have run its course, said analysts, with near-term rate cut hopes underpinning prices. 

 Two-year bond yields were up eight basis points to 5.60 percent, while five-year notes were down three points to 5.61 - still a shade above Wednesday's poorly-bid primary tender. 

 Analysts expect the central bank's 10-member Monetary Policy Council (MPC) to shave 25 basis points from its main rate - now at 6.75 percent - when it meets next week.

title: Hungary  forint eases, cenbank  intervention  seen.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 21 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint eased against the euro on Tuesday and a continued fall would likely provoke renewed central bank (NBH) interventions to resell part of the billions of euros bought by the bank last week, dealers said. 

 "Currently the market is consolidating at lower levels and prices do not move very hectically as there is interest on both sides," said Orsolya Liptai of K&H Bank. 

 At 0850 GMT the forint  was quoted at 246.30/60, or 10.8 percent above parity in its 30-percent-wide band, down from late Monday's 245.40/50. Against the dollar it eased to 231.00/30 from 230.00/30. 

 Dealers said foreign investors were on the selling side, while Hungarian exporters bought the euro, being happy with higher forint revenues after several weeks when the currency traded close to the top of its band at 234.69 versus the euro. 

 However, exporters were unlikely to soak up a big chunk of around 1,000 billion forints ($4.32 billion) sold by the NBH last week to fend off a speculative attack against the band. 

 "If the NBH is consistent, they have to step in again if the forint reaches the 248-250 range," Liptai said. "That's not too far now." 

 The NBH fended off the attack on the band by slashing interest rates and changing its deposit rules to force speculative money to leave the country through the currency market. 

 The flight of hot money began on Friday amid high volatility and NBH interventions to reverse falls of the currency. 

 The NBH posts gains by selling euros at lower forint levels than 234.69, where it bought the euros. Tuesday is the settlement day of most of last week's euro buying intervention, and after a relapse on Monday the market expects continued volatility. 

 With huge amounts of surplus forint liquidity seeking a home in the markets, they will pay close attention to a three-month government bill auction and the NBH's two-week deposit tender later on Tuesday, dealers said. 

 The government will offer three-month bills worth 25 billion forints, the usual weekly amount. The three-month bill is Hungary's shortest paper and the only one for which demand surged after the hot money outflow began. 

 As part of the measures to scare off hot money, the NBH limited deposits to be accepted at 100 billion forints at its tender, below the usual amount of around 200 billion forints. 

 The overnight interbank money market was in a standstill, with all excess money flowing into the NBH's overnight deposits at 3.5 percent. 

 "Everybody is awash with money and puts it into the NBH. Why should anyone pay more than 3.5 percent now?," said Balazs Hajdu of Commerzbank. 

 Speculators sitting on piles of forint positions, will find no comfort in overnight deposits either as the NBH cut the rate on its only remaining unlimited facility by 400 basis points to 3.5 percent, much below interest rates elsewhere in the region.

title: Hungary grain exports slow despite weak  currency .
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 20 (Reuters) - The weakening of Hungary's forint last week after central bank intervention and sharp interest rate cuts failed to boost grain exports, and the currency needs to lose more ground to boost grain sales, traders said on Monday. 

 Hungary's farmers have supplies of half a million tonnes of exportable wheat and at least twice as much maize, but demand was slow despite the weaker forint, they said. 

 "What we need is an even stronger dollar or higher international grains prices, but there's little immediate hope of either," said Robert Vajo, trader at brokerage Agrokont. 

 Last week's turmoil on Hungary's foreign exchange markets, left key interest rates 200 basis points lower at 6.50 percent, and weakened the forint to 230 to the dollar from 220. 

 The weakening forint was followed by a rise in grain futures prices of 600-1,000 forints per tonne, dampening potential export demand. 

 "Wheat is trickling out of the country to neighbouring destinations, but only in tens of thousands of tonnes at a time," said Janos Szojka, a trader at brokerage Swap. 

 Hungarian grains prices need to be reduced quite sharply to compete with cheaper alternative sources in the Ukraine and Russia, he said. 

 Earlier this month, the Jordanian government said it bought 100,000 tonnes of Russian, Kazakh and Hungarian origin hard wheat. 

 "Our only hope is that grains from the East will not have duty-free access to the European Union this year," Szojka said. 

 Agrokont's Vajo said a few truckloads of wheat found regular buyers in Romania and Yugoslavia but beyond that there was little in the way of new deals. 

 Szojka added that with hundreds of thousands of tonnes of grain in state-subsidised stores there was little pressure on farmers to go below current asking prices. 

 He added that grains returning from storage in the spring may not make too much difference either. 


On the Budapest Commodity Exchange, nearby March maize  closed at 21,990
forints ($92.58) per tonne on Monday, down 210 forints, May      lost 270
forints to 22,050 and July         fell 300 forints to 22,850.
March wheat  eased 70 forints to 22,580, but May          and August    were
unchanged at 22,750 and 23,000 forints respectively.

title: ANALYSIS-Poland's euro ambitions hinge on budget reform.
text:
WARSAW, Jan 17 (Reuters) - Poland's goal of adopting the euro by its target date of 2007 will slip out of reach if the government fails to tackle budget reforms now to boost investment and cut welfare handouts, analysts said. 

 But deep reform is unlikely given the government's weak economic record and its fear that unveiling spending cuts before a European Union referendum in June could hurt the "Yes" vote. 

 Recent ministerial changes, including Friday's sacking of Health Minister Mariusz Lapinski, risk further disruption to economic reforms already running behind schedule. 

 Poland needs to fix the budget so that it can absorb billions of euros in development funds from Brussels after the eastern European country's expected EU accession in May 2004. Such funds require co-financing by the beneficiary state. 

 The region's other main EU hopefuls, Hungary and the Czech Republic, are also struggling to bring their budget deficits below a ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product required by the Maastricht Treaty to qualify for the euro zone. 

 Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko had promised to present details of his budget reforms in the New Year but has still not revealed details, leaving the issue on the back burner for now. 

 But Jacek Tomkiewicz, an economist at Kolodko's "Tiger" think-tank and ministry aide, said some guidelines had been set. 

 "We will need to find an extra 10 billion zlotys ($2.6 billion) or so in our budget for EU-related costs. Our aim is to do this without increasing the deficit," Tomkiewicz said. 

 Poland has set its 2003 deficit at 39 billion zlotys, or 3.9 percent of GDP. Mandatory spending, such as index-linked rises in pensions, amount to nearly 70 percent of all outlays. 

 Changes could include a shakeup of the generous farmers' pension scheme, called KRUS, but that could run into heavy opposition from the Peasants Party, the junior partner in the ruling coalition. 

 "I don't expect a sweeping reform. Very few details will become public before the referendum," said Janusz Jankowiak, chief economist at BRE Bank in Warsaw. 

 IF NOT 2007, THEN WHEN? 

 The 14-month-old left-wing cabinet has freed up Poland's rigid labour code but failed to restructure loss-making heavy industries like coal mining, railways and shipbuilding, fearful of adding to a record 18 percent jobless rate. 

 "If the 2004 budget is glued together by an increase in the deficit, then talk about joining the euro zone in 2007 is completely unrealistic," said Witold Orlowski, economic adviser to Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski. 

 "Poland's price stability is not guaranteed and if we delay budget reforms and only meet fiscal entry conditions in five or six years, we may then find we don't meet other criteria." 

 Delayed euro entry would be a blow to convergence investors who have bet tens of billions of euros on early euro adoption and could be a disincentive for government reforms. 

 On the other hand, keeping the zloty longer would help Poland maintain natural steam vents for its developing economy - enabling it, for instance to run a higher inflation rate and see its currency appreciate. 

 "Meeting the Maastricht Criteria should be the basis of policy-making for any government regardless of the accession schedule," said Tim Ash, economist at Bear Stearns in London. "I am not convinced it wouldn't be better for Poland's economy to develop further ahead of EMU membership." 

 BUDGETS AND CURRENCY BANDS 

 This week's market meltdown in Hungary, where the central bankintervened heavily on currency markets and slashed interest rates to contain the forint, also highlights the risk of running a wide deficit while imposing a currency trading band. 

 High deficits, financed by debt issues, have sparked foreign portfolio inflows and boosted currencies across the region. 

 So unless borrowing needs are lowered, Poland and the Czech Republic - running a deficit of 6.3 percent of GDP in 2003 - risk similar problems once they ditch their free floating currency for the pre-euro Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2) band. 

 Boguslaw Grabowski, one of 10 members of Poland's rate-setting council, told Reuters joining the ERM's 30 percent trading band without a plan to fulfil the Maastricht criteria would be a "huge mistake". 

 The Czechs, who do not expect to adopt the euro before 2009, aim to curb their deficit to 3.7 percent of GDP in 2006 mostly by curbing welfare payments, sick leave and jobless benefits. 

 Hungary, whose inflation prospects are unclear following this week's fiasco, still eyes EMU membership in 2007 but faces a formidable challenge in reforming public finances first after the deficit topped eight percent of GDP last year.

title: UPDATE 5-Hungary c.bank changes tack, steadies forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 17 (Reuters) - Claiming to have beaten off speculative attacks that drove the forint to the top of its trading band this week, Hungary's central bank on Friday offloaded some of the billions of euros it earlier bought to support the currency. 

 After a roller-coaster two days in which the central bank cut interest rates by 200 basis points and bought 4-5 billion euros at 234.69 forints to defend its exchange rate regime, it reversed direction and sold euros at around 245 forints. 

 Analysts said the central bank (NBH) was trying to keep markets on their toes, signalling it wanted the forint to firm within the band, but not enough to move it back to the top where it had given speculators a clear target to attack. 

 "I believe the bank is, and will be, selling batches of euros...trying to stabilise the forint in a...range which would be a more difficult target for speculators to hit," said Istvan Zsoldos at CA IB Securities. 

 The forint closed around 244.50/80 to the euro, or 11.4 percent above parity in its 30 percent wide band versus late Thursday levels nearer 250. 

 ING Bank's Gyorgy Barcza said the NBH was playing cat-and-mouse with the markets, propping up the forint - which dropped around six percent on Thursday in the wake of the bank's shock rate cuts and market intervention - while keeping markets guessing as to its real goal. 

 "The bank's primary goal now is to scare off speculators, but it also wants to take profits on its long euro positions worth up to five billion euros," Barcza said, adding he reckoned the NBH had offloaded 500-800 million euros. 

 Others put the NBH's Friday euro sales at much lower levels. 

 NO BAND SHIFT 

 Finance Minister Csaba Laszlo said a concerted government and central bank effort had seen off the speculators. 

 He again ruled out any shift in the band for the next 18-24 months, by which time Hungary will be in the European Union and possibly inside the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2), the waiting room for euro zone members. 

 "It seems this (week's) speculative attack has not been successful and those who speculated on a forint band shift will suffer very big losses," Laszlo told reporters. 

 Traders, however, said they expected markets to stay choppy. 

 "The big amounts from the interventions are circulating, and looking for a home," said Peter Koppi at Raiffeisen Securities. 

 "There is uncertainty." 

 Bond dealers reported hectic trade, with prices gyrating as foreign investors sought to exit Hungary after being burnt by the NBH's unpredictable intervention and rate cut tactics. 

 "Selling was stronger, with foreigners fleeing the (bond) market," said Robert Barlai of Erste Bank Investment. 

 Some dealers said foreign investors had only wound up a small chunk of the short euro positions built up earlier in the week when the NBH intervened at 234.69 to the euro to defend the top of the band. 

 "The massive short positions are still here," one said. 

 "The longer it takes for the forint to go back above 240, the more investors will have to ask themselves how much loss they're ready to take," the dealer added. 

 Deutsche Bank trader Pal Geszti said the forint would stay between 240 and 250 to the euro for the next couple of weeks. 

 "Those holding short positions must bid...we expect them to step in if the forint rises above 240 to try and get out with as little a loss as possible," he said. 

 ROLLER-COASTER 


On Thursday, the NBH cut key interest rates by 100 basis points for the
second time in two days to 6.5 percent and lowered the overnight
deposit rate to 3.5 percent to depress the forint            from the
top of the band.



The band, designed to steady the forint, was widened in May 2001 as
part of Hungary's preparation for euro zone entry, possibly by 2007.



Hungary is central Europe's only EU candidate to have already adopted a
currency regime similar to the ERM.



The forint's roller-coaster ride knocked some of the shine off the
Slovak crown         and the Polish zloty                as investors
closed positions in the wake of Hungary's monetary mayhem.

title: WRAPUP 2- Hungary  slashes rates,  intervenes  to cool  currency .
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Hungary's monetary authorities fought to hold down the surging forint on Thursday, cutting rates sharply and staging huge market interventions to keep the currency within the upper limits of its ERM-2 type system. 

 The Hungarian central bank (NBH) cut its key interest rates by 100 basis points, the second such slashing of borrowing costs in two days, bringing rates down to 6.5 percent in an attempt to force speculators to abandon upward pressure on the forint. 

 Dealers fled the forint after the rate cut, buying back euro and sending the currency plunging to 250.00 from earlier levels of 234.69, the top of the trading band, where the central bank had to intervene aggressively to cool the unit. 

 The sharp cuts bring Hungarian interest rates a quarter point below nearby Poland's. While the cuts may send capital scampering for higher yielding Polish bonds they will make it hard for the NBH to meet its inflation-fighting targets. 

 "They managed to shift the forint from the strong end of the band, but they may have to intervene tomorrow from the other side," said Istvan Zsoldos of CAIB Securities in Budapest. 

 Analysts said the bank's move to limit the forint deposits it will accept at next week's fixed-rate tender to 100 billion forints ($448.5 million) was key to curbing foreign buyers. 

 "The restriction on deposits will definitely have a strong impact, as it nominally limits the gains on exchange rate speculation," said Dirk Woelfer at S&P MMS in Frankfurt. 

 "Changing the deposit rules was a very smart move," added Orsolya Nyeste at Postabank. 

 CONVERGENCE SPECULATION 

 Foreign capital had poured in to take advantage of Hungary's high rates and its security as a future European Union member. Investors expect interest rates to converge fast with lower euro-land levels, bringing easy profits on government bonds. 

 The speculative inflow has put the NBH in a policy quandary. It has abandoned its opposition to rate cuts to try to hold down the forint, but risks the unit falling to levels that will reignite inflation and put economic stability at risk. 

 "If interest rate levels drop so much that they hit the pain threshold of foreign investors a capital flight can set off, which can make it difficult for the bank to hold the forint at strong levels," said Gyorgy Barcza at ING Bank in Budapest. 

 Analysts said the delicate balancing act may be difficult to pull off and signalled the problems future EU members will have trying to find the right level to enter the euro currency if inflation and capital-enticing deficit levels are too high. 

INTERVENTION

 Dealers said the NBH had bought over four billion euros in constant interventions throughout Thursday, the second day it had been forced into the market. 

 Despite the turmoil in the markets Central bank chief Zsigmond Jarai and Finance Minister Csaba Laszlo said they were determined not to shift the current parameters of the 30 percent trading band. 

 "Today I consulted with Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy and ...Jarai and the common stance of us is: there will not be a band widening or shift," Laszlo said in a statement. 

 Jarai early on Thursday promised interest rate cuts quickly to stem the forint, prompting dealers to say that such a policy would effectively let the market set the price of borrowing. 

 "As market players have realized their power (to change central bank policy) a renewed attack on the forint can not be excluded at all. Moreover, a nominal key rate at 6.5 percent is still attractive," said Zoltan Torok of Raiffeisen Securities. 

 But NBH determination to put out speculative fires and resist upward forint pressure was underlined by it changing deposit rules and slashing overnight deposit rates to limit the ability of forint holders to find a home for the unit. 

 With falling yields on high-flying government bonds investors left with forint after the interventions now have few lucrative places to lodge Hungarian currency. 

 "The restriction on deposits will definitely have a strong impact on the currency as it nominally limits the gains on exchange rate speculation," said Dirk Woelfer of S&P MMS in Frankfurt. 

 "The central bank is a lot smarter than the market gave it credit for and policy is now directed solely at burning speculators and ensuring that they don't come back," said one Hungarian analyst. 

 EURO APPROACH 

 The NBH's woes are a precursor of the problems many ex-communist EU members-in-waiting will have as they try to enter the euro, which they are expected to join this decade. 

 Among eight east European states due to join the EU in May 2004 only Hungary is operating an ERM-2 style band system, which all will eventually have to adopt after agreeing parity rates to the euro with the European Central Bank and EU authorities. 

 The ERM-2 bands are supposed to steady a currency as it nears euro entry. Hungary's struggle to hold its currency down, protecting exporters, underlines the need to choose a credible parity rate that markets will not attack as unacceptably low. 

 Hungary's interest rates had been among the highest among the region's EU designees. 

 They still offer investors a 375 basis point carry over euro zone rates, suggesting speculators will not stay away for long and many analysts believe wealth catch-up and falling inflation also point to a higher forint.

title: Pressure on forint eases but  intervention  ongoing.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 16 (Reuters) - Upward pressure on Hungary's
forint  continued to force the central bank to
sell the currency at the top of its band in midday trade on
Thursday.
Activity had eased since the morning when investors sold up
to four billion euros to the central bank (NBH), but the bank
was seen cutting interest rates later on Thursday to avoid being
forced into further massive interventions, dealers said.
"They have to cut rates and they also said they would," one
dealer said. "Otherwise someone will ring at their door in the
morning saying they have brought forty trucks of euros."
Market players continued to buy forint at the top of the
30-percent-wide band at 234.69 against the euro at 1115 GMT, and
the dollar was also at the edge of the band at 221.90/222.20.



Earlier on Thursday NBH Governor Zsigmond Jarai told a news
conference that the bank was ready to intervene and further
reduce its interest rates after Wednesday's 100 basis point cut
if large interventions continued to be needed.
Traders said the market expected a new cut to come later on
Thursday.
Jarai, outlining a new NBH strategy amid the heavy capital



inflows, said the bank would cut rates to stem speculation but



needed the currency to remain near the top of the band to help



it defend its inflation targets.



He said the bank needed a strong forint since CPI targets



were threatened by the impacts of last years' bloated budget



deficit and surging wages.



The governor suggested that interest rates received on



two-week deposits placed with the NBH by market players who buy



forint now may be reduced to much lower levels by next Tuesday,



when the bank reopens its two-week facility to investors.



The facility is open once a week. Jarai's suggestion implies



sharp rate cuts before Tuesday.

title: Hungary Eurobond Issue Plans Could Be Scaled Back-Agency
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- Hungary may scale back its Eurobond issue plans for this year if the National Bank of Hungary needs to keep intervening on the currency market steadily to defend the forint's trading band, state news agency MTI quoted Minister of Finance Csaba Laszlo as saying Wednesday. 

 "If the central bank is forced to intervene continuously, and that pumps up the bank's foreign currency reserves, we may reconsider the issue of a further EUR1 billion in Eurobonds," Laszlo was quoted as saying. 

 Hungary said earlier this week that it plans to issue EUR1 billion in eurobonds, to be followed by other issues totaling a further EUR1 billion later this year. 

 But Wednesday the central bank was forced to intervene on the forint market to weaken the forint, as obliged legally when the currency hits its strongest spot in its trading band. The bank defended the forint's trading band by selling forints for euros. 

 Dealers said the bank sold forints worth several hundreds of millions of euros in the intervention. 

 The bank allows the forint to trade in a plus or minus 15% band with the band's midpoint fixed against the euro at HUF276.11. The strongest level of the forint against the euro is at HUF234.69, where the central bank needs to accept euros for forints. 

 -By Margit Feher, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0622; margit.feher@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary cenbank chief sees no room to cut rates.
text:
VIENNA, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank governor said on Wednesday that he saw no opportunity for interest rates cuts at present and insisted that a relatively strong currency was needed to achieve low inflation. 

 Zsigmond Jarai was speaking to an investment conference in Vienna just minutes before the National Bank of Hungary confirmed it was intervening in the foreign exchange market to stop the forint breaching the upper limits of its trading band. 

 He said he agreed with the government that there was no need at the moment to adjust the band. 

 "We don't see any room (for rate cuts) at the moment," Jarai said in answer to a question why Hungarian interest rates have not been slashed to weaken the strong forint. 

 "Why we didn't decrease the interest rate this week? The reason was heavy inflationary pressure in the economy," he added. 

 The NBH has come under pressure to cut rates from the strengthening forint, which the government says hurts exporters but Jarai said a strong currency helped to control inflation. 

 "We do believe that to achieve low inflation we need a relatively strong currency," Jarai added. 

 A Hungarian central bank spokesman in Budapest said on Wednesday the bank had stepped into the market to buy euros from domestic banks when the forint reached the 234.69 per euro strong end of its 30 percent trading band. 

 BUDGET DEFICIT 

 Jarai said that given the country's ballooning budget deficit there was no way the central bank could risk a weaker currency. 

 "We would be happy to achieve low inflation with a weaker currency if the deficit would be substantially lower and wage increases would be controlled by an income policy," he said. 

 He noted that the budget deficit had swollen from 4.1 percent of gross domestic product in 2001 to "nearly 10 percent" last year. While the official figure was 9.4 percent for 2002, he said it would soon be revised. 

 "The only good macroeconomic indicator (in Hungary) is the relatively low inflation," he said. 

 He said that if wage growth was under control and the budget deficit slashed, the central bank "might find the room to loosen monetary conditions". 

 "We fully agree with the government that there is no need to change the band," he said. 

 Regarding the strengthening of the currency, Jarai said Hungary's expected European Union entry in 2004 was playing a role in market sentiment. 

 "At the moment there appears to be euphoria in the market due to EU accession," he said. But he warned that a shift in sentiment in the opposite direction could easily come as a result of some unforseen event or development.

title: UPDATE 2-Hungary c.bank steps in to defend forint band.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank (NBH) intervened to defend the forint's trading regime on Wednesday, buying large batches of euros from domestic banks. 

 The NBH has to step in when the forint hits the top of its 30 percent wide trading band of 234.69 against the euro. 

 The intervention was the first since the band was widened in May 2001, part of a series of measures to prepare Hungary for membership of the euro single currency, possibly in 2007. 

 Hungary is central Europe's only European Union candidate to have already adopted a currency regime matching the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM-2), effectively the euro zone waiting room. 

 Dealers said the NBH began intervening at around 1030 GMT. 

 "Domestic banks started selling euros in batches of 10 million to the (central) bank," one dealer at K&H Bank said. 

 NBH spokesman Gabor Missura later confirmed the bank was buying euros for forints. 

 There was no immediate indication of how much the NBH may have spent in the intervention. 

 INFLATION GOAL 

 The NBH, whose primary goal is to check inflation, earlier signalled it would rather intervene than cut interest rates which, at 8.50 percent, are the highest in the region and offer a carry of over 550 basis points against the euro. 

 The bank has so far fended off pressure to cut rates because of the stronger forint, despite howls of protest from exporters, who traditionally drive Hungary's economic growth. 

 But NBH Governor Zsigmond Jarai has said the NBH cannot risk a weaker currency, given a ballooning budget deficit of over nine percent of GDP last year and fast rising wages. 

 Jarai, speaking during a central bankers' conference in Vienna, said he saw no room to cut rates for now, adding a relatively strong forint was needed to hit the bank's tough 4.5 percent end-2003 inflation goal. 

 The forint, which has risen around 12 percent against the euro since May 2001, has been knocking at the top of its band for days, briefly breaching the 234.69 level on Monday, but only after 1400 GMT, when the central bank had already closed. 

 On Tuesday, the forint  closed at 234.75/80 to the euro. 

 The currency gained strength on Wednesday after December data showed year-on-year inflation at 4.8 percent, better than the 5.1 percent many in the markets had forecast. 

 By 1150 GMT, the currency had eased back a touch, quoted at 234.66/235.16 to the euro. 

 The forint's protracted strength has prompted speculation the NBH and the centre-left government may be forced to revalue the flotation band, but Finance Minister Csaba Laszlo has stressed he sees no revaluation for at least 18-24 months. 

 Hungary is expected to join the EU in May 2004 and would be keen to go into the ERM-2 around the same time. 

 The forint has been pushed higher by heavy foreign capital - one local estimate puts this as high as eight billion euros - chasing high-yielding bonds ahead of gradual convergence with lower EU rates.

title: Hungarian Ctrl Bk Sees  Intervention  Costs Modest-CSFB
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- The National Bank of Hungary expects the costs of any intervention in the market to combat forint strength will be modest, Credit Suisse First Boston said in a research note Tuesday, citing sources at the bank. 

 The sources told CSFB that the bank would be willing to intervene at a scale similar to the EUR2.5 billion and EUR3 billion it spent annually between 1996 and 2001, during which time it intervened regularly. 

 The bank doesn't expect the amount needed to sterilize the impact of foreign funds will be that high, since the widening of the current account deficit will limit the pressure on the forint to strengthen, CSFB said. 

 However, CSFB believes that the central bank is downplaying the size of any interventions and "that hot and convergence money inflows will remain substantial," pushing up the forint. The current account deficit isn't cause for a headache, CSFB added. 

 The Hungarian forint is at record highs, and has been trading close to its strongest level against the euro for several days. The bank allows the forint to trade in a range of plus or minus 15% against the midpoint of its band against the euro. Around 1200 GMT the forint was trading at HUF234.95 ($1=HUF221.96), very close to its strongest level of HUF234.69. 

 The remarks come a day after the central bank left its key interest rate unchanged at 8.5%, surprising economists who expected a cut due to the forint's strength. 

 The decision probably reflects the bank's concerns that it could miss its 4.5% annual inflation target in December, CSFB said. But CSFB sees room for cuts totaling 100 basis points if the upward pressure on the forint persists, in addition to any foreign exchange intervention. 

 Minister of Finance Csaba Laszlo also said Tuesday that he sees room for the central bank to ease its rates. 

 -By Margit Feher, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0622; margit.feher@dowjones.com

title: Hungary finmin says strong HUF limits bank's options.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Hungarian Finance Minister Csaba Laszlo said on Monday the forint's firming to the top of its trading band would limit the independent central bank's (NBH) room for manouevre over monetary policy. 

 Laszlo told Reuters he did not want to comment on the bank's decision earlier to keep key interest rates on hold at 8.50 percent despite the strong forint and market expectations for a rate cut. 

 However, he indicated that continued upward pressure on the currency could force the bank to cut rates in the near future. 

 "The fact that the forint hit the strong end of its band... signals that the manoeuvring room of the bank's monetary policy will narrow in the future," he said. 

 The bank's decision to leave rates on hold, prompted the forint to rise to the strong end of its 30 percent wide band for the first time since the regime was introduced in May 2001. 

 Analysts said convergence-led capital inflows and speculation about a revaluation of the forint band were likely to keep up the pressure on the band, but the NBH, concerned over inflation, may prefer costly intervention to rate cuts. 

Hungary plans to join the European Union in May 2004 and is eyeing adoption of the euro in 2007. 

 High interest rates have attracted heavy foreign capital inflows into central Europe since late last year. 

 Hungary's forint has also firmed on speculation the bank and centre-left cabinet may have to shift the currency's band at some stage, though both have ruled out any change to the current forint regime in the next 18-24 months.

title: UPDATE 1-Forint tests band, c.bank says not  intervened .
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint         tested its
trading band for the first time on Monday after the central bank (NBH)
disappointed some in the market by leaving key interest rates on hold.



Dealers said the currency, buoyed recently by keen foreign demand
chasing high yields ahead of future euro zone entry, traded at 234.69
to the euro, a maximum 15 percent above the band's central rate.


 "There's been a deal at 234.69 versus the euro in electronic trade," said Attila Behan at K&H Bank. 

 Other dealers confirmed the forint hit the top of its band for the first time since the trading range was widened to 15 percent either side of parity in May 2001. 

 At that level, the NBH has to intervene, buying euros for forints to defend the regime. 

 But a central bank spokesman told Reuters the bank had not sold forints on the market. 

 "(Market players) are trading among themselves," Gabor Missura said. "We're open to 3 p.m. (1400 GMT) and, until then, no one came to us to buy forints." 

 NO RATE CUT, NO INTERVENTION

 NBH Governor Zsigmond Jarai said recently the bank would not intervene in the market before the forint hit the top of its band, but once there, it would defend the regime. 

 Another possible way to ease forint pressure is to trim interest rates but, despite some expectations for a 50 basis point cut on Monday, the NBH opted to keep rates on hold at 8.50 percent. 

 Analysts said the bank was keen to show its policy continued to focus on cutting inflation. Hungary is due to join the European Union in May 2004, and could enter the ERM-2, the euro zone waiting room, around the same time. It is the only central European EU candidate to have already adopted an ERM-type currency band. 

 The strong forint has hit exporters, who traditionally drive the country's economic growth, and who are already reeling as main markets like Germany are in the doldrums. 

 The forint's rise highlights the bank's dilemma on how to defend its 4.5 percent end-2003 inflation target with a tight monetary policy when it can only curb the forint by cutting interest rates. 

 Hungary's inflation, at around five percent, is also one of the highest among the pre-EU states. The NBH wants to bring down inflation to 2-3 percent next year in readiness for euro zone entry, possibly by 2007. 

 During recent forint rallies, analysts said speculative inflows could force a revaluation of the band's parity rate. 

 But both the centre-left government and the independent NBH have said the band would not be revalued before Hungary joins the ERM-2. 

 The cabinet opposes revaluation as this would further dent export competitiveness. It would prefer to see lower interest rates, temporarily sacrificing the NBH's tight inflation target.

title: ANALYSIS-Hungary c.bank baffles markets, wins time.
text:
BUDAPEST, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank (NBH) has bought time by sowing confusion in the markets amid fevered speculation over the strong forint and possible interest rate cuts, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 Last week, the bank took markets by surprise by lopping half a percentage point off key rates - changing tack on a long-standing policy of monetary tightening due to inflation pressures from a soaring budget deficit and surging wages. 

 On Monday, it surprised markets again - leaving rates unchanged amid wide expectations of a cut of anything between 25 and 100 basis points. 

 All the while, the forint has continued to gain, hitting new highs on Tuesday at around 235.60 against the euro, triggering complaints from exporters. 

 The currency's strength is due to heavy capital inflows on the prospects of a smooth European Union entry in 2004 and a fall in interest rates to lower euro zone levels. 

 Analysts said Monday's non-move on rates probably cost a lot of market players a lot of money, showing Hungary's markets are not yet just a one-way bet. 

 "Yesterday's decision leads us to believe that causing confusion could be the bank's strategy," said Mojmir Hampl, analyst at Ceska Sporitelna in Prague. 

 Hampl said a rate cut this week would merely have triggered expectations for further reductions. 

 "By leaving rates steady, the bank proved to be an active player, leaving the ball in the market's court," he said. 

 He said the market was split between those continuing to bet on the bank eventually giving in and cutting rates, and those who were increasingly nervous that the bank may hold firm. 

INTERVENTION TOOL 

Hungary's interest rates are still the highest in pre-EU Central Europe, and bearish stock markets and alternative emerging markets have helped sustain keen interest in the region's assets, analysts said. 

 Hungary's five-year government bonds traded at yields around seven percent on Tuesday, compared with 5.8 percent on the corresponding Polish and 3.8 percent on German five-year bonds. 

 By 1530 GMT, the forint was back down at around 236.20 to the euro, still near the 234.69 top of its trading band, enough to keep speculation alive that Hungary may have to revalue the band's parity upwards in the months ahead. 

 Analysts said the NBH had bought time with its two surprise rate announcements, and had not yet used all the tools it has to discourage speculation if investors get too confident. 

 The risk of the bank using these tools - primarily direct intervention - now hangs over investors, they said, adding that with no rate cut this week the NBH has more room to cut if needed. 

 The head of Hungary's second biggest commercial bank, K&H, earlier said the NBH could curb the forint by intervening, sending a signal that the forint can move into reverse, too. 

 Other central banks in the region, like Slovakia, have used direct intervention to win time, analysts added. 

 "Intervention is useful not because it can cause a temporary currency easing...but it can cause losses and make speculators uncertain," said Dirk Woelfer at Standard & Poor's MMS in Frankfurt. 

 "(Both sides) are now testing each other and contemplating how far the other side is ready to go," he added. 

 Current Hungarian yields offer investors lucrative returns, but some analysts warned it could be difficult to sustain recent gains in central Europe and there could be a hard landing. 

 In Hungary, concerns over a high budget deficit and inflation may resurface, in addition to the risks involved in trying to fathom central bank policy, they said. 

 ""For safety reasons, we recommend not raising Hungarian exposure," said Ceska Sporitelna's Hampl said. "Short-term investors should think about profit-taking." 

 Others, however, said convergence play would continue and the NBH would finally surrender to massive inflows. 

 "(The NBH) will almost certainly cut rates in two weeks time (to spur growth)," HSBC said in a regional report. 

 "...some time next year, it will have to choose between watering down or abandoning its inflation targeting..., or revaluing central parity to allow further forint appreciation."

title: ANALYSIS-Easing,  intervention  won't halt C.Europe  fx  bulls.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Nov 20 (Reuters) - EU candidates' central banks face a tough fight to contain their surging currencies, as bullish foreign investors flock to central Europe knowing juicy returns await them when the region joins the euro zone. 

 Polish, Hungarian and Slovak policy makers look destined to repeat the battle waged by the Czech central bank, which bought billions of euros this year and slashed interest rates below euro-zone levels to stop hot-money inflows pushing up the crown. 

 Like the Czechs, other EU candidates fear that appreciation caused by capital inflows will hit exports and growth as they gear up to join Europe's single market in 2004 and, later in the decade, adopt the euro. 

 Poland, where analysts still see room to ease and pressure on the zloty is not so great, might be able to take a lesson in how the Czechs tamed the crown. But the twin-track defence of rate cuts and intervention may not work for Hungary or Slovakia. 

 Those countries don't have the Czechs' tame inflation and risk stoking price rises if they ease aggressively, while interventions may turn into a blank cheque to speculators. 

 "Is buying a billion euros going to ease the pressure? Two billion? Five billion? Well, if you believe in the convergence play, then no. All it's going to be is a one-way bet for people to play into," said Deutsche Bank analyst Jeff Gable. 

 "Then it becomes a much more difficult choice. If central banks are going to cut interest rates dramatically, then it begins to have implications for their inflationary path." 

 OPENING SHOTS FIRED 

 Investors have rushed to central Europe, where, regardless of fundamentals, they believe debt bought now in future EU members will earn healthy returns as currencies strengthen and the region's interest rates drop to euro-zone levels. 

 Slovakia's central bank fought back last week as foreign inflows pushed the crown to record highs. It bought over 500 million euros over three days and then walloped the market with a 150-basis-point cut in its main rate to 6.5 percent. 

 Hungary followed on Monday with a surprise half-point cut, bringing its key rate to 9.0 percent, as the forint neared the strong end of its 30-percent-wide band against the euro. 

 But the cuts failed to scare away investors, who kept piling on bets that there will be further rate cuts soon, putting the credibility of Hungary's inflation-and exchange rate-targeting regime on the line. 

 Just as in the Exchange Rate Mechanism crises which preceded the creation of the euro, the forint band creates a target which markets can aim at. Only this time, the pressure is on to revalue, not devalue, as Britain and Italy had to in the 1990s. 

 "It's a very difficult situation for the central banks. The question is how far they can go with rate cuts," said Commerzbank's Radomir Jac. "Those we have seen are not working enough to weaken the currencies... and even more rate cuts are unlikely to stop the appreciation." 

 The free-floating Slovak crown, which has firmed more than seven percent since July, has returned towards record highs of 41.12 per euro since the rate cut and interventions. 

 Analysts were unsure as to whether the forint would test the strong side of its band against the euro this year, but noted that the rate cut had not pushed it lower. It was 14.1 percent above its central parity at 237.30 per euro on Wednesday. 

 HOW FAR WILL THEY GO? 

 Analysts said Slovakia and Hungary will likely cut again soon if buying persists, but any such move must be backed by intervention to have any effect. And even then market enthusiasm has a good chance of persisting. 

 "The Czechs only really managed to turn around the crown once their rates were below those of the ECB," said IDEAglobal analyst John Davitte. 

 The Czech central bank's two-week repo rate stands at 2.75 percent, 50 basis points below the European Central Bank's main rate. 

 Davitte said that, with other euro-zone aspirants looking to hit tough targets on inflation and borrowing to qualify for the euro, "I don't think they can afford to cut rates to those kind of levels". 

 Lower rates would mean Hungary's central bank may have to scrap its 2003 inflation target, as the finance ministry has baulked at revaluing the forint band. Rate cuts could also fuel domestic demand in Slovakia and swell an already-wide trade gap. 

 If they feel they can no longer reduce borrowing costs, the banks will be left with only one weapon - intervention - which could result in a long and costly campaign. 

 "It could be that eventually (rate cuts) will stop, and the central banks will have to rely only on interventions. The question then would be whether those would last for a couple of months or even a couple of years," said Jac.

title: UPDATE 1-Hungary PM, c.bank head talk down surging forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Hungary's prime minister and central bankintervened on Friday to talk down the country's soaring currency, and the forint retreated a touch from a new record high against the euro. 

 The forint edged down to 237.10/20 following comments by Premier Peter Medgyessy, at a regional summit in Warsaw, and central bank (NBH) Governor Zsigmond Jarai. 

 It earlier steamed to a new high of 236.10 to the euro as foreign buyers chased high-yielding interest rates amid speculation the authorities could be forced to raise central parity in the forint's 30-percent-wide flotation band. 

 The top of the band, introduced in May 2001 in preparation for Hungary's eventual entry into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM II), is set at 234.69 against the euro. 

 To defend that, the NBH would have to intervene directly by buying euros to weaken the forint. 

 Medgyessy told Reuters on the sidelines of a meeting of European Social Democrat leaders in Warsaw that he wanted to see a realistic exchange rate for the forint, adding he would not move parity in the currency's trading band. 

 "The forint should be valued realistically," he said. 

 JARAI SEES NO NEED TO CHANGE PARITY RATE 

 Separately, on the sidelines of a business conference in Budapest, NBH head Jarai said he saw no need to change the parity rate - fixed at 276.10 to the euro last year - before joining the ERM II, a precursor to signing up to the single currency euro zone. 

 "We think the forint has come a little bit close to the edge of the band," Jarai said. "I would like to state that under no circumstances will we lift the band... there's no need." 

 "With forint strength within the band we can comfortably meet our end-2003 inflation target (of 4.5 percent)," he added. 

 "If the exchange rate (settles) between 238 and 240, our (end-2003) inflation forecast can change to 4.3 percent (from 4.6), well within the 4.5 percent target," Jarai added. 

 Other central European currencies have come under pressure as optimism rises over a smooth EU enlargement in 2004. 

 The Slovak central bank shocked markets earlier with a 150 basis point interest rate cut to curb its surging crown. 

 "It was mainly Hungarians who were very active in the past couple of hours, but Poles and Slovaks have also been buying (in the forint market)," one dealer said. 

 High bond yields, coupled with improved EU entry sentiment, have boosted foreign capital inflows into foreign exchange and fixed income markets. 

 The forint had posted a new euro high of 237.75 on Thursday as government bond auctions attracted strong subscriptions. 

 JP Morgan earlier recommended selling euros and buying forints, saying they offered the best carry trade in central Europe. 

 Hungary's base rate of 9.50 percent is the region's highest. 

 JP Morgan said the forint would remain under upward pressure, which could force the NBH and centre-left cabinet to lift parity, within the next four to six months. 

 HSBC also said the forint rise could force the currency band's revaluation by the middle of next year. - Additional reporting by Andras Muller, and Douglas Busvine in Warsaw.

title: Emerging  FX -E.Europe units rally as Irish approve Nice.
text:
LONDON, Oct 21 (Reuters) - The main emerging European currencies rallied strongly on Monday after Ireland's approval of the Nice Treaty on European Union enlargement at the weekend removed a major obstacle standing in the way of the process. 

 The Irish approved the treaty by a convincing margin, with 63 percent voting in favour to 37 percent against, prompting a collective sigh of relief from the 10 candidate countries hoping to be admitted to the EU in 2004. 

 The Czech crown, Hungarian forint and Polish zloty all jumped when local trade resumed on Monday and analysts said the rally could continue over the next few sessions. 

 "The rally might extend over the next couple of days," said Koon Chow, central Europe currency strategist at CSFB. 

 "Even though there was anticipation of a 'yes' vote, investors had been holding hedging positions in currencies and the interest rate market, because they thought a 'no' result would trigger a more violent reaction." 

 Emerging European currency and bond markets have been seeing strong inflows for much of this year as investors bet on their economies converging to EU standards ahead of EU and euro entry. 

 Chow added that distinction should be made between the different countries, with domestic economic fundamentals now likely to come back into focus. 

 "The currency rally is likely to have the most longevity in Poland, where domestic fundamentals are the most persuasive. 

 "In the Czech Republic, the central bank still stands against appreciation with rate cuts and direct intervention, while in Hungary there are still question marks over the direction of the twin deficits." 

 At 0930 GMT, the zloty traded up 0.48 percent against the euro from late Friday at 4.03, the forint was up 0.75 percent at 242.98, while the crown was 0.2 percent firmer at 3.48. 

 FOCUS TURNS TO BRUSSELS 

 Some analysts said a more cautious tone could return to the market ahead of the Brussels summit on enlargement later this week. 

 The meeting is set to discuss the terms of accession for the candidate countries and the negotiations are likely to be tough, particularly on the contentious issue of agricultural subsidies. 

 There are also worries about the stance of the Dutch after their centre-right government collapsed last week, in part over disagreements on the enlargement issue. 

 Two junior partners in the coalition opposed admitting Poland, Slovakia and Cyprus to the EU - though constitutional experts have stressed that the caretaker government has the legal authority to approve enlargement at the Brussels meeting. 

 "(The summit) would normally be seen as a formality, but instead could prove the venue for some serious wrangling, as the Dutch and other EU governments play hardball over accession terms," said analysts at Credit Agricole Indosuez, in a daily research note. 

 POLL BOOST FOR HUNGARIAN GOVERNMENT 

 The forint made the most headway of the regional currencies on Monday, getting an additional lift from the strong showing of the ruling centre-left coalition at Hungary's weekend local elections. 

 Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy's Socialists and their liberal Free Democrat coalition allies won a majority of 17 out of 19 counties in Sunday's vote, according to early results. 

 The result should strengthen Medgyessy's hand in his efforts to rein in Hungary's twin budget and current account deficits. 

 "We now need to see evidence of a fall in the budget deficit - the weekend local elections have cleared a major political obstacle for the government, making it more confident to cut back spending," said Chow at CSFB. 

 The Israeli shekel continued its recent strong run, rising over half a percent to fresh one-month highs around 4.7260. 

 A strong rebound in U.S. technology stocks has powered the rally, with many Israeli tech firms quoted on the U.S. Nasdaq stock index. 

 The Nasdaq rallied around six percent last week after some encouraging signs on the corporate earnings front.

title: ECOFIN:  Hungary  To Run  Forex Intervention  Only In Euros
text:
OVIEDO, Spain -(Dow Jones)- The Hungarian central bank intends to conduct future intervention in the foreign exchange market exclusively in euros, National Bank of Hungary Governor Zsigmond Jarai said Sunday. 

 The decision was made recently due to the important role of the euro in Hungary's economy and financial markets. More than 80% of the volume traded in the country's interbank currency market is in euros, and conducting intervention in euros would heighten transparency for markets, Jarai noted. 

Hungary didn't intervene in the currency markets at all in 2001, nor has so far in 2002. Jarai was speaking at a euro seminar of central bankers, officials and business leaders at this weekend's informal Ecofin meeting. 

 Hungary is one of up to 10 accession countries seeking European Union membership in 2004, and it would like to join the euro zone "as soon as possible," Jarai said, indicating a target date of 2007. 

 After joining the E.U., accession countries must fully meet the economic and fiscal criteria spelled out in Maastricht Treaty. What's more, the currencies of accession countries must enter a trading band against the euro known as the exchange rate mechanism, or ERM II, for at least two years before they can join the euro zone. 

 "We also accept and we believe it's a good decision to wait at least two years in the ERM II system," Jarai said.

title: POLL-Forint seen falling ahead of election, surging later.
text:
BUDAPEST, Feb 25 (Reuters) - The forint is seen falling against the euro ahead of Hungary's general election in April, but then rebounding and nearing the top of its flotation band by next year, a monthly Reuters poll of analysts showed on Monday. 

 The consensus in the survey , conducted between February 20 and 22 with 15 participants, sees a fall in the forint exchange rate against the euro to 245.25 by the end of March from Friday's close at 243.60/86. 

 The most pessimistic analyst projected a slump to 252.00. 

 Hungary will hold two rounds of elections on April 7 and 21. 

 PRE-ELECTION FALL SEEN TEMPORARY 

 The main election rivals - ruling centre-right Fidesz-MPP and opposition Socialists - are neck-to-neck in opinion polls. 

 Both are emphasising Hungary's bid to join the European Union (EU) in 2004, but analysts are worried that Fidesz may be corralled into a coalition with the extreme right MIEP party. 

 Analysts' main scenario is that the forint quietens after the vote and economic fundamentals fuel a rise. Some analysts even say the rise may lead Hungary to revaluing the parity rate in the 30-percent-wide forint flotation band. 

 The forint, one of the main Central European currencies seen benefitting from convergence with the EU, came into the limelight earlier this month after rises to record highs. 

 The currency surged to 239.60 against the euro after Prime Minister Viktor Orban projected a 3-5 percent rise every year in the run-up to euro zone membership, expected for 2006 or 2007. 

 The forint retreated last week after a sharp upwards revision in the 2001 current account deficit, verbal intervention by the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) and a 50 basis point cut in the NBH's two-week deposit rate to 8.50 percent last Monday. 

 PARITY CHANGE A RISK 

 According to analysts' consensus the forint is expected to firm to 242.37 by the end of this year and to 238.63 by the end of 2003. The average forecasts were slashed by 1.66 and 3.21 forints, respectively, after Orban's comments on the forint. 

 The consensus projects softer levels than the top of the 30-percent-wide forint band at 234.69, but most analysts said an upwards revaluation of the parity rate is likely by the end of 2003 as the central bank wants to avoid speculative attacks. 

 Two of 11 analysts projected an upwards 10 percentage point parity rate revaluation for the second half of this year, five forecast a change for 2003, two said no revaluation was expected this year, while two said a change would not come before 2004. 

 Analysts said the revaluation risk rose after the prime minister's comments. 

 "We expect no modification...this year," Lehman Brothers said in its weekly outlook for Hungarian markets. "However, Pandora's box was opened, and from now on the market may start to price in some chance of an early parity appreciation."

title: Hungary  bonds, forint weaken on rate cut,  intervention .
text:
BUDAPEST, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Hungarian government bonds eased on Monday but activity was limited as investors digested news of a revision to 2001 current account data as well as a 50 basis point rate cut, traders said. 

 The Hungarian forint , which eased after the data revision, weakened further as the central bank verbally intervened to curb a recent rise in the currency, dealers said. 

 The Government Debt Management Agency (AKK), which fixes yields on benchmark securities once a day at around 1330 GMT, set the yields by up to five basis points higher. 

 The three-year 2005/G was set at 7.44 percent, up four basis points and the five-year 2006/E at 7.19 percent, up three. 

 Dealers said government bonds rose about five basis points after the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said in the morning that it revised the final current account deficit to 1.262 billion euros from 518 million but eased back later in the day. 

 "Bids inched higher by some five basis points during the day but everybody waited to see what the NBH would do in the afternoon," one government securities trader said.
