title: ANALYSIS-Czechs' crown problem mirrored across region.
text:
LONDON, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Czech authorities have adopted a high risk strategy in trying to curb the crown's rise, highlighting a problem facing other emerging European currencies as EU accession triggers strong foreign investment flows. 

 The Czech National Bank (CNB) intervened on Monday and cut interest rates by 25 basis points in an effort to curb the crown's sharp appreciation, but buyers soon returned to the market after an initial spike lower. 

 Analysts said the CNB's move did little to address the fundamental reasons behind crown strength and, while it may hold up the crown's rise in the short term, it might also store up problems for a later date. 

 "If you ask whether this intervention is in line with Czech fundamentals, the answer is no," said Callum Henderson, emerging markets currency analyst at Citibank. 

 Poland and Hungary, which like the Czech Republic are seen likely to join the European Union (EU) in 2004, are also facing problems posed by strong currencies. 

 However, analysts see currency intervention as a high-risk strategy, from which Poland and Hungary have shied away. 

 While authorities in some emerging markets would welcome hefty inflows of foreign investment, for the Czechs they are mainly causing headaches. 

 A deal between the government and the central bank last week arranged to lock away 25 billion Czech crowns ($683 million) in privatisation proceeds in the bank's foreign reserves until 2007. 

 "Even if all privatisation revenues are kept off the market this year, which will be difficult, the Czechs are still going to see strong portfolio inflows," Henderson said. 

 Yet with privatisation revenues of around 144 billion crowns due, and more expected to follow, few believe that the deal will be enough to stem the crown's steep ascent. 

 The Czech bond market also is expected to continue to attract capital inflows as its economy converges ahead of EU accession and interest rates fall towards euro zone levels. 

INTERVENTION AS SMOOTHING MECHANISM 

 While many market players agree the authorities will not be able to stop the crown strengthening over the long term, some accept the central bank has at least managed to slow it down. 

 "One can assume that if the central bank wasn't there the (euro/crown) market would be trading much lower," said a senior dealer at a bank in London. 

 The amount of Monday's intervention was estimated by traders at between 200-400 million euros, and with average daily turnover in the region of 450 million euros it's clear that those amounts can have a significant impact. 

 However, the dealer said the central bank might be storing up trouble for the future if it continues to intervene. 

 The central bank's short crown position is likely to lose money if, as even the authorities expect, the unit strengthens over the long term. This loss will have to be accounted for in the government budget, which is already deep in deficit. 

 Persistent intervention and rate cuts to combat crown strength could also lead to inflationary pressure. 

 DIFFERENT APPROACH IN POLAND, HUNGARY 

 In some ways strong local currencies are more of a headache for Hungary and particularly Poland, because their economies aren't performing as well as in the Czech Republic. 

 But so far the authorities have limited their actions to verbal intervention and monetary easing. 

 "In Poland, the central bank has strongly committed to non intervention since moving to a free-float exchange rate," said Marco Annunziata, chief economist for emerging Europe at Deutsche Bank. 

 Cezary Jozefiak, a member of the Polish Monetary Policy Council, earlier this month reiterated the bank's long-standing view that intervention was not an option. 

 Polish officials believe the market should be left to find its own level and recognise there is little they can do to reverse the trend in the zloty, Annunziata added. 

 In Hungary, the central bank has embarked on an aggressive series of rate cuts which has seen the key two-week deposit rate reduced by 2.5 percent since last May. 

 The cuts are not undertaken to weaken the forint, but justified on the view that currency strength has helped bring inflation down, offering more scope for monetary easing. 

 "Hungarian policy has been far more accommodative of a strong currency than the Czechs'," said Juliet Sampson, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America. 

 "They're unlikely to intervene because they're content with the level of the forint, at least for now, and everything they have said confirms that," she added. 

 Sampson said Czech sensitivity stems from a trade and current account balance hit by currency strength in the past. 

 But she added that there was, as yet, little evidence that strong currencies in emerging Europe were having a major negative impact on exporters. 

 "We're yet to see deficits ballooning, with productivity gains so far helping to offset currency strength."

title: WRAP: Hungary Can Live With Strong Forint - Jarai
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- Hungary's strong forint, which has soared under pressure from strong investment inflows, poses no threat to growth, said National Bank of Hungary President Zsigmond Jarai Friday. 

 Hence, he said, no intervention in the market or in the managed exchange rate regime is needed, adding that the currency's strength supports the central bank's 2002 and 2003 inflation goals. 

 But any further rise is not needed to meet inflation targets, he added. 

 "With the current 243-248 forint level (versus the euro), we can comfortably meet our inflation targets. We don't target an exchange rate. Further firming is not necessary. We don't want to undershoot the 2001 inflation target, but it doesn't require any intervention," Jarai said. 

 The bank seeks to lower annual inflation to 4.2-4.5% in December 2002 and 3.5% in December 2003 from an expected 7% or thereabouts in December 2001, he said. 

 "There's room to reduce rates if the exchange rate remains in the current range and inflation falls," Jarai added. The last time the bank cut its key rate was on Monday, by 25 basis points to 9.5%. 

 Jarai made his comments in response to market speculation that the recent firming of the forint against the euro would prompt the central bank to talk down the forint, or even change the current managed exchange rate mechanism, which limits the forint's trading range. 

 But the system will remain in place until 2004, the date Hungary plans to join the European Union, Jarai said. 

 "We'll need to renegotiate the regime with the European Union, and then we'll need to readjust the (forint's central) parity, but we won't change the fluctuation band," Jarai said, talking to a small group of journalists after a press conference held jointly with government ministers on Hungary's economic outlook for 2002. 

 The forint's central parity is set at HUF276.105 around which the bank allows a variation of plus or minus 15%. 

 The forint had firmed to over 12% on the strong side of its parity prior to Monday's rate cut and also Thursday on continued strong portfolio receipts chasing interest rate carry trades on Hungarian government bonds over the euro. Hungary's sound economic standing and convergence prospects are also sucking money in. 


               EU Compliance Drives Policy



By Friday afternoon, the forint regained its early-session losses and
trading calmed down, following the Polish zloty's recovery from a steep
fall and Jarai's comments.



At around 1500 GMT it was trading at HUF244.37 against the euro, much
firmer from HUF248 early Friday and slightly weaker than late Thursday's
HUF244.00-30.



As to the outlook for 2002, the central bank and government will press
ahead with their current fiscal and monetary policies in pursuit of
ultimate compliance with E.U. requirements.



"We want to launch the euro in 2006," Jarai reiterated Friday. "Our
fiscal, monetary and overall economic policy targets take that into
account first."



In spring 2001, the bank widened the forint's band from +/-2.25% in
preparation for joining the E.U.'s Exchange Rate Mechanism II. It also
launched an inflation-targeting policy because Hungary's number one task
when joining the euro zone is to lower inflation.



With a wider band, the forint strengthened last year to HUF246 against
the euro from HUF265 at the start of 2001.



However, productivity gains have offset the negative impact of the
strong forint on exports, which are driving the country's growth.



The stronger forint has been forcing small and medium-size firms - the
hardest hit by the stronger currency - to modernize, Minister of
Economic Affairs Gyorgy Matolcsy said Friday.



Gross domestic product is expected to rise between 3.5-4% this year,
somewhat slower than around 4% in 2001, Minister of Finance Mihaly Varga
said at the press conference.



The current account deficit, which the bank and the government expect
below EUR1 billion in 2001, will widen to between EUR1.5-2 billion in
2002, both benign figures, reflecting how strongly Hungary can weather
the global economic slowdown, they said. The deficit totaled EUR1.62
billion in 2000.



-By Margit Feher, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0622;
margit.feher@dowjones.com

title: Hungary cbank says no need to curb strong forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Hungary's central bank said on Friday that no market intervention was needed to curb the forint after the currency's recent rise. 

 National Bank of Hungary Governor Zsigmond Jarai told a news conference that the 2002 inflation target of around 4.5 percent for December could be achieved with the current forint levels. 

 "The current forint level poses no risk to economic growth or balance," Jarai said. 

 "There is no need for a market intervention...we can sit back comfortably, unruffled by speculation concerning the currency band," Jarai added. 

 In the New Year the forint has been trading at strong levels of between 243 and 245 against the euro, compared with 265 a year ago.

title: Hungary govt, c.bank expected to talk forint down.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Hungary's government and central bank are expected to intervene verbally on Friday to try and curb a rising forint after substantial capital inflows in recent weeks, analysts and dealers said on Thursday. 

 National Bank of Hungary Governor Zsigmond Jarai, Finance Minister Mihaly Varga and Economics Minister Gyorgy Matolcsy are due to hold a joint news conference on Friday (1000 GMT) on the economic prospects this year. 

 "We don't think (exchange rate) measures will be announced, but they will try to talk (the forint) down," said Istvan Gere, dealer at K&H Bank. "This is is a trend in Central Europe, the Polish and Czech situation is also similar." 

 Varga told reporters on Thursday that "foreign observers" currently see the forint, the Czech crown and Polish zloty as strong. 

 "The strong forint obviously has an impact on the economy. We will have talks with the central bank and Economics Minister on Friday and certainly we will also speak about that," he said. 

 Answering a question, Varga did not rule out officials talking about the forint at Friday's news conference. 

 The forint has firmed to below 244 against the euro since early last month when it was more than than 250. 

 Government bond yields have fallen sharply on fresh capital inflows, with the amount held by foreign investors rising some 100 billion forints ($366.8 million) to above 1,100 billion. 

 The forint is near its all-time high of 241 to the euro hit last July and is just three percentage points below the top of its 30-percent-wide flotation band. 

 CONVERGING REGION, SURGING CURRENCIES

 The forint's surge fits a regional trend fuelled by falling inflation and relatively high fixed income yields as several states get closer to European Union membership, analysts said. 

 Hungary and other countries in the region hope to join the EU in 2004 and enter the euro zone two or three years later. 

 "Strong currencies cause a headache for policy makers in the CEE countries as the generally unfavourable external environment mixed with strong currencies hits export opportunities," said Zoltan Torok, analyst at Raiffeisen Securities. 

 The Polish and Czech governments are also considering measures to curb their currencies amid strong portfolio capital and foreign direct investment inflows. 

 NEW HUNGARY REGIME SEEN STANDING PRESSURE 

 Hungary widened the forint's 4.5-percent band to 30 percent last May as part of a series of moves to prepare the currency for the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM II), the euro anteroom. 

 Analysts said the new broader band was likely to withstand the pressure. 

 "Before ERM II, an exchange rate adjustment will be needed anyway, but an adjustment two years before ERM would make no sense," said Marton Nagy of ING Investment Management. 

 "If the forint reaches 13-14 percent above parity in the band, many investors will start to think the top is too close and begin to liquidate positions," he said. 

 Other analysts did not rule out the chance that capital inflows could push the forint near to the top of the band, but they said verbal intervention and central bank interest rate cuts, widely expected in the market, were sufficient to contain the currency's rise. 

 "The 25 basis point rate cut (on Monday) was just a signal that the central bank is uncomfortable with the forint so strong," Nagy said.

title: Hungary's forint opens firmer as exporters hedge.
text:
BUDAPEST, Oct 1 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint firmed to 7.2 percent above parity in its band after the opening on Monday, as Hungarian exporters were hedging their foreign currency revenues with forward transactions, traders said. 

 "Hungarian exporters have been heavily selling foreign currency in the past two weeks hedging their revenues with forward deals, which provides support for the forint," said Attila Behan at K&H Bank. 

 On Friday the forint closed at 6.86 percent above central parity in its 30-percent-wide flotation band. 

 Behan said remarks by central bank governor Zsigmond Jarai on Friday that the country did not need to need to change its inflation targets as the forint stabilised after recent falls, had no impact on the forint. 

 Jarai also said that Hungary will not need to take up any new loans from abroad in 2002 to refinance its expiring debt. 

 Against the euro, the forint firmed to 256.20/70 from Friday's close at 256.90/257.00, while against the dollar it traded at 281.80/282.80, easing from 280.90/281.40 on Friday. 

 Behan said the forint would likely trade in a range between 255 and 260 forints to the euro in the near future. 

 He said the termination of the forint's crawling peg devaluation system on Monday had no significant impact on the currency. 

 Hungary on Monday ended the forint's crawling peg devaluation system, as one of the last steps of a monetary overhaul in its run-up to European Union membership and the forint's joining the euro zone. 

 The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) set the forint at the middle of the intervention band at 276.1 forints per euro. 

 The forint now floats in a 15 percent-wide range on either side of this parity. Hungary expects to join the EU in 2004 and the eurozone about two years later.

title: Hungarian Forint Slide Leaves  Central Bank  In A Quandary
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- The National Bank of Hungary finds itself in a policy quandary. 

 Just as the central bank's policy board prepares to meet on Monday, the forint has fallen through a key support level against the euro, a victim of the mounting global tension which is souring sentiment in emerging markets. 

 The move took the currency to more than HUF260 against the euro on foreign selling in late afternoon trade Friday. That's the weakest it's been since May, and it's expected to weaken further next week. 

 "We broke an important support," said Zoltan Szabo at WestLB in Budapest. "Liquidity is pretty low since it's a Friday afternoon. Next week (when trade picks up) I see some further weakening. The forint could fall to 262-263." 

 Investors are now looking to the National Bank of Hungary for action. 

 There's been no sign of intervention, however, dealers said. Central bank executives have been unavailable to comment. 

 "The National Bank is keeping quiet. It should raise interest rates, I think," Szabo said. 

 "But it just lowered them last week. They're just thinking very hard right now about what to do." 

 At around 1200 GMT, the forint was trading at HUF260.80-20 or 5.5% on the strong side of its trading band, weaker than HUF258.00-30, or 6.5% on the strong side of its band, in the morning. 

 "HUF260 was a great watershed, foreigners are selling forints and buying euros," said a dealer at Raiffeisen. 

 The central bank allows the forint to trade in a plus or minus 15% band around a midpoint it sets daily against the euro. 

 But its current level is far from the central bank's target of HUF245-250, which it set to reduce annual inflation in December to 7%, down from 10.1% in December 2000. 

 More encouragingly, meanwhile, local bonds are faring much better than the currency. The amount of Hungarian bonds in foreign hands has been mostly steady since last Tuesday, even slightly higher, at around HUF950 billion, data from the state debt management center AKK show. 


                      Sound Economy



Hungary's economy is sound, with inflation on a downward path. But the
gathering global crisis, following last week's atrocities in the U.S.,
has driven investors into the safest boltholes, such as U.S. short-term
debt.



Stock markets, meanwhile, have suffered agonizing selloffs throughout
the world and many emerging market currencies, such as the forint, have
been exchanged for safer bets like the Swiss franc, which is at a record
high against the euro.



In such conditions, a rise in rates to support the forint would make
the bank look to be out of control and smack of economic mismanagement.



Only last week the central bank cut its key rate by 25 basis points to
11%, citing, among other factors, an earlier 25 basis point cut by the
European Central Bank. However, a bank executive said Tuesday it won't
immediately follow this week's 50 basis point cut by the ECB.



The most likely outcome is for the bank to stand pat in view of the
weak forint, though most analysts see more rate cuts to come this year
on the back of slowing inflation.



Credit Suisse First Boston economist Istvan Racz takes that line. He
sees unchanged rates Monday but a good chance of a quarter-point cut
10.75% at some point in October.



"This could take place if, as we and the market expect, there's a
further drop in year-on-year inflation to 8.1% in September from 8.7% in
August," Racz said in a research note Friday.



Rate cuts will likely total 50 basis points altogether for the rest of
the year as fiscal policy will get considerably looser and inflation
will only fall moderately in the fourth quarter, Racz added.



Investors must also keep an eye on general elections in neighboring
Poland over the weekend.



Unlike the forint, the Polish zloty firmed markedly Friday, but
experience shows that the forint and the zloty often correlate as both
are 'emerging Europe' currencies.



"Next to the (sometimes) close correlation in the currencies, the
issue of European Union accession deserves special attention in the
Polish elections," Hungarian retail bank IE-New York Broker said in a
research note Friday.



Hungary and Poland plan to be among the first countries to join the
E.U. sometime after 2004.



-By Margit Feher, Dow Jones Newswires; +361-267-0622;
margit.feher@dowjones.com (Balazs Koranyi contributed to this item.)

title: Hungary forint eases as global uncertainty weighs.
text:
BUDAPEST, Sept 20 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint closed weaker at around 6.20 percent above parity in its trading band on Thursday and traders said if foreign currency purchases continue, the forint might fall even further. 

 "We saw continuous foreign currency buys today, though not heavy buys," said Orsolya Liptai at K&H Bank. 

 "The 259 (forints to the euro) level has supported the forint so far, but if foreigners keep buying (euro) we can go above 260," she added. Liptai said at such levels the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) should already consider a possible intervention to prop up the Hungarian currency. 

 The forint closed on Wednesday at 6.50 percent above midline in its 30-percent-wide trading band. 

 Against the euro the forint closed at 258.70/259.20, easing from Wednesday's close at 258.00/30. 

 That is well below the 245-250 level which the central bank has said was needed to reach inflation targets of 6-8 percent for this year and 3.5-5.5 percent for 2002. 

 Analysts said on Thursday that the NBH should intervene at least verbally to support the forint if global market uncertainty continues to weigh on the currency. 

 "We expect the central bank to do something in the short term, at least verbally," Lehman Brothers analyst Gabor Bekes told a news conference. "There is a risk that investors begin to doubt that the NBH is ready to act for a stronger forint." 

 A likely retaliation by the U.S. may make the forint fragile as investors may avoid emerging markets amid global uncertainty, regardless of Hungary's strong fundamentals and its convergence with the European Union, analysts said. 

 Versus the dollar the forint ended at 278.70/279.30, compared with 278.90/279.20 on Wednesday. 

 The forint floats in a 15 percent-wide range on either side of a parity rate set daily by the National Bank of Hungary against a euro currency basket. From April 1, the forint has been devalued every working day at a 0.2 percent monthly rate. 

 The central bank will terminate this crawling peg devaluation as of October 1.

text:

 "We expect the central bank to do something in the short term, at least verbally," Lehman Brothers analyst Gabor Bekes told a news conference. "There is a risk that investors begin to doubt that the NBH is ready to act for a stronger forint." 

 The unit was quoted at 258.10/50 against the euro at 1310 /1110 GMT, down from its close at 252.25/50 last Monday before the attacks on the U.S.. 

 The forint was well below the 245-250 level which the central bank has said it needed to attain to reach its inflation targets of 6-8 percent for this year and 3.5-5.5 percent for next. 

 Bekes said Hungary could achieve the targets even if the forint was slightly weaker than planned as a slowdown in the global economy was expected to cut import prices.

 Zoltan Torok of Raiffeisen Securities said the NBH should not cut its interest rates in the short term as the current risk premium was part of the forint's defence against further falls. 

 "Our fear is that even if we do not see a large selling wave selling pressure will weigh on us," said Zoltan Torok. "In a situation like this an early rate cut would not be responsible behaviour." 

 Other analysts said the NBH may still reduce its interest rates at the next meeting of its Monetary Council scheduled for Monday after rate cuts in the U.S. and Europe.

title: Hungary  forint opens flat, averts  intervention  risk.
text:
BUDAPEST, June 2 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint was steady against its flotation band in early trade on Monday as no news provided it with new fuel to restart its recent rally, dealers said. 

 They said the central bank was unlikely to intervene so as to curb the forint's strength after the forint retreated from record highs on Friday and stayed at the lower levels. 

 "(Preliminary May) current account data will come out tomorrow, and a lot will depend on them," one dealer said. 

 The forint traded at 11.1 percent above parity in its 30-percent-wide flotation band at 10:20/0820 GMT, steady from Friday's close. 

 Against the euro it eased to 243.75/95 from 243.20/80, while versus the dollar it softened to 288.60/289.00 from 287.40/90. 

 The currency retreated in profit-taking on Friday, after rises to record highs at above 11.7 percent last week despite warnings from the central bank that it was too strong. 

 The National Bank of Hungary also confirmed last week that it intervenes only if the forint reaches the top of the band. But dealers still saw a risk that the bank steps in earlier to prevent an advance of the forint to the edge of the band. 

 Dealers said on Monday that the forint's retreat temporarily averted the risk of a market intervention by the central bank. 

 The currency firmed nine percent within the band since May 4 when the band was widened to 15 percent either side of a daily-set central parity rate, from 2.25 percent. 

 Dealers did not exclude that the currency may strengthen further this week. Current account data may give indications to the market, they added. 

 Analysts' consensus forecast for the May current account deficit was 90 million euros in a recent Reuters survey. 

 May was the first month when the strengthening forint began to make imports cheaper and exports more expensive, but analysts said any impact on data would appear with a delay of months. 

 However, the poll conducted two weeks ago also showed that most analysts did not expect a deterioration in the current account despite the strong forint. 

 The forint floats in a 15-percent-wide range on either side of a parity rate set daily by the National Bank of Hungary against a euro curency basket. From April 1, 2001, the forint is devalued every working day at a 0.2 percent monthly rate.

title: Hungary forint firms to 11.65 pct on bond buying.
text:
BUDAPEST, July 2 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint strengthened to close at 11.65 percent above parity on Monday, despite expectations in early trade that the currency would ease on a lack of market-moving news, dealers said. 

 After opening steady from its close on Friday, at 11.1 percent above midline, a flurry of buying in government bonds coupled with a National Bank of Hungary bond auction pushed the forint higher in its flotation band, said Attila Behan, dealer at K&H. 

 "After weakening this morning there were signs it would weaken further - but suddenly the picture just changed at midday," he said. "It was (due to) trading in Hungarian bonds." 

 Behan said the forint could easily rise to 12 percent above midline in its band in the rest of the week. 

 Against the euro the currency ended at 242.60/90, firming from Friday's close of 243.20/80. Versus the dollar it closed at 287.10/50, from 287.40/90. 

 The currency retreated in profit-taking on Friday, after rises to record highs at above 11.7 percent last week despite warnings from the central bank that the forint was too strong.

text:

title: Hungary cbank seen acting soon to harness forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, June 26 (Reuters) - The Hungarian central bank may be forced to intervene in the foreign exchange market to stop the forint strengthening further if verbal warnings do not do the trick, analysts said on Tuesday. 

 The forint has firmed steadily since the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) overhauled its monetary regime in May by widening the forint trading band, making it fully convertible, and launching an inflation-targeting policy. 

 Last Friday NBH general manager Zsolt Ersek told Reuters the bank did not think the forint should strengthen further, as its current level was "sufficient for us to meet the several percent inflation target for the end of the year". 

 A NBH spokesman said further verbal intervention and an interest rate cut were possible if the forint firmed more. 

 But the impact of the NBH's words was short-lived. 

 On Monday the forint surged to a new all-time high at 11.50 percent above parity in its band. And on Tuesday it ended at 11.36 percent, firming over nine percent since its band was widened in early May. 

 "It was a pretty weak attempt at verbal intervention...if they really wanted to stop the forint from appreciating then they would have to be more persuasive," said Juliet Sampson at Bank of America in London. 

 Sampson said the forint would firm further in the days ahead, but the NBH would wait with open market intervention until the currency tested the strong end of its trading band. 

 Finance Minister Mihaly Varga also said earlier on Tuesday that intervention was not yet on the agenda. 

 However, most analysts say a "real" intervention could come soon - possibly as early as this week. 

 "It could happen any time, as they (NBH) like to cause a surprise," said Istvan Zsoldos, analyst at Concorde Securities in Budapest. "It may happen as early as tomorrow, as a basic rule of intervention is that it should be unexpected." 

 Zsoldos said he expected the bank to step actively into the market when the forint rose to around 13 percent. 

 Gabor Bognar at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein in London also said the NBH will not allow the forint to test the top of its band, because then the bank's monetary policy would be just as limited as it was before the band widening. 

 "I expect that around 12-13 percent there will be an intervention which is more than a verbal intervention," Bognar said, adding that Hungary's economy was too open and the impacts of exchange rate changes too unpredictable for the forint to be allowed to rise much higher. 

 FORINT BEST CHOICE IN REGION 

 Hungary's robust economic growth and stable economy are two key factors attracting a massive flow of foreign capital to the country's foreign currency and government securities markets. 

 Hungary is seen as the best choice in the region now - with Poland struggling with economic difficulties and political uncertainty due to an election and the Czech Republic trying to bring its budget deficit under control. 

 "If I were a portfolio investor, I would bring my short-term money to Hungary rather than Poland for now," Bognar said. 

 "The forint has outperformed in the last few weeks because it is catching up (with other currencies in the region)," Sampson added. 

 Though analysts said it would be too early to estimate the size of a possible open-market intervention, they said even a low-scale move could restrain the forint's rise for a while. 

 "In such a speculative market with a small amount they can have a relatively significant impact," Zsoldos said. 

 "In this case (when the forint needs to be weakened) the central bank has practically unlimited munition to intervene," he added. The only factor to consider would be an eventual rise in the money supply which may push up inflation. 

 The NBH said when it widened the forint's band that the currency's appreciation would help meet its target for seven percent year-on-year inflation by the end of 2001. 

 The widening was part of a general overhaul in the monetary regime to prepare the forint for European Union (EU) and eurozone membership, expected by 2004 and 2006, respectively. 

 The overhaul included launching an inflation-targeting monetary policy and allowing foreigners to trade in short-term debt and currency derivatives. 

 Bognar at Dresdner said the NBH might cut its key two-week deposit rate when it intervenes - initially by 25 basis points - depending on the actual size of the intervention. 

 "I think if the size is more a few hundred millions of euros then a rate cut would also be considered by the bank," he said. 

 However, Zsoldos said the NBH would cut rates only around October, when inflation is seen falling to around 8 to 9 percent year on year - down from a peak at 10.8 percent in May.

title: Hungary forint rises ahead of full convertibility.
text:
BUDAPEST, June 15 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint extended its gains on Friday, the last trading day before full convertibility. 

 Analysts said further rises may come next week and the central bank may be prompted to intervene. 

 "We expect the authorities to intervene verbally shortly so as to stabilise the forint around the current levels at 10 percent (above parity in the trading band)," said Istvan Racz of Credit Suisse First Boston. 

 The government published a decree on full forint convertibility on Friday, removing restrictions on short-term capital flows. The move had been widely expected but it does not come into force until Monday. 

 The forint closed at 10.2/10.3 percent above parity in its 30-percent-wide flotation band, retreating from the day's peak at 10.45 percent or 245.55 against the euro, but well up from Thursday's finish at 10.0 percent above midline. 

 It strengthened to 245.90/246.20 against the euro from 246.00/80 and to 284.55/90 against the dollar from 290.20/40. Government bonds firmed in the early afternoon on a buying wave by foreigners encouraged by liberalisation, but returned to earlier levels amid profit-taking in late trade. 

 The main question about near-term market movements is whether foreign capital pours into the market in one wave after it is freed up on Monday, or comes in gradually, dealers said. A surge might be followed by corrections, they added. 

 Opinions were mixed but most market participants expected liberalisation to lift the forint early next week. 

 Dealers said liberalisation would also lead to a surge in turnover but London may benefit more than Budapest. 

 "I fear most of the trade will go to London," one delaer said. "Foreigners will determine the market and if they can trade among themselves they will do that - we can't do anything against that." 

 FORINT SEEN UP, INTERVENTION A QUESTION 

 Analysts said liberalisation was likely to boost the forint further to levels around 12 percent above parity. 

 "I expect the forint to peak at 12 percent at the strongest," said Kornelius Purps of HypoVereinsbank. 

 "After that, and this process might start already on Monday afternoon, the forint is expected to weaken to levels below 10 percent," he added. 

 Purps said the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) was unlikely to intervene because the forint was affected by one-off factors, adding that the central bank could step in only if the currency settles at levels far above 10 percent in two weeks time. 

 Marton Nagy of ING Investment said the currency would retreat after peaking at 11-12 percent above parity next week, also pushed down by probable NBH interest rate cuts in line with falls in inflation from July. 

 Gabor Bekes of Lehman Brothers said the forint was unlikely to rise above 11 percent next week but if it continues to firm, the government or the NBH would warn of its strength. 

 A money market intervention and even interest rate cuts by the central bank, however, were unlikely until the forint reaches 13-14 percent above parity in the band, Bekes added.

title: Investors await Hungary decree on freeing forint.
text:
BUDAPEST, June 15 (Reuters) - Hungarian markets were waiting on edge for a government decree on Friday, which is expected to make the forint convertible later in the day, fully opening its markets for the first time in 70 years, analysts said. 

 The decree, widely expected for weeks, is unlikely to cause dramatic price rises after a recent sharp rise of the forint and bonds, but market participants said they would keep eyes open. 

 "Nobody knows yet what is the final text of the new law," a forex dealer said. "I think lawyers will read it as fast as they can and give advice to traders on what they can and cannot do... it will be a very interesting day." 

 The decree will lift short-term capital flow restrictions, allowing foreigners to trade derivatives and short-term debt. 

 Analysts said it could lure new investment fund players into Hungary, dominantly from Europe, but new U.S. investors - who like short-term investment opportunities - may also appear. 

 FOCUS ON FORINT AND BILLS 

 The market free-up will open business opportunities so far unseen in Hungary for investment funds, banks and companies. 

 In the past two weeks forint eurobond issues mushroomed, with foreign banks exploiting a strong interest in forint assets ahead of the free-up as the number of currencies in Europe is decreasing because of the EU's single currency, analysts said. 

 Interest is likely to focus on the forint and the short-term debt market, but in the future the half-dead derivatives market could also come to a buzzing life due to inflows, analysts said. 

 "There are people who keep a substantial portfolio of bonds expiring in the coming months, and they may try to replace them with T-bills now," said Gabor Bekes, analyst at Lehman Brothers. 

 The forint rose 7.75 percent within its trading band, to end at 10 percent above parity on Friday, since it was widened on May 4 to 15 percent either side of parity, from 2.25 percent. 

 Analysts said the forint may firm further, but the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) may intervene to curb it verbally or by commissioning a commercial bank to buy foreign currency. 

 The NBH cannot allow a forint rise to the top of the band as that could show that its exchange rate target may contradict its new inflation-targeting monetary policy, analysts added. 

 "The forint can firm further by one or two percent before the central bank begins to fear that large-scale intervention will be needed (at the top of the band)," said Bekes.

title: Hungary short bonds firm as foreigners buy.
text:
BUDAPEST, May 8 (Reuters) - Hungarian short-term government bonds extended their gains on Tuesday as foreign investors continued to buy, encouraged by a firming of the forint in its trading band which was widened last week, traders said. 

 "I'm sure that five or 10 billion forints in net terms came in from abroad today and also yesterday," said Karoly Misky of Bondtrade, adding, however, it was difficult to predict the levels where foreign investors would take profits. 

 Short-term bond yields fell by some 15 basis points, with the 2001/C-series trading at around 10.60 percent 3:30 p.m./1330 GMT. 

 Longer bonds, however, were volatile, and retreated by about 10 basis points by the afternoon from Monday's levels as domestic investors were selling, traders said. 

 Local investors feared that a further firming of the forint could trigger selling by foreigners, traders said. Market rumours that the central bank may intervene if the forint firms to beyond a certain level also sparked selling, traders added. 

 "The central bank wanted a stronger forint, but not to the extremes," one trader said. "An intervention is not an impossible idea." 

 National Bank of Hungary (NBH) governor Zsigmond Jarai announced last Thursday a widening in the forint band to 15 percent either side of a central parity rate, set daily by the NBH, from 2.25 percent. 

 Jarai said the bank would intervene in the market only if the currency would reach each end of the new band. 

 On Tuesday the forint closed at 5.75/5.80 percent above parity, compared with 4.9/5.07 percent above the midline on Monday.

title: Hungary Jarai Vows No  Forex  Intevention In New Wider Band
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- The National Bank of Hungary won't intervene within the forint's newly-widened intervention band, central bank governor Zsigmond Jarai said Friday. 

 At a press conference, the governor also predicted the forint's monthly devaluation rate could be eliminated in the first half of 2002 if inflation falls. 

 In a surprise move late Thursday, the authorities widened the band to +/-15% around a midpoint fixed to the euro daily, from +/-2.25% previously. 

 Friday, the forint strengthened to about 4% on its strong side by midday. 

 "We didn't widen the band just to say we've widened it. In the first several weeks we'll definitely let the forint float within the band and we'll not intervene even after that," Jarai said. 

 That contradicts dealers' expectations that the bank will maintain an 'inner band' and intervene to keep it there. 

 "Right now, we're seeing the forint strengthening about 2.5% (on its latest and firmest spot at 2.25% in the old band), and that's more or less in line with our expectations," Jarai said. "But it's too early to tell how things will develop. Friday's usually a casual Friday among dealers so we'll wait till next week to see what really happens." 

 While widening the intervention band, the central bank maintained its monthly devaluation of the forint's middle rate in the band by 0.2% against the euro. 

 Later, the bank wants to abolish the devaluation - or the 'crawling peg,' as it is known - probably next year, but only if inflation falls below 7%, said Jarai. 

 "We'll need to think about the crawl if inflation falls below 7%; there's no sense in devaluation below 7% inflation," he added. 

 "If annual inflation falls to 6-7% in December as we now predict, that signals a trend which allows us to eliminate the crawling peg, perhaps in the first half of next year," Jarai explained. 

 The authorities widened the intervention band to try to reduce persistently high inflation of around 10%, but it won't cool down this year, so they have maintained their 2001 inflation projection of 8-9%, and around 6-7% next year, Jarai said. 

 The wider band "won't affect Hungarian businesses' competitiveness this year," he said. "It won't change unemployment and it won't increase the current account deficit."

title: Hungary Jarai:Wider Euro/Forint Band In 12-18 Mos-Paper
text:
BUDAPEST -(Dow Jones)- The Hungarian forint's trading band could be widened in 12 to 18 months, recently appointed central bank governor Zsigmond Jarai told business daily Vilaggazdasag in an interview published Thursday. 

 "We could introduce an exchange rate system similar to ERM II earlier (than 2004), a year or a year and a half from now," Jarai was quoted as saying. 

 Under the European Monetary System's exchange rate mechanism, the ERM II, the forint would be fixed to the euro but allowed to fluctuate plus/minus 15% before intervention is necessary. 

Hungary hopes to join ERM II at the start of 2004, when it expects to join the European Union, Jarai added. 

 At present, the forint is traded in a narrow, plus or minus 2.25% band around its midpoint, which is fixed to the euro daily. The central bank devalues the midpoint 0.3% against the euro monthly. The bank will cut the devaluation rate, or crawling peg, to 0.2% from Apr. 1. 

 Jarai believes that the crawling peg system needs to remain in place until the need for devaluation is eliminated. 

 "I believe there's a need for two more cuts in the devaluation rate. At present, we don't want to widen the (trading) band because the (resulting) appreciation (of the forint) wouldn't be beneficial to the economy," Jarai said. 

 "Except for banks, the income increase wasn't so large (last year) in the corporate sector that it would stand a further appreciation of the forint," Jarai added. 

 The forint appreciated 5% against the euro last year in real terms. 

 "With growth slowing in the E.U., it wouldn't be right to take steps to strengthen the forint," Jarai added. 

 As Hungary's robust growth is driven by exports, a further currency appreciation would hinder its competitiveness. 

 Jarai added that he sees real interest rates on the short end low at present, but not too low for the longer end of the bond curve. The governor noted though that "interest rates don't make such an impact on Hungary's economy as (in developed countries)." 

 The reason is that corporate loans only amount to 70% of gross domestic product while in western Europe the same indicator is 200%. Household loans are only 5% of consumption while the same indicator is around 100% in western Europe, Jarai said. 

 Regarding the current account, which posted a much higher-than-expected deficit in January, Jarai pointed out that this partly reflects high natural gas prices, which lag the rise of crude oil prices by about six months.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Rebound as Latam worries ease.
text:
LONDON, July 14 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies rebounded on Wednesday as the latest flurry of Latin America worries appeared to ease. 

Currencies that took a knock earlier this week on talk that Argentina might not service its debt were mostly firmer, with the Polish zloty and South African rand showing the clearest recovery. 

 Emerging Asian units saw a more muted reaction but held up well despite substantial sell-offs on regional stock markets and tension between Taiwan and China, analysts said. 

 Taiwanese stocks plunged nearly four percent on Wednesday, rattled by Taipei's break with the "One China" policy that had helped smoothe relations with Beijing, but traders said the stand-off was partly used as an excuse to take profits. 

 South Korean stocks closed 3.4 percent down and Hong Kong's Hang Seng index lost nearly three percent. 

 "We're moving into a corrective phase for Asian stocks, which is not surprising given the huge gains since the beginning of this year," said Mitul Kotecha, emerging markets economist at Standard Chartered in London. 

 "That, and growing concern on competitiveness, will filter into the currencies' performance at some point, and should prevent further appreciation in the near term. But the medium-term trend is to strength." 

 The Taiwan dollar was little affected by the China tensions, but South Korea's won slipped as local banks bought dollars to meet a government deadline on loan loss provisions. 

 Latin American stock markets stabilised on Tuesday and currencies recouped much of their lost ground. 

 Most analysts were already seeing this week's Latin America-inspired sell-off as vastly overblown when the man largely responsible for triggering the panic, Argentine presidential candidate Eduardo Duhalde, denied late on Tuesday he had ever called for a debt pardon. 

 Kotecha said currencies such as the rand, Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso, which are underpinned by investors seeking high yield, had been hardest hit by the Latin America jitters as players fled to safer havens such as U.S. Treasury bonds. 

 The rand bobbed back on Wednesday, although it was still some way off the levels of around 6.1 to the dollar seen at the end of last week, and far from the 6.0 mark tested in late June. 

 The Polish zloty, often the Central European currency most vulnerable to wider emerging market sentiment, jumped to open at 5.62/5.58 percent above its basket parity from late Tuesday's 5.03 percent. 

 The Slovak crown also rebounded sharply, helped by comments by the European Union's executive body that it expected the country to be admitted to formal EU membership talks at the end of this year. 

 But the Czech crown was more subdued, dipping after a local newspaper quoted an unnamed central bank board member as saying he was in favour of intervening against the currency. 

Hungary's forint, largely insulated by its semi-convertible status from the Latin America worries, showed no reaction to Tuesday's 25-basis-point cut in the two-week repo rate. 

 "To some extent it was expected," said Jan Pudil, a local currency debt trader at Westdeutsche Landesbank's emerging markets division in London. 

 "It just paves the way for a further easing. The real level of interest rates is so excessively high compared to other countries in the region." 

 Analysts said the strength of the forint was the main factor behind the easing, despite central bank worries about the government's fiscal policies and strong import demand. 

 The currency has been pushing at the top end of its tight 4.5 percent-wide trading band for well over a month, requiring frequent central bank interventions to keep it in check. 

 "Continued large-scale capital flows into the country will provide new impetus for the discussion (at the central bank and between the central bank and the government) on the future shape of the exchange rate regime," Salomon Smith Barney analyst Wike Groenenberg said in a briefing note. ** Following is a table of key emerging market exchange rates, including the change versus late New York trade the previous day and the change in the year to date.. ** The Czech, Polish, Hungarian and Slovak currencies, formerly quoted against the mark, are now quoted against the euro to reflect new market norms. title: Hungary forint eases vs band on commercial orders.
text:
BUDAPEST, April 12 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint ended morning trade weaker on Monday, at parity in the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) 4.5-percent-wide intervention band, pushed down by small-scale commercial orders, dealers said. 

 "This is (banking) customer business," said Gabor Butor of Raiffeisen-Unicbank, adding that foreigners showed little interest after a general rally in the country's markets on Thursday and early Friday. 

 The forint began to ease Friday amid profit-taking after a rally triggered by Thursday's better-than-projected current account data and the NBH's return to its interest rate cut policy which was expected by some analysts to boost foreign investors' confidence. 

 The NBH cut its benchmark rates by 50 basis points early Friday. The forint closed on Friday at 0.35/0.4 percent above parity. 

 Dealers said the forint may firm a little in the afternoon as a correction of the fall, but will stay close to parity. 

 Against the dollar the Hungarian currency finished morning trade at 234.65/75, slightly firmer than Friday's close at 234.90/235.20, while versus the euro it it softened to 254.80/255.00 from 253.10/60. 

 The NBH fixed the forint at noon at 235.10 to the dollar an at 254.75 to the euro. 

 The forint fluctuates by 2.25 percent on either side of a parity rate set by the central bank according to the value of a basket of 30 percent dollars and 70 percent euros.

title: Hungarian forint eases vs band after profit-taking.
text:
BUDAPEST, April 12 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint opened easier against the central bank's intervention band on Monday in slow trade, due to currency buying following profit-taking in the country's markets late Friday, dealers said. 

 "I can imagine that (banks) who remained short on Friday are closing positions now," one dealer said. "But turnover is very low, almost nothing happens." 

 The forint was quoted at 0725 GMT at 0.12 percent above parity in the 4.5-percent-wide intervention range, compared with 0.35/0.4 percent above mid-line at Friday's close. 

 The forint began to ease Friday afternoon amid profit-taking in the country's markets after a general rally following better-than-expected current account data released on Thursday and a 50-basis-point central bank rate cut Friday morning. 

 The rate cut was expected by some analysts to help restore foreign investors' confidence in the Hungarian economy after earlier current account and budget figures triggered concerns. 

 Since the initial rally on Friday, Hungarian markets have become calm again and foreigners are showing little activity, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the forint was expected to move in a narrow range around parity on Monday. 

 Against the dollar the Hungarian currency was quoted at 234.70/235.30, compared with Friday's end at 234.90/235.20, while against the euro it eased to 254.30/255.00 from 253.10/60. 

 The forint fluctuates by 2.25 percent on either side of a parity rate set by the central bank according to the value of a basket of 30 percent dollars and 70 percent euros.

title: Hungary forint ends weaker against band.
text:
BUDAPEST, April 9 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint closed weaker on Friday within the central bank's currency basket as profit-taking trimmed early gains inspired by a good current account figure, traders said. 

 "There was profit-taking as those who opened long positions when the forint was around parity (within the central bank's basket) closed them now," said Balazs Benczedi of WestLB Hungaria. 

 The forint closed at 0.35 to 0.40 percent above parity within the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) 4.5 percent wide intervention band, slightly below Thursday's close at 0.5 percent above parity but significantly weaker than Friday's opening level of 0.85/95 above mid-line. 

 "A similar profit-taking happened in government securities, and equity purchases (by foreign investors) could not compensate for that," Benczedi said. 

 The forint ended higher against the dollar at 234.90/235.20 compared with Thursday's close at 235.65 but was little changed against the euro at 253.10/60 compared with 253.40 on Thursday. 

 Benczedi said that the weakening of the forint was probably temporary and it should rise again early next week. 

 "Friday is a short trading day and the atmosphere was more suited for profit-taking, but the forint should strengthen next week, because confidence is returning," he said. 

 The forint opened stronger against the band at 0.7 percent above parity after the NBH cut its benchmark rates by 50 basis points in the morning. 

 A rate cut can normally ease a currency by reducing the demand of foreigners for government securities, but analysts said the NBH's move could increase confidence in the economy and could trigger capital inflows. 

 Hungary's markets have been depressed for months due to investors concerns over the budget and current account deficit. 

 The NBH released good current account data on Thursday, showing a preliminary accumulated deficit of $239 million, compared with analysts' average forecast of $340 million. 

 The forint fluctuates by 2.25 percent on either side of a parity rate set by the central bank according to the value of a basket of 30 percent dollars and 70 percent euros. 

 ((Budapest newsroom +36 1 327 4042 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Hungary's forint weakens vs band by midday.
text:

     "The forint weakened somewhat between 9:30 and 10:30 (0830

title: Forint may be pressured if c/a data unfavourable-Nomura.
text:
BUDAPEST, March 5 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint may attract some pressure next week if January current account data, due on Monday, are unfavourable but it is unlikely to suffer an attack, Nomura Research said. 

 "The forint...is likely to see further pressure if Monday's current account figures are unfavourable," London-based analysts said in Nomura's "Emerging European Daily" report dated March 4. "However, we do not expect any substantial fall in the forint. 

 The forint ended on Friday at 0.25/0.3 percent below parity in the 4.5-percent-wide intervention band, up from Thursday's close at 0.7/0.8 below parity on what some dealers attributed to market talk that the current account data will be good. 

 The data will be released after market close on Monday, at 1500 GMT. 

 Market participants have said the forint could fall to the bottom of the intervention band, where the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) sells foreign currency, if the January current account deficit is higher than the consensus forecast of $290 million. 

 But Nomura said the central bank proved itself willing to defend the forint's narrow band in the wake of the Russian crisis last year. 

 "The market will be unwilling to re-test the NBH as their intervention and higher interest rates were painful to those who bet against the forint last year," the analysts said. 

 ((Sandor Peto, Budapest newsroom +36 1 327 4044 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Forint opens steady vs band in volatile market.
text:
BUDAPEST, March 1 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint opened little changed against the central bank's currency basket in volatile trading on Monday, but a slowdown in producer price inflation could help the currency, traders said. 

 Industrial producer prices rose 0.2 percent in January and 4.4 percent from a year earlier, the Central Statistical Office said earlier, adding that the increases were much smaller than in the first months of the past five years. 

 "This PPI figure means that at least there will be no added pressure on the forint from the inflation side, but the current account figure is the more worrying one," said Attila Vago of Budapest Bank. 

 In early trading the forint hovered 0.1 percent on either side of parity level of the National Bank of Hungary's 4.5 percent wide intervention band compared with Friday's close at mid-level. 

 Another trader said a possible increase in demand for government securities may prop up the currency. 

 "If there is indeed demand on that side, that could help," the trader said. 

 Against the dollar, at 0914 GMT the forint stood at 230.60/80, down from Friday's close at 230.15/55, while against the euro it stood at 253.90/254.00, little changed from 253.70/254.15. 

 The forint floats against a basket comprising 30 percent dollar and 70 percent euro. ((Budapest newsroom +36 1 327 4042 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Hungary forint steady vs band, shrugs off debt rise.
text:
BUDAPEST, Feb 23 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint opened steady against the central bank's basket on Tuesday, shrugging off Monday's central bank announcement of an $834 million December rise in the country's net foreign debt, traders said.

title: Hungary  central bank  says won't widen forint band.
text:
BUDAPEST, Jan 22 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) does not intend to widen the intervention band in which the forint floats, NBH Deputy Governor Gyorgy Szapary said on Friday. 

 "Today we have no intention whatsoever to expand the exchange rate band because we think once something is functioning well, we don't have to repair it," Szapary told journalists at a Budapest conference on the euro currency and Hungary. 

 "The system has operated well, is operating well and we have no intention to change it for the time being," he said. 

 Some analysts have suggested in recent weeks that the National Bank of Hungary should and could widen the 4.5-percent-wide forint band to give the bank greater ability to use monetary policy and cut the costs of maintaining the current band. 

 The Hungarian government initiated a "crawling peg" exchange rate mechanism in 1995 which allows the forint to fluctuate by 2.25 percent on either side of a parity rate set by the national bank and devalued by 0.6 percent each month. 

 The currency floats against a basket comprised of 30 percent dollars and 70 percent euros. 

 The currency has been trading close to the strong end of the band since early-December after falling to the weak end during the Russian financial crisis. ((Daniel Langenkamp, Budapest newsroom +36 1 327 4043 budapest.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Hungarian Forint Weakens Further To 0.4% On Trading Band
text:
BUDAPEST (Dow Jones)--The Hungarian forint is falling further Wednesday afternoon following its steep morning losses in its trading band, with more declines expected on worries over Brazil's economic health. 

 Around 1340 GMT, the forint was at 0.4% from the midpoint on the strong side of the central bank's trading band, down from around 1.5% at 1015 GMT and also down from 2.25% late Tuesday. 

 The central bank allows the forint to move a maximum of 2.25% from the midpoint, which is fixed using a basket of 30% dollar and 70% euro. The bank devalues the forint by 0.6% each month against the basket. 

 "This doesn't seem to be the end," said Istvan Hideg, currency trader at Erste Bank Hungary in Budapest. "The forint may not stop falling until it's at the midpoint." 

 However, Hideg didn't rule out a more severe weakening that would push the forint into the weak side of the band. The forint last traded in the weak side in mid-December. 

 Despite the sharp fall of the forint, the National Bank of Hungary hasn't intervened in the market, and dealers said the central bank probably won't step in unless the forint appears likely to hit the weakest side of the trading band. 

 A central bank spokesman declined to comment on Wednesday's developments. 

 Around 1340 GMT, the dollar was at HUF217.15-217.35, up from HUF216.24-216.44 at 1015 GMT and also higher from HUF216.25-216.45 in late trading Tuesday. 

 The euro was at HUF255.20-255.58, up from HUF253.23-253.58 at 1015 GMT and higher from HUF249.25-249.45 late Tuesday.

title: MONDAY IN BRIEF - Hungary - Dec 22.
text:
--------- GENERAL NEWS ------------------------------------- 

 * Hungary's biggest railway union will hold a two-hour warning strike on Tuesday in support of their wage demand after engine drivers' strike on Monday, a union official said on Monday. 

 -FORINT- * 

 Hungary's forint is expected to continue to trade at the top end of the central bank's currency basket into next year, benefiting from the first sustained capital inflow since Russia's crisis, analysts said on Monday. 

 * On Monday the forint closed at 1.75 percent above parity within the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) 4.5 percent wide intervention band compared with .075 percent above parity at Friday's close. Against the dollar, the Hungarian unit closed at 213.50/70 compared with Friday's close of 215.00/10. 

 - INTEREST RATES - 

 * The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) said on Monday it cut all its three repo rates by 25 basis points each. The overnight repo rate was cut to 19.50 percent, the overnight reverse repo rate to 14.00 percent and one-month reverse repo rate to 16.75 percent. 

 * The National Bank of Hungary (NBH) surprised the markets on Monday by cutting all three repo rates by 25 basis points and analysts said more rate cuts would follow early next year if inflation continues to decline. 

 * Hungary's interbank overnight (O/N) rates ended slightly higher at 16.875 percent (before the NBH rate cuts) in very low trade on Monday after closing Friday at 16.75 percent, dealers said. 

  ----------- EQUITIES ----------------- 

 * Hungarian shares finished firmer on Monday in lively trade, driven by a rising trend in European markets and strong domestic macroeconomic fundamentals, traders said. 

 The BUX index finished at 6,111.20 points, up 213.38 points or 3.62 percent. Spot share turnover rose to 25.109 billion forints ($115.9 million) from 14.417 billion forints on Friday, the BSE said in a statement. 

 * Russia's Gazprom and Hungary's MOL signed a barter agreement under which Hungary will pay with food and drugs for up to one billion cubic meters of imported natural gas until the end of 1999, the clearing bank said on Monday. 

 * Hungarian regional electricity distributors Dedasz Rt and Titasz Rt have submitted their applications to the bourse to list their stocks on the Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE), the BSE said in a statement. 

 * Hungarian oil and gas group MOL said on Monday it signed a $150 million multi-currency revolving syndicated loan agreement. 

 * Nomura Equities Research said on Monday it maintained a "buy" recommendation on shares on Hungarian brewery Brau Union Hungaria, saying it expected strong profit growth next year. 

  ----------- ECONOMIC INDICATORS ------ 

 * Hungary's gross domestic product rose 5.6 percent in the third quarter of the year from the same period of 1997 and was up by 5.1 percent year-on-year in the January-September period, the Central Statistical Office said on Monday. 

 * Hungary's third-quarter economic growth of 5.6 percent is higher than expected, but analysts said a strong rise in imports and a slowdown in export growth were warning signs for the current account.

title: Hungary forint ends higher vs band, dollar.
text:
BUDAPEST, Dec 21 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint closed significantly higher against the central bank's currency basket helped by good macroeconomic news but also a very low turnover on the forex market, traders said on Monday. 

 "The forint rose some two percent within the basket since last Wednesday," said Gabor Butor of Raiffeisen Unicbank. 

 On Monday the forint closed at 1.75 percent above parity within the National Bank of Hungary's (NBH) 4.5 percent wide intervention band compared with .075 percent above parity at Friday's close. 

 But Butor said part of the rise was due to the fact that the market became one-sided, with virtually no demand for foreign currencies. 

 "This is a highly illiquid market...and a two percent rise in three days is too much," he said. "This can only really happen in emerging markets." 

 Against the dollar, the Hungarian unit closed at 213.50/70 compared with Friday's close of 215.00/10.
